# **1.  Executive Clinical Summary**

| **The 60-Second Take** Klotho (named after the Greek Fate who spins the thread of life) is a transmembrane protein with a circulating soluble form. It is one of the most powerful endogenous regulators of aging that humans produce — and almost no one outside longevity medicine knows it exists. Removing the gene in mice cuts lifespan by ~30%. Overexpressing it extends lifespan by ~19–31%. Levels decline with age and are crushed by chronic kidney disease, oxidative stress, inflammation, depression, and senescent cell burden. Clinically, alpha-Klotho serum levels are now testable (Jinfiniti, ClothoYears, others). Levels can be modulated through lifestyle, exercise, sleep, hormones, vitamin D, ACE-inhibition, statins, GLP-1 agonists, certain nutraceuticals (cordyceps, curcumin, resveratrol, vitamin D, fisetin), senolytic protocols, and emerging recombinant/gene-therapy approaches. Klotho should be viewed alongside FOXO3, Sestrin-2, irisin, and follistatin as the four endogenous longevity proteins worth tracking and optimizing in a comprehensive program. |
| --- |

## **Why this matters in your practice**

- Your complex patients (mold/CIRS, post-viral, autoimmune, post-COVID) carry a high inflammation/senescence burden. Inflammation and angiotensin-II directly **suppress** Klotho — so chronic-illness patients run low even when their kidney function looks normal.

- Klotho is bidirectionally linked to nearly every modality you already use: BHRT, peptides (Epitalon, GHK-Cu, BPC-157, thymic peptides, SS-31, humanin), exosomes, stem cells, FFP, and senolytics.

- It gives you an objective serum endpoint for whether your longevity protocol is actually working — most other longevity markers (telomere length, epigenetic age) are slow-moving. Klotho responds within months.

- It is one of the few biomarkers where there is **both** mechanistic mouse data showing 30% lifespan extension **and** a commercially available human assay you can order today.

# **2.  History ****&**** Discovery**

Klotho was discovered in 1997 by Makoto Kuro-o and colleagues, working on a transgenic mouse line at the National Institute of Neuroscience in Tokyo. A spontaneous insertional mutation in the upstream regulatory region of an unknown gene produced a strikingly accelerated-aging phenotype: short lifespan (~8–9 weeks), kidney calcification, vascular calcification, osteoporosis, skin atrophy, emphysema, infertility, ectopic calcification, and premature thymic involution.

Reversing the mutation (restoring normal expression) abolished the phenotype. Overexpressing the gene extended murine lifespan by ~19–31%. The team named it after Klotho (Clotho), the Greek Moirai who spins the thread of human life.

Since the 1997 Nature paper (Kuro-o M et al., Nature 1997;390:45–51), more than 3,000 publications have linked Klotho to chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, cancer, sarcopenia, osteoporosis, and overall mortality. Kuro-o's 2019 review in Nature Reviews Nephrology remains the canonical synthesis (Kuro-o M, Nat Rev Nephrol 2019;15:27–44).

| **Clinical pearl** If you take a normal mouse and delete Klotho, it lives ~30% shorter. If you take that same mouse and overexpress Klotho, it lives ~30% longer. That is a 60-percentage-point swing on a single protein. No other endogenous longevity factor has been shown to do that. |

# **3.  Molecular Biology of Klotho**

## **3.1 The KL gene and its three isoforms**

The KL gene (chromosome 13q12) produces three distinct family members through alternative splicing and separate genes:

| **Isoform** | **Primary tissue** | **Primary partner / function** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| α-Klotho | Distal nephron (kidney), choroid plexus, parathyroid, sinoatrial node | Co-receptor for FGF23 — phosphate/Vitamin D homeostasis. **The longevity-relevant isoform.** This is what serum assays measure. |
| β-Klotho | Liver, adipose tissue, pancreas | Co-receptor for FGF19 (satiety/bile acids) and FGF21 (starvation hormone, metabolic flexibility, GLP-1 cross-talk) |
| γ-Klotho (KLPH) | Eye, skin | Function still under investigation; presumed FGF co-receptor role |

## **3.2 Membrane-bound vs. soluble Klotho**

α-Klotho exists in two clinically distinct forms — and this distinction matters when you are interpreting labs and choosing therapies:

- **Membrane-bound α-Klotho** — the full-length transmembrane protein anchored at the cell surface, where it acts as the obligate co-receptor that allows FGF23 to bind FGFR1c, FGFR3c, and FGFR4. This is the version that controls renal phosphate handling and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D synthesis.

- **Soluble (secreted) α-Klotho** — the extracellular domain (KL1 + KL2) is cleaved off the membrane by ADAM10 and ADAM17 (sheddases) and released into blood, urine, and CSF. Soluble Klotho is the **endocrine, hormone-like form** that circulates throughout the body and is responsible for most of the systemic anti-aging effects. **This is what the Jinfiniti and ClothoYears assays measure.**

- There is also a smaller secreted form produced by alternative splicing, but it appears to be a minor contributor in humans.

## **3.3 Enzymatic activity of soluble Klotho**

Soluble α-Klotho is not just a passive signaling molecule — it has its own enzymatic activity:

- **β-glucuronidase activity** — hydrolyzes steroid β-glucuronides; provides modest control over insulin sensitivity.

- **Sialidase activity** — removes sialic acid residues from cell-surface glycoproteins, which exposes the underlying galactose and stabilizes ion channels (notably TRPV5 in the kidney for calcium reabsorption and ROMK1 in the kidney for potassium handling).

- **Indirect FGF23 receptor inhibition** in tissues that lack membrane Klotho — this is the basis of its systemic effects.

# **4.  Mechanism of Action**

## **4.1 The Klotho-FGF23 axis (mineral homeostasis)**

In the kidney, membrane α-Klotho binds FGF23 (a phosphaturic hormone secreted by osteocytes when phosphate is high). The FGF23–Klotho–FGFR complex triggers:

- **Phosphaturia** — internalization and degradation of NaPi-2a and NaPi-2c phosphate co-transporters in the proximal tubule → urinary phosphate excretion.

- **Suppression of 1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1)** and induction of 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1) → ↓ active vitamin D (1,25-(OH)₂D) → ↓ intestinal phosphate absorption.

- **Suppression of PTH** secretion.

- **Stabilization of TRPV5** in the distal tubule → ↑ calcium reabsorption.

- **Suppression of TRPC6** in intestine and elsewhere → reduces inappropriate calcium influx into cardiomyocytes (cardioprotective).

| **Clinical relevance** Patients with declining renal function develop **elevated FGF23 long before serum phosphate rises**, because Klotho falls first. This is why early-stage CKD patients have FGF23 elevation: the body is fighting to maintain phosphate excretion as nephrons drop out and Klotho expression collapses. **Elevated FGF23 with normal phosphate = early Klotho insufficiency, even before eGFR is overtly abnormal.** |

# **5.  The Klotho Decline Curve**

Klotho is a developmental protein. Levels peak in young adulthood and decline progressively with age, but the rate of decline is **highly modifiable** by lifestyle, disease burden, and intervention.

Population data (multiple cohorts, Jinfiniti aggregate data) show:

- Healthy young adults (20–35): typically 800–1,600 pg/mL (Jinfiniti units) or ~5–17 ng/mL depending on assay

- Average decline of ~6–10% per decade in healthy individuals

- Steeper decline accelerates after age 40, paralleling DHEA, growth hormone, and sex steroid decline

- In the InCHIANTI cohort, the lowest tertile of soluble Klotho had **2.2× higher all-cause mortality** at 6 years vs. the highest tertile (Semba RD et al., J Gerontol 2014)

- Patients with CKD, long COVID, untreated CIRS/mold illness, severe depression, autoimmune disease, or active cancer often run at a fraction of age-expected values

| **Suppressor** | **Mechanism / clinical correlate** |
| --- | --- |
| **Aging itself** | Loss of nephron mass, cumulative DNA damage, transcriptional drift |
| **Chronic kidney disease** | Direct loss of expressing tissue; dose-dependent with eGFR |
| **Inflammation (NF-κB)** | TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β all suppress KL transcription |
| **Oxidative stress** | Establishes feed-forward loop because Klotho protects against ROS |
| **Angiotensin II** | Direct suppression — explains why ACEi/ARBs raise Klotho |
| **Cellular senescence** | SASP cytokines (IL-6, MMPs, TGF-β1) suppress Klotho expression |
| **Psychological stress / depression** | HPA axis cortisol reduces renal Klotho expression |
| **Hyperphosphatemia** | Even chronic mild dietary phosphate excess (processed foods, colas) |
| **Vitamin D deficiency** | Vitamin D directly upregulates KL transcription (VDRE in promoter) |
| **Sedentary lifestyle** | Exercise is one of the most reproducible upregulators |
| **Chronic latent viral load (CMV, EBV, HSV, post-COVID)** | Drives immunosenescence and SASP, indirect suppression |
| **Smoking, alcohol excess, microplastic burden** | All increase oxidative stress and inflammation |

# **6.  Clinical Conditions Linked to Low Klotho**

Low Klotho is not a disease per se — it is a vulnerability state. Treat it as you would treat low DHEA, low testosterone, or low vitamin D: as a modifiable risk-amplifier present across the entire chronic disease spectrum.

| **System / Condition** | **What the data show** | **Clinical implication** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Chronic Kidney Disease** | Klotho falls before eGFR; tracks CKD stage; predicts progression and mortality independent of eGFR | Check Klotho in any patient with eGFR <90, even without overt CKD |
| **Cardiovascular disease** | Low Klotho → vascular stiffness, calcification, LVH, heart failure; lowest tertile = ~2× CV mortality | Combine with hsCRP, ApoB, Lp(a), homocysteine |
| **Hypertension** | Klotho deficiency upregulates RAAS; ARBs/ACEi partially restore Klotho | Klotho-low hypertensives may respond better to RAAS blockade |
| **Heart failure (HFpEF and HFrEF)** | Inverse correlation with NT-proBNP; predicts mortality | Track in HF patients on full GDMT |
| **Type 2 diabetes / metabolic syndrome** | Low Klotho impairs insulin sensitivity via IGF-1/IRS-1 axis | GLP-1 agonists, metformin, exercise all raise Klotho |
| **Cognitive decline / Alzheimer's** | Higher Klotho → preserved hippocampal volume, better memory; KL-VS heterozygotes resist Alzheimer's | Important biomarker in cognitive optimization protocols |
| **Parkinson's disease** | Low Klotho associated with disease severity and motor decline | Adjunct to standard neuroprotective strategies |
| **Sarcopenia ****&**** frailty** | Klotho regulates muscle satellite cells; low levels predict frailty in elderly | Combine with grip strength, gait speed, DEXA |
| **Osteoporosis / fragility fractures** | Klotho-null mice are profoundly osteoporotic; low Klotho associates with fracture risk | Especially relevant in postmenopausal women |
| **COPD** | Klotho protects alveolar epithelium from oxidative stress; low in smokers and COPD | Track in patients with mold exposure or CIRS |
| **Depression / neuropsychiatric** | Klotho is suppressed by chronic stress and depression; low in MDD | Address mental health as part of longevity workup |
| **Long COVID / post-viral syndromes** | Spike protein, latent viral load, and senescence all suppress Klotho | Combine senolytic + antiviral + Klotho-raising strategies |
| **Cancer (low Klotho)** | Many tumors silence Klotho via promoter methylation; low Klotho = poorer prognosis in breast, colon, lung, pancreatic, RCC | Klotho re-expression is being studied as anti-tumor strategy |
| **Skin atrophy / aging** | Skin loses Klotho with age; topical recombinant Klotho improves elasticity, hydration, wrinkle depth in clinical study | Aesthetic regenerative applications |
| **Vision (macular degeneration, cataract)** | Klotho protects retinal pigment epithelium from oxidative stress | Adjunct to standard ophthalmologic care |

# **7.  When Klotho is Too High — The Cancer Caveat**

| **Important nuance — Klotho follows a U-shaped curve in oncology** In **most** solid tumors (breast, colorectal, pancreatic, lung, renal cell, hepatocellular), Klotho expression is **suppressed** by promoter hypermethylation, and low Klotho is a poor prognostic sign. Restoring Klotho is being investigated as anti-tumor therapy in these settings. However, **some cancers — especially certain hematologic malignancies and a subset of aggressive epithelial tumors — show paradoxically elevated serum Klotho**, possibly via altered shedding by ADAM proteases or tumor-derived production. Markedly elevated Klotho on a serum panel in a patient with otherwise normal markers warrants oncologic surveillance, not celebration. **Practical rule:** Aim for restoration to age-appropriate or upper-age-tertile values, not for supraphysiologic elevation. If a patient's Klotho is dramatically above expected for age and they have not changed lifestyle, look for an occult driver. |

## **8.2 Interpreting Klotho values**

Reference ranges are assay-dependent. Always interpret using the laboratory's own reference framework. Below are typical Jinfiniti-assay benchmarks (units: ng/mL):

| **Range (Jinfiniti, ng/mL)** | **Clinical interpretation** |
| --- | --- |
| ≥ 5 ng/mL | **Optimal** — youthful pattern; maintain |
| 3 – 5 ng/mL | **Suboptimal** — typical of many midlife adults; intervene with lifestyle ± nutraceuticals |
| < 3 ng/mL | **Abnormal** — common in CKD, long COVID, severe inflammation, late midlife with multiple stressors; aggressive intervention warranted |
| < 1 ng/mL | **Very abnormal** — usually indicates significant renal dysfunction or end-stage senescent burden |
| Markedly elevated above age-expected | **Investigate** — possible occult malignancy, paraneoplastic shedding, or rare KL gene polymorphism (KL-VS) |

| **Key pearl from clinical experience** Following the same patient longitudinally is more useful than comparing them to population norms. A patient who moves from 1.3 to 3.7 ng/mL on a structured longevity protocol is doing extraordinarily well, even if 3.7 still reads as 'suboptimal.' Trend > snapshot. |

# **9.  Therapeutic Strategies to Raise Klotho**

Klotho is responsive — that is the main reason it is worth measuring. Strategies fall into five categories. The strongest results come from combining categories rather than relying on any single intervention.

## **9.1 Lifestyle interventions**

| **Intervention** | **Effect on Klotho** | **Practical guidance** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Aerobic exercise** | Among the most robust and reproducible upregulators in human studies | 150–300 min/wk moderate intensity; Zone 2 base + 1–2 weekly Zone 4–5 intervals |
| **Resistance training** | Increases muscle Klotho expression; supports satellite-cell function | 2–3 sessions/wk, compound movements |
| **Caloric restriction / time-restricted eating** | ↑ Klotho via FOXO and AMPK activation | 16:8 or alternate-day; avoid in underweight/elderly frail |
| **Sleep (7–9h, deep sleep ≥1.5h)** | Restorative sleep ↓ inflammation → ↓ Klotho suppression | Track with WHOOP/Oura; address apnea aggressively |
| **Sauna (infrared or traditional)** | ↑ heat-shock proteins, ↓ microplastic burden, ↓ inflammation; indirect Klotho support | 4–7 sessions/wk, 20–30 min @ 165–180°F |
| **Cold exposure** | ↑ PGC-1α, ↑ irisin (a Klotho ally) | Cold plunge 2–11 min, 2–3×/wk |
| **Mediterranean / anti-inflammatory diet** | ↓ inflammation → preserves Klotho | Heavy on EVOO, fatty fish, berries, leafy greens; minimize ultra-processed |
| **Microplastic reduction** | Microplastics drive oxidative stress and DNA damage | Eliminate plastic water bottles; never microwave plastic; use glass/stainless |
| **Stress / depression treatment** | Cortisol and SNS overdrive directly suppress Klotho | HRV training, meditation, therapy, SSRI when appropriate |
| **Phosphate moderation** | Hyperphosphatemia drives FGF23 ↑ → Klotho ↓ | Limit colas, processed cheese, deli meat, baked goods with phosphate additives |

# **12. Senescence, Inflammation, and Klotho — Why You Treat Them Together**

| **Core clinical concept** Senescent cells secrete the SASP (senescence-associated secretory phenotype) — a soup of IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, MMPs, and TGF-β1. Every one of these directly suppresses Klotho transcription. Inflammation and senescence are upstream of Klotho deficiency. This means: **clearing senescent cells is one of the most powerful indirect ways to raise Klotho.** And restoring Klotho in turn protects remaining stem cells from becoming senescent. It is a self-reinforcing positive loop once you break it. |
| --- |

## **12.1 Senolytic protocols (Klotho-supportive)**

**Pulsed monthly senolytic protocol** (synthesized from current longevity practice — individualize per patient):

- **Fisetin 1,500–3,000 mg/day × 5–7 days, once monthly**

- **Quercetin 1,500–2,000 mg/day × same window**

- **Apigenin 50–100 mg/day** (also a CD38 inhibitor → preserves NAD+)

- **Spermidine 1–10 mg/day** continuously

- **Curcumin 500–1,000 mg/day** continuously

- **Optional, specialist co-managed:** **Dasatinib 100 mg + Quercetin 1,000 mg** × 2–3 consecutive days, repeated every 4–12 weeks per protocol (Mayo Clinic / James Kirkland trials)

| **Important caveats around senolytics** • **Active malignancy** is a relative contraindication for D+Q senolytic protocols — discuss with oncology. • **Anticoagulation:** Quercetin and fisetin have mild antiplatelet effects; caution in patients on warfarin/DOACs. • **Drug interactions:** Dasatinib is a CYP3A4 substrate — many drug-drug interactions; specialist oversight required. • Take cycles **off** between pulses — receptors and the cellular system need recovery. • Track senescent-cell burden via Jinfiniti β-galactosidase; track Klotho on the same panel quarterly. |

# Thymic / Immune Peptides — Category Overview

The thymus is the master training school of the adaptive immune system. T-cells produced in the bone marrow migrate to the thymus, where they are educated to distinguish self from non-self, mature into CD4+ helpers and CD8+ killers, and are released to populate lymph nodes, spleen, and tissues. The thymus undergoes progressive involution starting at puberty — by age 60, most thymic tissue has been replaced by fat. This is part of why immune function declines with age: there is simply less infrastructure to train new T-cells against new threats.

Chronic illness accelerates this. Mold/mycotoxin exposure, Lyme co-infections, chronic viral reactivation (EBV, CMV, HHV-6), prolonged stress, severe nutritional deficits, and chemotherapy/radiation all atrophy the thymus prematurely. The clinical phenotype: recurrent infections, slow recovery from illness, post-viral fatigue that doesn't resolve, viral reactivation patterns, low CD4:CD8 ratios, low NK cell function, and a 'tired' immune system that cannot mount or resolve responses appropriately.

Thymic peptides address this in two distinct ways: (1) restoring thymic signaling output even when thymic mass is reduced (Thymalin and Thymagen do this through epigenetic reactivation), and (2) directly polarizing peripheral immune responses toward Th1 antiviral/anticancer activity (TA-1's specialty). The choice between them is one of the most important clinical decisions in complex chronic illness.

### What it is

Thymalin is a complex polypeptide preparation originally extracted from calf thymus glands and characterized by Russian researchers (Khavinson, Morozov) starting in the 1970s. Two versions are now available: (1) Classic Thymalin — multi-component biologic from calf thymus tissue, containing dozens of small peptides and protein fragments that collectively reproduce the regulatory output of a healthy thymus gland; this is the original Russian formulation. (2) Synthetic Thymalin — produced by research peptide manufacturers (e.g., ABM) that reproduces the active polypeptide sequence without bovine source material. Both versions perform similarly in clinical practice for broad thymic restoration. The synthetic version eliminates alpha-gal/bovine allergy concerns and is preferred in tick-exposed patients (Texas, Northeast US), though some clinicians feel the calf-derived version has slightly broader spectrum due to its multi-component nature. The thymus undergoes progressive involution starting at puberty — by age 60, most thymic tissue has been replaced by fat. Thymalin's role is to restore signaling output even when thymic mass is reduced, by epigenetically reactivating residual thymic epithelial cells and reprogramming peripheral T-cell maturation.

### Mechanism of action

- Restores thymic epithelial cell function — re-engages the maturation environment for naive T-cells, even in age-involuted thymus.

- Normalizes the Th1/Th2 balance — corrects both Th1-dominant (autoimmune) and Th2-dominant (allergic/atopic) skew.

- Increases CD4+ helper T cell production and the CD4:CD8 ratio in immune-exhausted patients.

- Restores IL-2 production by mature T cells — key cytokine for adaptive immunity.

- Strongly suppresses IL-6 and TNF-α — drops chronic inflammatory tone in CIRS, autoimmune, post-viral states.

- Inhibits NF-κB pathway broadly — anti-inflammatory at the transcriptional level.

- Restores thymulin production from residual thymic tissue (zinc-dependent).

- Modulates dendritic cell maturation — improves antigen presentation in immune-deficient patients.

- Increases natural killer (NK) cell number and lytic activity.

- Restores apoptosis-mediated negative selection of autoreactive T cells in the thymic periphery.

- Acts at multiple immune checkpoints simultaneously — accounts for its broad efficacy and gentle side-effect profile.

### Clinical indications

- Mold/mycotoxin illness and CIRS — broad immune normalization across the Th profile

- Chronic Lyme disease and tick-borne co-infections (Bartonella, Babesia, Ehrlichia)

### Dosing rationale & timing

The 10 mg/day loading dose × 10 days reflects the original Russian clinical protocols, which consistently produced normalization of CD4 counts, NK cell function, and Th1/Th2 ratios within the first cycle. Each 20 mg vial yields 2 doses (10 mg each). The transition to maintenance at 10 mg 2–3 times weekly extends benefits without diminishing returns — daily continuous dosing is unnecessary and wasteful. Two complete cycles (10-day load + 1–2 month maintenance, repeated) is standard in immune-exhausted patients. Subcutaneous absorption is reliable; some clinicians prefer IM for the first 1–2 doses if rapid onset is needed, then transition to SQ. No food restriction. Morning dosing is generally preferred — the immune system has its own circadian rhythm tied to cortisol, and AM dosing aligns with peak T-cell receptor responsiveness. In severe immune collapse (post-chemo, post-CIRS), some clinicians extend the loading phase to 14–20 days. Reconstituted vials are stable refrigerated for ~14 days.

### Evidence base

Robust Russian and Eastern European clinical literature spanning 40+ years — multiple controlled trials in elderly populations, post-radiation immune recovery, chronic infection, and longevity outcomes. The Anisimov mortality study (long-term Thymalin cycles in elderly Russian populations) showed reduced all-cause mortality with periodic Thymalin administration. Mechanistic studies have characterized the peptide constituents and demonstrated thymic epithelial cell reactivation. Western RCT data is limited because Thymalin is not FDA-approved and is sourced through research peptide channels. The clinical track record in functional medicine practices (post-2010) is strong for broad immune restoration in chronic illness — this is the workhorse for complex patients where TA-1 is too stimulating.

### Contraindications

- Pregnancy and lactation

- Active untreated malignancy involving the immune system (lymphoma, leukemia) — coordinate with oncology

- Acute organ transplant patient on immunosuppression — opposing mechanism

- Known allergy to bovine proteins — applies to CALF-DERIVED Thymalin only. Synthetic Thymalin (ABM and similar manufacturers) eliminates this concern and is the preferred choice in alpha-gal patients.

- Severe IgE-mediated atopy without mast cell pre-stabilization

- Active acute infectious illness with high fever — defer until afebrile

### Drug interactions

Generally minimal pharmacologic interactions. Pharmacodynamic considerations: opposes calcineurin inhibitors and other immunosuppressants — do not combine in transplant patients. Pairs favorably with antimicrobial peptides (LL-37) and anti-inflammatory peptides (KPV, BPC-157). Synergistic with zinc supplementation (zinc is required cofactor for thymulin activity). Vitamin D sufficiency (≥50 ng/mL) augments thymic function. May reduce the dose of biologics required in mild autoimmune disease (coordinate with rheumatology). No cytochrome P450 interactions. Caution if combining with TA-1 in autoimmune patients — Thymalin alone is preferred; if combination is necessary, start Thymalin first to establish regulatory tone before adding TA-1's stimulatory signal.

Thymalin is the foundation of immune protocols and is typically started early — often alongside SS-31 in mold/CIRS patients (the two peptides target different systems and don't compete). ### Clinical pearls

- Thymalin is the 'architect' that rebuilds the thymus — Thymagen is the 'electrician' that fine-tunes signaling — TA-1 is the 'security system' that activates frontline defense. Use them in that mental model.

Verify the patient does not have alpha-gal syndrome (red meat allergy from tick exposure) before starting calf-derived Thymalin — anaphylaxis risk. - Cycling matters — continuous daily dosing past 30 days produces no additional benefit and may desensitize the response. Always include the 2–3×/week maintenance phase.

### What it is

Thymosin Alpha-1 is a synthetic 28-amino-acid peptide identical in sequence to the natural alpha-1 fragment of prothymosin alpha, originally isolated from bovine thymus by Allan Goldstein at George Washington University in the 1970s. Unlike Thymalin (a multi-component biologic), TA-1 is a single, well-characterized molecule and has been pharmaceutically developed under the name Zadaxin (sold internationally for hepatitis B/C, immune deficiency, and as an adjunct in cancer). FDA approval has not been granted in the US, but TA-1 is approved in 35+ countries. It is the most studied immune peptide in the world — over 100 published clinical trials and decades of safety data. TA-1 functions specifically as a Th1 polarizer and is the strongest pharmacologic activator of cytotoxic T-cell and NK-cell function available outside of biologics like interferon.

### Mechanism of action

- Activates Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) on dendritic cells and macrophages — primary innate immune sensor for intracellular pathogens.

- Strongly polarizes immune response toward Th1 — antiviral and anticancer adaptive immunity.

- Increases interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) production dramatically — the master antiviral cytokine.

- Increases IL-2 production — drives T-cell proliferation and survival.

- Increases CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell number and lytic activity — the cells that kill virus-infected and tumor cells.

- Increases NK cell number and lytic activity — innate antiviral and antitumor surveillance.

- Reduces IL-4 (Th2 cytokine) — corrects allergy/atopy-skewed immune profiles.

- Mild reduction in IL-1β (less than Thymalin/Thymagen) — preserves the inflammatory response needed for pathogen clearance.

- Modulates IL-12 to drive cell-mediated immunity.

- Promotes maturation of T-cell precursors via thymic and extra-thymic pathways.

- Enhances dendritic cell antigen presentation — bridges innate and adaptive immunity.

- Suppresses regulatory T cell (Treg) function in tumor microenvironment — releases anti-tumor immunity (relevant to oncology).

### Clinical indications

- Chronic viral reactivation (EBV, CMV, HHV-6, HHV-7, HHV-8) — gold-standard peptide indication

- Hepatitis B and C (FDA-approved abroad, off-label in US)

- Acute viral infections — influenza, COVID, severe respiratory viral illness (PRN dosing 3–8 mg)

- Chronic Lyme disease with viral reactivation overlay

- Cancer adjunct — multiple myeloma, melanoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, NSCLC; coordinate with oncology

- Sepsis adjunct (ICU use abroad)

- Vaccine response augmentation in elderly or immunocompromised

- Recurrent infections in CVID, common variable immunodeficiency

- Late-stage HIV (immune reconstitution adjunct)

- Pre-/post-surgical immune support in cancer patients

- Severe Candida, recurrent fungal infections in immunocompromised

### Dosing rationale & timing

The 1.6 mg subcutaneous dose 2–3 times weekly is the established Zadaxin dosing for hepatitis and chronic immune deficiency, validated across 100+ trials. This dose produces measurable Th1 activation (IFN-γ rise) within 2–4 weeks and clinical immune benefit over 8–12 weeks. The 3–8 mg PRN dose is reserved for acute infections — typically administered daily for 5–10 days during acute illness, then tapered or discontinued. SQ and IM produce equivalent absorption; SQ is generally preferred for outpatient use (easier patient self-injection). Empty stomach not required. Morning dosing aligns with cortisol rhythm and immune circadian. The duration matters: 8 weeks is the minimum for chronic conditions; 12 weeks is more reliable for viral reactivation. Maintenance dosing (1×/week) can be considered after a successful 12-week course in patients with recurrent issues. Crucially: TA-1 dose escalation does NOT track with Thymalin — TA-1 is potent at 1.6 mg, and higher doses do not produce proportionally better outcomes outside acute infection.

### Evidence base

By far the most-studied immune peptide. Approved in 35+ countries. Hepatitis B and C trials demonstrated viral suppression and improved interferon response. Cancer adjunct trials in melanoma (Italian trials with Maio et al.), hepatocellular carcinoma, and multiple myeloma showed survival benefit when combined with standard therapy. Sepsis trials in China showed mortality reduction. COVID-19 trials during the pandemic showed reduced mortality in severe disease (Italian and Chinese cohorts). The mechanistic foundation is the strongest of any peptide in this category — TLR9 binding is well-characterized at the molecular level. Safety profile is excellent — millions of patient-doses with rare serious adverse events.

### Contraindications

- Active autoimmune flare WITHOUT cytokine-panel guidance — TA-1 polarizes Th1 and can worsen RA, lupus, MS, Hashimoto's, psoriasis, IBD if used reflexively. NOTE: Stable, cytokine-mapped autoimmune patients with anergic/stuck immune profiles may benefit from TA-1; see clinical pearls.

- Active organ transplant on immunosuppression — opposing mechanism

- Pregnancy and lactation

- Severe asthma or atopic disease without pre-stabilization (less risky than autoimmune disease but still a concern)

- Hyperthyroidism or active Graves' disease

- Known peptide hypersensitivity

### Drug interactions

Pharmacodynamic synergy with interferon — TA-1 was developed alongside IFN-α for hepatitis. Combinations with checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4) are being explored in oncology — coordinate with oncology if patient is on these. Opposes calcineurin inhibitors and immunosuppressants. Pairs favorably with antiviral medications (acyclovir, valacyclovir) — synergistic against herpesvirus reactivation. Vitamin D sufficiency improves response. Zinc 30–50 mg/day is supportive (TLR signaling depends on adequate zinc). No CYP450 interactions of note. Caution with biologics for autoimmune disease (TNF-α inhibitors, IL-6 inhibitors) — opposing mechanisms in some respects.

TA-1 is best deployed in patients with a clear viral, intracellular infection, or oncology indication. ### Clinical pearls

- TA-1 is the most studied immune peptide in the world. When patients ask 'is this proven?', this is the one with the strongest answer.

- Cytokine-guided TA-1 use in autoimmune patients: A 'stuck' or anergic immune system in chronic illness can LOOK autoimmune but actually needs Th1 reactivation. Order a cytokine panel (IL-2, IFN-γ, IL-4, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10) before deciding. Patterns that suggest TA-1 may help even in autoimmune-labeled patients: low IL-2 + low IFN-γ + paradoxically elevated TNF-α + chronic viral reactivation overlay. These patients are not in a Th1-driven flare — they're in immune exhaustion masquerading as autoimmunity. Start at 0.8 mg (half-dose), monitor weekly.

- The blanket 'no TA-1 in autoimmune' rule is for ACTIVE FLARES without cytokine data. Stable autoimmune patients with low-output immune profiles can be candidates with careful cytokine mapping and clinical monitoring.

- When in doubt and no cytokine panel is available, default to Thymalin or Thymagen — they normalize immune signaling without forcing Th1 polarization.

- Always screen ANA, anti-TPO, RF before starting TA-1 in patients without a known autoimmune diagnosis. A 'soft positive' ANA does not contraindicate; symptomatic autoimmunity does without cytokine support.

- In the IntellxxDNA framework: TA-1 is preferred when viral burden is the driver. Thymalin/Thymagen are preferred when autoimmune drift is present without cytokine-confirmed anergy.

- The Th1 polarization is felt by the patient — flu-like symptoms in week 1 are NORMAL and signify response. Counsel in advance to prevent panic and discontinuation.

- Acute COVID dosing protocol from the Italian and Chinese trials: 1.6 mg twice daily for 5 days, then 1.6 mg daily for 5 days, then 1.6 mg every other day until resolution. This works.

- EBV reactivation responds particularly well — patients with chronic post-EBV fatigue often see VCA IgG titers normalize by 12 weeks.

- Cancer adjunct use must be coordinated with oncology. Some oncologists welcome it (especially European-trained); others are unfamiliar. Bring published trial data.

- Higher doses (3–8 mg) are NOT for chronic use — they're acute infection rescue dosing. Going above 1.6 mg chronically does not produce better outcomes and increases side effects.

- If patient develops new joint pain, rash, dry eyes, or unexplained fatigue >2 weeks into TA-1, suspect autoimmune emergence. Stop, reassess, switch to Thymalin or Thymagen.

- Thyroid is the most common site of unmasked autoimmunity — check TSH, free T3/T4, and antibodies if any thyroid symptoms develop.

- PRN dosing for acute respiratory illness in elderly/vulnerable patients can be a clinic mainstay — 1.6 mg SQ on day 1 and day 3 of illness produces measurable benefit.

- MCAS patients need careful pre-stabilization (cromolyn, ketotifen, quercetin) before starting — Th1 polarization can trigger mast cell flares.

- Don't combine TA-1 + Thymalin + Thymagen all at once in a 'shotgun' approach — sequence them. Start with Thymalin to establish baseline regulatory tone, then add TA-1 if Th1 stimulation is needed. Thymagen can be added as a 'finisher' for NF-κB and oxidative stress in long-haul cases.

- Reconstitution: standard 10 mg vial → 1 mL BAC water → 100 mcg per unit → 1.6 mg = 16 units. Stable refrigerated 28 days.

### What it is

Thymagen (also called Thymogen or Bestim, scientifically Glu-Trp) is a synthetic dipeptide developed at the Saint-Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology by the Khavinson group. Despite being only two amino acids, Thymagen exerts powerful epigenetic effects — it's one of the prototype Khavinson short peptides that demonstrated DNA-binding capacity and gene expression modulation. Functionally, it sits between Thymalin (broad polypeptide complex) and TA-1 (single 28-mer): smaller and more precise than Thymalin, but acts on different pathways than TA-1. Its hallmark mechanisms are the strongest NF-κB inhibition of any thymic peptide, robust Treg induction, and a 'gentle' immune signal that makes it the safest choice in autoimmune-prone, MCAS-prone, and post-cancer patients.

### Mechanism of action

- Strongest NF-κB inhibitor of the thymic peptides — epigenetic suppression of inflammatory transcription.

- Antioxidant effect via direct radical scavenging and Nrf2 pathway support.

- Strongly suppresses IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α — broad anti-inflammatory.

- Strongly increases IL-10 — anti-inflammatory and Treg-supportive.

- Strongly increases IL-12 — drives Th1 differentiation when needed.

- Increases IL-2 production (more than Thymalin, less than TA-1) — balanced T-cell support.

- Activates regulatory T cells (Tregs) — reduces autoimmune drift and Th17 overactivation.

- Promotes T-cell maturation through extrathymic pathways — useful when thymus is severely involuted.

- Modulates dendritic cell function with a tolerogenic bias — reduces unnecessary immune activation.

- Improves immune recovery after chemotherapy and radiation.

- Restores cytokine production in immune-exhausted patients (low IL-2, low GM-CSF, low IFN-γ patterns).

- Crosses cell membranes and binds DNA directly — true epigenetic regulator (Khavinson mechanism).

### Clinical indications

- Post-cancer immune reconstitution (post-chemo, post-radiation)

- Post-viral immune exhaustion (long COVID, post-EBV/CMV, chronic post-viral fatigue)

- Mold/mycotoxin illness in patients who cannot tolerate TA-1 or Thymalin loading

- MCAS with immune dysregulation — gentlest of the thymic peptides

- Autoimmune-prone patients where TA-1 is contraindicated

- Mild immune dysregulation, recurrent minor infections in otherwise healthy patients

- Chronic stress-induced immune suppression

- Maintenance phase after Thymalin or TA-1 loading

- Pediatric immune support (research stage; coordinate with pediatric specialist)

- Healthy aging / immune longevity programs

- Adjunct in chronic Lyme co-infection treatment

- Recurrent shingles or herpes outbreaks where TA-1 is too stimulating

### Dosing rationale & timing

Thymagen has a wide dosing range that covers different clinical purposes — this is unique among the thymic peptides and worth understanding. The LOW dose (100–200 mcg/day IM, 5–10 units) is the maintenance / 'immune whisper' dose: changes gene expression, safe for long-term use, ideal for sensitive patients, autoimmune-prone, MCAS-prone, or situations where you want to avoid immune shifts. This dose is NOT enough to: reprogram immune signaling, lift suppressed cytokines, restore thymic output, or correct immune exhaustion. The REPROGRAMMING dose (10 mg/day × 10–14 days, max 20 days) is the 'physical therapy for the immune system' dose: teaches the immune system how to work again. Two cycles are common in immune-exhausted post-oncology and post-viral patients; three cycles maximum if tolerating and cytokines (IL-2, GM-CSF, IFN-γ) haven't moved. Slow onset is a hallmark — improvement may not be obvious until week 3–4 of a reprogramming cycle. IM is preferred for the reprogramming dose; SQ is acceptable for the maintenance dose. Empty stomach not required.

### Evidence base

Russian and Eastern European clinical literature spanning 30+ years. Studies in radiation injury (Chernobyl), post-chemotherapy immune recovery, chronic infection, and burn injury. Mechanistic work has characterized the DNA-binding and NF-κB inhibition. Cytokine outcome data exists for IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10. Western RCT evidence is limited; clinical use in functional medicine is well-established for sensitive immune patients where Thymalin or TA-1 are too stimulating. The Khavinson laboratory has published mechanistic and animal work in English-language journals.

### Contraindications

- Pregnancy and lactation

- Active organ transplant on immunosuppression

- Known hypersensitivity to peptide compounds

- Active acute infection with high fever — defer until afebrile (less stringent than for TA-1)

### Drug interactions

Generally minimal pharmacologic interactions. Thymagen is the most 'forgiving' of the thymic peptides — it pairs with most other agents without conflict. Synergistic with Thymalin (sequence: Thymalin → Thymagen for layered immune restoration). Pairs favorably with NAD⁺ (both modulate inflammatory transcription via different routes). Vitamin D and zinc support its action. No CYP450 interactions. Compatible with most anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial peptides. Caution if combining with active immunosuppression; less stringent than for TA-1.

### Stacking & synergy

Thymagen is the 'plays well with everyone' peptide of the immune category. Pairs especially well with: (1) Thymalin — sequence Thymalin × 10–20 days first, then Thymagen for finishing/maintenance — this is the gentlest immune restoration sequence; (2) After TA-1 cycle — Thymagen as 'cool down' phase to settle inflammation while preserving the Th1 gains; (3) BPC-157, KPV — synergistic anti-inflammatory effect; (4) SS-31 and MOTS-c — energy support for newly reactivated immune cells; (5) NAD⁺ — both modulate inflammation epigenetically; (6) Senolytics (FOXO4-DRI, fisetin) — clearing senescent immune cells while Thymagen restores function; (7) MCAS-prone patients respond well when combined with cromolyn, ketotifen, or quercetin. ### Clinical pearls

- Thymagen is the 'electrician' that fine-tunes immune signaling — quieter and more precise than Thymalin or TA-1.

- When in doubt about which thymic peptide to use in a sensitive patient, start with Thymagen at the low dose. It's the safest entry point.

- The dose paradox is real: 100–200 mcg/day is for maintenance, 10 mg/day is for reprogramming. There is no in-between. Choose your goal first, then choose your dose.

- Slow onset matters — set patient expectations. Improvement may not be obvious until week 3–4. Patients who expect TA-1-like rapid effects are disappointed.

- The classic reprogramming candidate: low IL-2 + low GM-CSF + low IFN-γ + history of severe immune insult (chemotherapy, severe COVID, prolonged Lyme). These patients respond best.

- Post-chemo immune reconstitution: Thymagen 10 mg IM daily × 10–14 days, repeat in 4 weeks. Two cycles often produce clear improvement in CD4 counts and infection frequency.

- MCAS patients tolerate Thymagen better than any other thymic peptide. When TA-1 or Thymalin trigger flares, Thymagen at low dose often works.

- Three reprogramming cycles is the maximum — if cytokines haven't moved by then, reassess for occult driver (mold, hidden infection, gut dysbiosis, malignancy).

- Pairs beautifully with Thymalin — Thymalin builds the architecture, Thymagen fine-tunes the electrical wiring. Sequence them, don't combine simultaneously at full doses.

- IM > SQ for the reprogramming dose because of better depot effect and slower release into circulation. Some clinicians use SQ for maintenance dosing for patient comfort.

- The NF-κB inhibition is its signature pharmacologic effect — useful to remember when treating chronic inflammatory states (CIRS, autoimmune, atherosclerosis) where NF-κB is the master switch.

- Russian protocols often combine Thymagen with vitamin C and zinc — these support the antioxidant and Treg-promoting effects. Worth replicating.

- Reconstitution: 20 mg / 5 mL = 4 mg/mL = 40 mcg per unit. So 100 mcg = 2.5 units, 200 mcg = 5 units, 10 mg = 250 units (will need split injection or smaller-volume vial).

- Healthy aging / immune longevity: Thymalin pulse 10 days twice yearly + maintenance Thymagen 200 mcg 2×/wk

- Autoimmune patient who needs immune support: Thymagen low dose ONLY — never TA-1, careful with Thymalin

## Required adjunct supplements

- Zinc 30–50 mg/day with food (TLR9 signaling and thymulin cofactor)

- Vitamin D₃ titrated to 60–80 ng/mL serum

- Selenium 200 mcg/day (T-cell function, viral defense)

- Vitamin A 5,000–10,000 IU/day from cod liver oil or beta-carotene (mucosal immunity)

- Adequate protein: 1.0–1.2 g/kg lean body mass minimum

- Glutathione (oral liposomal 500 mg/day or IV) — cysteine substrate for immune cell function

- Vitamin C 1,000–2,000 mg/day in divided doses

- Methylated B-complex with B12 1,000 mcg, folate 400–800 mcg

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Using TA-1 reflexively in active autoimmune flare WITHOUT cytokine guidance — most common serious mistake

- Conversely: refusing TA-1 in stable autoimmune patients with anergic/stuck immune profiles when cytokine data shows it is needed — this is a missed clinical opportunity in chronic illness

- Skipping the autoimmune screen (ANA, anti-TPO, RF) before starting TA-1

- Skipping the cytokine panel in autoimmune-labeled patients before deciding for or against TA-1

- Treating the flu-like first week as 'failure' and discontinuing — it's the response, not the problem

- Giving Thymagen low maintenance dose to a patient who needs reprogramming — wasted time

- Giving Thymagen reprogramming dose to a sensitive maintenance patient — unnecessary flare risk

- Combining all three thymic peptides at once at full doses — sequence them, don't shotgun

- Ignoring zinc, vitamin D, and protein adequacy — peptides cannot work in deficiency

- Continuing Thymagen reprogramming cycles past 3 without reassessment — look for occult driver

- Forgetting alpha-gal syndrome screen in tick-exposed patients before CALF-DERIVED Thymalin (synthetic Thymalin is alpha-gal safe)

- Discontinuing during a 'Herx' reaction without supporting binders — slow down, don't stop

*Disclaimer: Educational reference for licensed practitioners. Doses are starting suggestions; adjust per individual response, comorbidities, labs, and state scope of practice. Always coordinate cancer adjunct use with oncology. Always screen for autoimmune disease before TA-1.*

# Anti-inflammatory / Mucosal Peptides — Category Overview

Three peptides anchor this category, but they are very different from each other in scope, safety, and clinical application. Understanding the distinctions is essential — these are not interchangeable, and using them in the wrong setting can cause harm or wasted treatment cycles.

Safety hierarchy (lowest to highest risk): KPV → BPC-157 → VIP. KPV's mechanism (NF-κB inhibition + mast cell stabilization via MC1R) produces no significant systemic vasoactive or pancreatic effects. BPC-157's mechanism (VEGFR2 angiogenesis + microvascular repair) raises only theoretical malignancy concerns at standard doses. VIP's mechanism (broad VPAC1/VPAC2 receptor activity affecting vascular tone, immune regulation, AND pancreatic exocrine function) is more powerful — and correspondingly carries more pre-treatment requirements.

KPV is the gentle workhorse — a tripeptide α-MSH C-terminal fragment that quiets NF-κB and stabilizes mast cells with minimal side effects. It is among the safest peptides in clinical use and pairs with virtually any other agent. KPV is appropriate for almost any chronic inflammatory condition, particularly where mast cell or gut mucosal involvement is present.

BPC-157 is the regenerative workhorse — a synthetic gastric protein fragment with VEGFR2-mediated microvascular repair, fibroblast activation, and tight junction restoration. It is the most-asked-about peptide in patient communities and the most-used regenerative peptide in functional medicine. Its safety profile is excellent at standard doses, with the caveat that VEGF-mediated angiogenesis raises theoretical concerns in active malignancy.

VIP is the master neuroimmune regulator and the FINAL phase of Shoemaker's CIRS treatment sequence. It is fundamentally different from the other two — VIP requires a specific prerequisite sequence of treatments before it can be safely introduced. Misordered VIP carries pancreatitis risk. Practitioners using VIP must understand the Shoemaker sequence in detail.

| **The category decision tree** **Question 1: Does this patient have CIRS that has been sequentially treated through Shoemaker steps 1–11?** → YES, fully sequenced: VIP may be appropriate (with all baseline labs confirmed normal). → NO or partially sequenced: Use KPV and BPC-157 to manage inflammation and barrier issues. Defer VIP until sequence is complete. **Question 2: Is the dominant clinical problem inflammation, mast cell instability, or barrier dysfunction?** → Mast cell or skin/gut inflammation: KPV first-line. → Tissue injury, microvascular dysfunction, or gut barrier repair: BPC-157 first-line. → Both: combine KPV + BPC-157 (this is the most common pairing in functional medicine). |
