| **KPV (Lys-Pro-Val)**  —  *Tripeptide α-MSH C-terminal fragment — anti-inflammatory and mast cell stabilizer* |
| --- |
| **Vial** | **Dose** | **Route** | **Cycle** |
| 10 mg / 1 mL  (also 5 mg / 1 mL; oral capsule available) | 250–500 mcg/day SQ; 1 mg for flares; oral 500 mcg–1 mg/day | Subcutaneous (preferred) or oral | 20–50 days continuous; 4–8 weeks for gut conditions; PRN for flares |

### What it is

KPV is a tripeptide consisting of three amino acids — lysine, proline, and valine — corresponding to the C-terminal sequence (residues 11–13) of α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH). Despite being only three amino acids, KPV retains most of α-MSH's anti-inflammatory activity without the pigmentation, sexual, or appetite effects of the parent hormone. This makes it a uniquely 'clean' anti-inflammatory peptide. It was first characterized in the 1990s when researchers were searching for the minimal active fragment of α-MSH for therapeutic use. KPV crosses cell membranes readily, is orally bioavailable (rare among peptides), and acts at multiple inflammatory checkpoints simultaneously. It is one of the most underutilized peptides in current functional medicine — clinically powerful, safe, and inexpensive relative to its effects.

### Mechanism of action

- Binds melanocortin receptors (MC1R, MC3R, MC5R) on immune cells — same receptor family as α-MSH but with a more selective anti-inflammatory profile.

- Strongly inhibits NF-κB activation and nuclear translocation — blocks the master inflammatory transcription factor.

- Inhibits NLRP3 inflammasome assembly — prevents IL-1β and IL-18 maturation and release.

- Reduces TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8 production at the transcriptional level.

- Stabilizes mast cells — reduces histamine, tryptase, and prostaglandin release; this is one of its most clinically valuable effects.

- Restores gut tight junction proteins (claudin-1, occludin, ZO-1) — directly repairs intestinal barrier permeability.

- Inhibits leukocyte migration into inflamed tissues — quiets the local inflammatory response.

- Modulates the gut-brain axis through vagal afferent signaling.

- Activates Nrf2 antioxidant pathway secondarily.

- Anti-microbial action against Candida albicans, Staphylococcus aureus, and several other pathogens (direct antimicrobial peptide effect).

- Inhibits melanocyte proliferation but does NOT cause pigmentation (unlike α-MSH or PT-141).

- Crosses the blood-brain barrier in modest amounts — central anti-inflammatory effect on neuroinflammation.

### Clinical indications

- Inflammatory bowel disease — Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis (oral KPV has IBD-specific data)

- Leaky gut / increased intestinal permeability syndromes

- Mold/mycotoxin illness (CIRS) — addresses the gut-immune-mast cell axis simultaneously

- Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) — one of the few peptides safe and useful in MCAS

- Chronic urticaria and atopic dermatitis

- Eczema and inflammatory skin conditions

- Psoriasis (off-label, modest data)

- Inflammatory arthritis as adjunct (not first-line)

- Post-viral inflammatory states (long COVID with mast cell or GI involvement)

- Gut-brain axis disorders (anxiety with GI symptoms, cyclic vomiting, irritable bowel)

- Recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, lichen planus

- Recurrent Candida overgrowth (gut, vaginal, skin)

- Dental and periodontal inflammation

- Chronic sinusitis with mast cell component

### Dosing rationale & timing

The 250–500 mcg subcutaneous daily dose is the standard maintenance range, sufficient for most chronic inflammatory and barrier-repair indications. The 1 mg dose is reserved for active flares — IBD exacerbation, MCAS crisis, severe atopic flares — and is typically used short-term (5–10 days) before tapering back to maintenance. Oral KPV (500 mcg–1 mg) has unique clinical value because the peptide survives gastric digestion better than most peptides AND has direct local effect on the gut mucosa AND systemic absorption. Twice-daily dosing is acceptable when continuous coverage is needed. Subcutaneous absorption is rapid and complete; intramuscular offers no advantage. Empty stomach is unnecessary. Morning or pre-meal dosing pairs well with gut indications. Reconstituted vials are stable refrigerated for 28 days. The peptide is one of the gentler ones — patients rarely report flares from initiation, even when other peptides have caused issues.

### Evidence base

Human RCT data exists primarily in inflammatory bowel disease — oral KPV (formulated as KPV nanoparticles or standard oral preparations) has shown reduction in disease activity scores, mucosal healing, and symptom improvement in pilot trials. Mechanistic foundation is robust: NF-κB inhibition, NLRP3 inflammasome blockade, and tight junction restoration are well-characterized at the molecular level. Animal data spans IBD, allergic airway disease, atopic dermatitis, vitiligo (paradoxically — anti-inflammatory effect with no pigment-modulating activity), and septic shock models. The UCLA Karbach group and several European centers have published on KPV mechanism. Functional medicine clinical experience is strongly positive for MCAS, leaky gut, and CIRS-related inflammation — outcomes consistently good with minimal side effects.

### Contraindications

- Pregnancy and lactation (no human data)

- Known hypersensitivity to peptide compounds

- Active malignant melanoma (theoretical concern given melanocortin receptor activity, though KPV does NOT stimulate melanocyte proliferation)

- Severe hyponatremia (rare consideration; α-MSH family modestly affects ADH)

- No other major contraindications — KPV is among the safest peptides clinically

### Drug interactions

Minimal pharmacologic interactions. KPV does not interact with cytochrome P450 enzymes, drug transporters, or protein binding sites in clinically meaningful ways. Pharmacodynamic synergy with: BPC-157 (gut barrier repair from complementary angles — this is a classic combination); Larazotide (zonulin antagonist + tight junction restoration); cromolyn and ketotifen (mast cell stabilization); quercetin and DAO supplementation (histamine pathway support); curcumin and boswellia (NF-κB inhibition). Compatible with most pharmaceuticals including biologics for IBD (TNF-α inhibitors, anti-integrins). Caution if combining with high-dose corticosteroids — opposing mechanisms in some respects, though clinically the combination is often used and tolerated. No concerns with antimicrobial peptides (LL-37, ARA-290).

### Baseline labs & monitoring

- Baseline: hs-CRP, ESR, fecal calprotectin (if GI-focused), tryptase (if MCAS-focused), CBC with eosinophils

- Inflammatory bowel disease: ileocolonoscopy / disease activity index at baseline and post-8-week course

- MCAS: serum tryptase, urinary N-methylhistamine, prostaglandin D2 metabolites if available

- Mid-cycle (week 3–4): symptom check, GI tolerance, mast cell symptom diary

- Post-cycle (week 6–8): repeat hs-CRP, fecal calprotectin if relevant, tryptase if relevant

- Long-term users: every 3–6 months CBC, hs-CRP, symptom-based monitoring

### Side effects

*Common (mild, dose-limiting only if severe):*

- Mild injection site reaction

- Transient mild GI upset (oral form) — usually resolves in days

- Mild headache rare

- Most patients report no acute side effects — KPV is unusually well tolerated

*Serious (stop and reassess):*

- Very rare. No notable serious AEs in clinical use.

- Rare anaphylaxis (any peptide)

- Theoretical concern with active melanoma but no clinical reports of harm

### Stacking & synergy

KPV is a 'plays well with everyone' peptide and is foundational to many protocols. Pairs especially well with: (1) BPC-157 — the classic 'gut healing duo' addressing both barrier integrity (BPC-157) and inflammation (KPV); (2) Larazotide — together they target the trifecta of leaky gut: zonulin antagonism, tight junction restoration, and inflammation reduction; (3) Mast cell stabilizers (cromolyn, ketotifen, quercetin) — synergistic for MCAS and chronic urticaria; (4) Thymalin or Thymagen — KPV reduces inflammatory tone while thymic peptides restore adaptive immunity; (5) LL-37 — KPV calms inflammation while LL-37 addresses pathogen burden; (6) GHK-Cu — both have skin/mucosal repair effects from different mechanisms; (7) Glow blends (which often contain KPV) — single-vial convenience for skin + gut + inflammation. AVOID stacking concerns: minimal — KPV can be combined with nearly any peptide protocol without conflict.

### Clinical pearls

- KPV is dramatically underused. In MCAS, leaky gut, IBD, and CIRS, it should be near the front of the protocol — not buried in the appendix.

- The oral form is genuinely useful and rare among peptides. Most peptides are destroyed in the GI tract; KPV is small enough and stable enough to survive partial digestion. For IBD specifically, oral may be preferred over SQ.

- In MCAS patients who flare on every other peptide, KPV is often the first one they tolerate. Start at 250 mcg SQ and titrate. The mast cell stabilizing effect is clinically obvious within 1–2 weeks.

- Pair with BPC-157 for any leaky gut or post-mold gut work — together they address inflammation + barrier repair from complementary angles. This is one of the most reliable peptide combinations in functional medicine.

- For active IBD flare, 1 mg/day SQ × 5–10 days, then 500 mcg/day SQ × 4 weeks, then 250 mcg/day maintenance is a typical taper.

- Counsel patients that KPV is a 'quiet' peptide — they may not feel a dramatic acute effect, but inflammatory markers and symptoms improve over weeks. Track objective metrics (calprotectin, tryptase, symptom diary).

- In chronic urticaria and atopic dermatitis, often paired with low-dose naltrexone (LDN) and quercetin for additive effect.

- The melanocortin receptor activity does NOT cause pigmentation — KPV is the C-terminal fragment without the alpha-MSH N-terminal pigmentation sequence. This is a common patient question.

- Stable in oral capsule form for travel — useful for patients who flare during travel disruption (food, water, stress).

- In Glow 70 (with KPV) and similar blends, the KPV component is what reduces the skin inflammation while GHK-Cu and BPC-157 provide regeneration. Single-vial convenience.

- Veterinary use: KPV is used for canine and feline IBD with good success — a useful talking point for patients researching the peptide.

- Reconstitution: 10 mg / 1 mL = 10 mg/mL = 100 mcg per unit. 250 mcg = 2.5 units, 500 mcg = 5 units, 1 mg = 10 units. Easy math.

| **BPC-157 (Acetylated)**  —  *Body Protection Compound — gut and microvascular repair, anti-fibrotic* |
| --- |
| **Vial** | **Dose** | **Route** | **Cycle** |
| 10 mg / 2 mL (acetylated; preferred for stability) — also 20 mg / 2 mL high-dose | 250–500 mcg/day; up to 1 mg for acute injury or refractory cases | Subcutaneous (preferred), oral (for gut indications), regional injection near injury site | 28–66 days per vial; 4–12 week courses; cycle 6 weeks on / 2 weeks off for chronic use |

### What it is

BPC-157 (Body Protection Compound 157) is a 15-amino-acid synthetic peptide derived from a partial sequence of human gastric protein BPC, originally isolated from human gastric juice in the 1990s by the Croatian research group led by Predrag Sikiric. Despite its 'body protection compound' marketing name, BPC-157 is not endogenous as a free circulating peptide — it is a synthesized fragment of a larger gastric protein. The acetylated form (preferred in clinical use) has improved stability and bioavailability compared to non-acetylated. After 30+ years of intensive Croatian preclinical work, BPC-157 has emerged as one of the most widely used regenerative peptides globally, with applications spanning orthopedic injury, inflammatory bowel disease, microvascular dysfunction, and post-surgical recovery. It is currently one of the FDA's targeted compounds for restriction discussion under the bulk substance compounding framework — practitioners should monitor regulatory status.

### Mechanism of action

- Upregulates VEGFR2 (vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2) → robust angiogenesis and microvascular repair.

- Activates focal adhesion kinase (FAK) and paxillin pathways → fibroblast and tendon cell migration.

- Increases endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) → vasodilation and improved tissue perfusion.

- Modulates the dopamine, serotonin, and GABA systems centrally — explains anxiolytic and mood effects.

- Stabilizes the gut-brain axis through vagal nerve pathways.

- Downregulates NF-κB and COX-2 → broad anti-inflammatory effect.

- Restores tight junction proteins (claudin-1, ZO-1, occludin) → gut barrier repair.

- Stimulates growth hormone receptor expression → indirect tendon and connective tissue repair signaling.

- Activates 4-hydroxynonenal scavenging → reduces oxidative damage in injured tissue.

- Promotes fibroblast outgrowth and tendon-to-bone healing — accelerates orthopedic repair.

- Counteracts NSAID-induced GI mucosal injury — restores gastric and intestinal mucosa.

- Reverses experimental fibrosis in animal models (lung, liver, skin scarring).

- Modulates platelet function — generally pro-healing without major bleeding risk.

### Clinical indications

- Tendon, ligament, and muscle injuries — rotator cuff, ACL, meniscus, muscle tears, tendonitis

- Post-surgical recovery (orthopedic, abdominal, anastomotic)

- Inflammatory bowel disease, gastritis, GERD, peptic ulcer

- Leaky gut / increased intestinal permeability

- NSAID-induced GI injury

- Microvascular dysfunction in mold/CIRS, post-COVID, dysautonomia

- Chronic pain syndromes with vascular component

- Post-concussion syndrome (emerging)

- Anxiety and mood support (emerging — central serotonergic effects)

- Wound healing — chronic ulcers, diabetic wounds, surgical wounds

- Inflammatory arthritis as adjunct

- Frozen shoulder / adhesive capsulitis

- Plantar fasciitis

- Achilles tendinopathy

- Post-radiation tissue injury

- Periodontal disease (mucosal application or systemic)

### Dosing rationale & timing

The 250–500 mcg/day dose is the workhorse range for most musculoskeletal and gut indications. Twice-daily dosing (every 12 hours) is biologically optimal due to the peptide's ~4–6 hour half-life — many clinicians simplify to once daily for compliance, accepting reduced efficacy. For acute injuries, doses up to 1 mg/day for 7–14 days produce faster resolution. The 20 mg high-dose vial (3–7.5 U/day) is used in chronic refractory cases or major orthopedic injuries. Subcutaneous near the injury site ('regional dosing') is more effective than distant SQ for orthopedic targets — inject within 1–2 inches of the injured tendon, muscle, or ligament. For abdominal/gut targets, periumbilical SQ is appropriate. Oral BPC-157 has unclear bioavailability — some preparations are stabilized for oral use, but SQ remains the gold standard for systemic effect. Empty stomach is unnecessary. The peptide should be cycled — 6 weeks on / 2 weeks off prevents tachyphylaxis in chronic users. For acute injuries, continuous dosing through resolution is acceptable. Reconstituted vials stable refrigerated 28 days.

| **Route matters: oral vs. subcutaneous — match the route to the target** BPC-157 is unusual among peptides in being **orally active**. It derives from a protein native to gastric juice and is stable in human gastric juice for over 24 hours — so unlike most peptides, it survives the gut rather than being destroyed by it. That stability is exactly why the oral route works, and why the choice of route is a clinical decision, not just a convenience. **Oral — for gut-targeted work. **Oral BPC-157 delivers the peptide directly to the gastric and intestinal mucosa, healing the lining “from the inside.” This is the preferred route for GI-localized pathology: leaky gut, gastritis, ulcer, IBD/IBS, reflux-related mucosal injury, and post-antibiotic or NSAID gut damage. Typical oral dosing is 250–500 mcg/day, most often split as 250 mcg twice daily, taken on an empty stomach. Capsules or stabilized liquid from a compounding pharmacy are the usual forms. **Subcutaneous — for systemic or distal repair. **For musculoskeletal, tendon/ligament, neural, or any target beyond the gut lumen, SQ achieves the systemic exposure oral cannot reliably reach. For orthopedic work, dose regionally (near the injury) where feasible. SQ remains the reference route for non-GI indications — the systemic bioavailability of oral BPC-157 for distant targets is debated, so do not rely on oral alone for systemic effect. **Practical rule: **gut in the lumen → oral (or oral plus SQ for transmural/severe disease); everything else → SQ, regional where possible. The dose range (250–500 mcg/day) is the same; the route follows the target. Keep corticosteroids apart from BPC-157 — they blunt its action. |
| --- |

### Evidence base

Massive preclinical foundation — over 200 published studies from the Sikiric group in Croatia covering tendon healing, GI ulcer protection, brain injury, dopaminergic protection, vascular biology, and toxicology. Animal evidence is robust across virtually every tissue type tested. Human RCT data is limited — the regulatory pathway has favored compounding pharmacy use rather than pharmaceutical development. Most human evidence is observational, case series, and clinical experience. No published toxicity at clinical doses across thousands of patient-years of use. The mechanistic foundation (VEGFR2, FAK, eNOS pathways) is well-validated. The peptide's clinical track record exceeds its formal RCT evidence — a typical situation for compounded therapeutics.

### Contraindications

- Active malignancy — theoretical concern via VEGF and angiogenic stimulation. RATIONALE: BPC-157 upregulates VEGFR2 to drive new blood vessel formation in injured tissues; the same angiogenic signaling can theoretically support tumor vascularization. No documented harm in human use, but mechanism-based caution is warranted. Coordinate with oncology in cancer survivors.

- Pregnancy and lactation — no human data; precautionary.

- Known hypersensitivity to peptide compounds.

- Recent or active hemorrhagic stroke (vascular effects unclear in this setting). RATIONALE: BPC-157's vasoactive and platelet-modulating effects have not been characterized in acute hemorrhagic states; defer until stable.

- Active uncontrolled bleeding (modest theoretical platelet effect). RATIONALE: BPC-157 has documented effects on platelet function and clot formation in animal models; in active hemorrhage, this is unpredictable.

- FDA regulatory status: practitioners should monitor — BPC-157 has been on the FDA's bulk substance review list for compounding restriction. Status may change. RATIONALE: regulatory access affects sourcing reliability and patient continuity of care; not a clinical contraindication but a practical one.

### Drug interactions

Minimal known drug interactions. BPC-157 does not interact with cytochrome P450 enzymes or drug transporters in clinically meaningful ways. Pharmacodynamic considerations: theoretical synergy with other angiogenic agents (TB-500, GHK-Cu) — generally favorable; may potentiate tissue repair when combined. Theoretical caution if co-administered with active anti-VEGF cancer therapies (bevacizumab, ranibizumab) — opposing mechanisms; coordinate with oncology. Synergistic with KPV for gut healing. Compatible with NSAIDs short-term (BPC-157 actually counteracts NSAID-induced GI injury). Compatible with biologics for IBD. May enhance the effect of growth hormone peptides on tendon repair. Caution combining with high-dose anticoagulants (theoretical platelet effect). No concerns with most cardiac, metabolic, or psychiatric medications.

### Baseline labs & monitoring

- No mandatory laboratory monitoring at standard doses for short courses

- Long-term users (>6 months): annual cancer screening per age-appropriate guidelines (mammogram, colonoscopy, PSA, etc.) — given theoretical VEGF concern

- Cancer survivor patients: coordinate with oncology; consider pause if active surveillance phase

- GI users: fecal calprotectin, hs-CRP, or symptom-based monitoring

- Orthopedic users: subjective pain/function scales; imaging if specific injury at baseline and post-treatment

- Hepatic and renal function in patients with pre-existing dysfunction — generally unaffected but worth tracking in long-term users

### Side effects

*Common (mild, dose-limiting only if severe):*

- Mild injection site reaction — redness, transient nodule, especially with regional dosing

- Mild headache in first few days — typically resolves

- Transient mild dizziness uncommon

- Transient mild nausea (oral form rarely)

- Most patients report no acute side effects

*Serious (stop and reassess):*

- No serious adverse events reported in published clinical use at standard doses

- Rare anaphylaxis (any peptide)

- Theoretical: cancer growth promotion in undiagnosed malignancy — not documented but biologically plausible; basis for cancer screening recommendation

### Stacking & synergy

BPC-157 is one of the most-stacked peptides in functional medicine. Pairs especially well with: (1) KPV — the classic gut-healing combination; KPV reduces inflammation, BPC-157 repairs barrier; (2) TB-500 — synergistic tissue repair (Wolverine combo) for major orthopedic injuries; (3) GHK-Cu — additive collagen synthesis and ECM remodeling; (4) Larazotide — three-prong attack on leaky gut (zonulin, tight junctions, inflammation); (5) Glutamine and zinc carnosine — gut mucosal nutrition that BPC-157 needs to work with; (6) Curcumin, boswellia — anti-inflammatory adjuncts; (7) For tendon/ligament: pair with adequate protein intake (1.2–1.5 g/kg) and collagen peptides; (8) For mold/CIRS gut work: BPC-157 + KPV + Larazotide + binders is a foundational stack; (9) Compatible with thymic peptides, antimicrobial peptides, GH peptides, GLP-1s. AVOID stacking concerns: active anti-VEGF therapy in cancer (coordinate with oncology); theoretical caution with active hemorrhagic conditions.

### Clinical pearls

- BPC-157 is one of the most asked-about peptides by patients — usually because of gym/biohacking forums. Set realistic expectations: it works best for acute/subacute injuries and gut repair, not chronic degenerative disease alone.

- Regional dosing (SQ near injury site) significantly outperforms distant SQ for orthopedic targets. Patient in for a rotator cuff: inject the deltoid or proximal anterior shoulder, not the abdomen.

- Oral bioavailability is debated. SQ remains gold standard for systemic effect. For pure gut indications, the oral form may have direct mucosal benefit, but combine with SQ for systemic action.

- Sikiric's research suggests BPC-157 works upstream of growth factors — restoring the body's OWN repair signaling rather than supplying exogenous factor. This is a useful framework for patient education.

- In mold/CIRS protocols: don't start BPC-157 until after mast cell stabilization is achieved (KPV + cromolyn + quercetin first). Flares are possible if started too early in unstable MCAS.

- FDA regulatory status is unstable as of recent years. BPC-157 has been targeted for compounding restriction. Track this — if access becomes restricted, plan alternative regenerative strategies (TB-500, GHK-Cu, Wolverine).

- Cancer history is the most common patient question. The honest answer: theoretical VEGF concern based on mechanism; no documented harm in human use; most longevity-medicine clinicians use BPC-157 in patients years out of remission with oncology coordination; active disease is generally a contraindication.

- Patients on long courses (>6 months) should cycle: 6 weeks on / 2 weeks off prevents tachyphylaxis and gives the body a 'reset' window.

- Counsel patients on injection technique — many push-injecting too fast causes local burning. Slow injection over 30 seconds is better tolerated.

- Cyclic vomiting syndrome and gastroparesis show response in some patients via the gut-brain-vagal mechanism — underused indication.

- Anxiety and mood improvements are real but unpredictable. Some patients report dramatic anxiolytic effect, others nothing. The serotonergic central mechanism is genuine but not universal.

- For a 250 mcg dose from 10 mg/2 mL vial: 5 mg/mL = 50 mcg per unit, so 250 mcg = 5 units. Easy to remember.

- If a patient flares on BPC-157 (rare), the most common cause is undiagnosed MCAS that wasn't pre-stabilized. Stop, treat MCAS, restart at quarter dose with mast cell support.

- Wolverine (BPC-157 + TB-500 combination) is a popular single-vial product but doses each component lower than separate vials would. Use Wolverine for moderate injuries or compliance-challenged patients; use separate vials for major injuries.

| **VIP (Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide)**  —  *Master neuroimmune regulator — final phase of Shoemaker CIRS sequence* |
| --- |
| **Vial** | **Dose** | **Route** | **Cycle** |
| Compounded intranasal spray, typically 50 mcg per spray (varies by pharmacy) | 1 spray (50 mcg) intranasal QID × 1 month → BID × 1 month → daily ongoing (Shoemaker protocol) | Intranasal exclusively for chronic CIRS use | Long-term — months to years; titrated based on labs and symptoms |

### What it is

Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) is a 28-amino-acid neuropeptide produced endogenously throughout the body — most prominently in the central and enteric nervous systems, the lungs, and the immune system. It functions as both a neurotransmitter and a hormone, with profound effects on vascular tone, immune regulation, neuroinflammation, and cellular metabolism. In the context of CIRS (Chronic Inflammatory Response Syndrome) and biotoxin illness, VIP deficiency is a well-documented downstream consequence of chronic exposure to mold mycotoxins, Lyme co-infections, and other biotoxins — these illnesses systematically deplete VIP, leading to capillary hypoperfusion, neurocognitive symptoms, and inability to recover even after exposure ends. Intranasal VIP replacement, developed and standardized by Dr. Ritchie Shoemaker, is the FINAL PHASE of the CIRS treatment sequence — it cannot be safely started until earlier phases are completed. The rationale for sequence completion is mechanistic: VIP acts on VPAC1 receptors that are densely expressed on pancreatic acinar cells, where it stimulates cAMP-mediated exocrine secretion. In a patient with ongoing biotoxin exposure, persistent MARCoNS colonization, or unresolved inflammatory state, the elevated systemic inflammatory tone amplifies VIP's pancreatic stimulatory effects beyond physiologic limits — risking acute pancreatitis. Sequence completion (binders, MARCoNS clearance, exposure resolution, ADH/osmolality stabilization) reduces this inflammatory amplification before VIP is introduced. The Shoemaker protocol specifies monthly lipase monitoring throughout VIP therapy as the standard of care.

### Mechanism of action

- Binds VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors on immune cells, vascular endothelium, neurons, and pulmonary tissue.

- Restores cerebral microvascular perfusion — corrects the capillary hypoperfusion that drives 'CIRS brain' (cognitive dysfunction, executive function loss).

- Strongly anti-inflammatory at the central nervous system level — reduces neuroinflammation independent of systemic markers.

- Modulates Th1/Th2/Th17 balance toward regulatory T cell (Treg) dominance — reduces autoimmune drift.

- Strongly suppresses TNF-α, IL-6, IL-12, IL-23 in neuroinflammatory contexts.

- Increases anti-inflammatory IL-10.

- Restores MSH (melanocyte stimulating hormone) production from the hypothalamus — MSH is profoundly suppressed in CIRS, and VIP is the upstream regulator.

- Improves pulmonary vascular tone and reduces pulmonary hypertension in CIRS patients.

- Reduces TGF-β1 — the fibrotic cytokine elevated in CIRS.

- Restores hypothalamic-pituitary axis function — corrects ADH:osmolality dysregulation, sex hormone production, growth hormone pulses.

- Improves olfactory function — many CIRS patients regain sense of smell within weeks.

- Modulates vagal tone — restores autonomic balance.

- Pancreatic exocrine and endocrine effects — relevant to safety considerations (see contraindications).

### Clinical indications

- Chronic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (CIRS) — final phase, after Shoemaker steps 1–11 completed

- Persistent CIRS symptoms despite cleared MARCoNS, normalized ADH/osmolality, and resolved exposure

- Pulmonary hypertension associated with CIRS (Shoemaker-validated indication)

- Persistent cognitive dysfunction in post-CIRS patients

- Persistent fatigue and exercise intolerance after CIRS treatment

- Selected post-COVID patients with CIRS-overlapping phenotype (off-label, requires CIRS-trained provider)

- Persistent ADH or osmolality dysregulation despite earlier interventions

- Persistent low MSH after other CIRS treatment phases

- Olfactory dysfunction in CIRS context

- Reactive airway disease with CIRS overlap

### Dosing rationale & timing

The standardized Shoemaker dosing protocol is: 1 spray (50 mcg) intranasally FOUR TIMES DAILY for the first month, then twice daily for one month, then daily for one month, with reassessment based on clinical response and biomarkers. Many practitioners now use a more gradual titration in sensitive patients (1 spray daily × 2 weeks → 2×/day × 2 weeks → titrate up as tolerated), but the original Shoemaker protocol specifies the QID loading because the goal is rapid restoration of MSH production and normalization of TGF-β1, MMP-9, and C4a — biomarkers that respond to intensity of dosing. RATIONALE FOR INTRANASAL ROUTE: VIP has a serum half-life of approximately 1–2 minutes — far too short for systemic dosing to maintain therapeutic levels. Intranasal administration produces direct CNS uptake via the olfactory and trigeminal nerve pathways, bypassing systemic degradation and delivering peptide directly to the brain regions where neuroinflammation is most prominent in CIRS (anterior cingulate, hippocampus, brainstem). Subcutaneous or IV VIP does NOT reproduce these CNS effects and carries significantly higher systemic side effect risk. RATIONALE FOR THE QID LOADING: The Shoemaker biomarker data (2013 publication) demonstrated that TGF-β1 and C4a normalize at the 4×/day dose; less frequent dosing produced incomplete response. RATIONALE FOR LIFETIME-OR-LONG-COURSE TREATMENT: VIP-deficient CIRS patients have chronic loss of upstream regulation; replacement is restorative rather than curative. Some patients can taper after sustained recovery (years); others remain on maintenance indefinitely. Re-exposure to biotoxins (water-damaged building, contaminated food) requires immediate discontinuation, re-evaluation of exposure status, and restart only after exposure is resolved.

### Evidence base

Foundational work by Dr. Ritchie Shoemaker — multiple peer-reviewed publications documenting VIP deficiency in CIRS, restoration of MSH, normalization of pulmonary artery pressures, cognitive improvement, and immune marker recovery. The Shoemaker protocol has been validated in retrospective cohort analyses of biotoxin-exposed populations. Mechanistic foundation in VIP biology is robust — decades of basic science on VPAC receptors, neuroinflammation, and pulmonary vascular biology. Endogenous VIP biology has been extensively studied since its discovery by Said and Mutt in 1970. The CIRS-specific application is more controversial outside the Shoemaker community — some functional medicine practitioners use VIP without strict adherence to the prerequisite sequence, which the Shoemaker group strongly opposes due to safety concerns.

### Contraindications

- PANCREATITIS RISK — see safety details below. RATIONALE: VIP stimulates pancreatic acinar cell exocrine secretion via VPAC1 receptors and cAMP-mediated signaling. In an inflammatorily-amplified state (active biotoxin exposure, MARCoNS colonization, unresolved CIRS inflammation), this physiologic effect can become pathologic. Sequence completion reduces background inflammation before VIP is introduced. The Shoemaker protocol specifies monthly lipase monitoring for this reason.

- History of pancreatitis (any cause) — absolute contraindication. RATIONALE: previously injured pancreatic tissue has reduced functional reserve and altered acinar cell signaling, raising the risk of recurrence with any pancreatic stimulant.

- Active gallbladder disease or recent cholecystitis. RATIONALE: VIP relaxes the sphincter of Oddi and can precipitate biliary-pancreatic events in patients with biliary pathology.

- Current MARCoNS colonization (must be cleared first). RATIONALE: MARCoNS produces biofilm-protected staphylococcal enterotoxins that maintain systemic inflammation and amplify VIP's pancreatic effects. Cleared MARCoNS = lower inflammatory amplification.

- Current biotoxin exposure (must be resolved first). RATIONALE: Ongoing exposure perpetuates the cytokine storm that VIP is meant to resolve; treating with VIP during ongoing exposure is treating the symptom while ignoring the cause, AND amplifies pancreatitis risk.

- ADH or osmolality not yet stabilized. RATIONALE: VIP modulates the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Introducing it before ADH/osmolality is corrected can produce unpredictable fluid-electrolyte shifts.

- Untreated subclinical pulmonary hypertension (relative — actually an indication once safety is confirmed, but baseline echo and PA pressures must be measured). RATIONALE: VIP affects pulmonary vascular tone via VPAC2 receptors; you need to know what you're starting with to interpret response.

- Pregnancy and lactation

- Known hypersensitivity

- Active cancer (case-by-case; coordinate with oncology). RATIONALE: VIP has growth-modulating effects on some tumor cell lines that express VPAC receptors.

- Acute infection (defer until resolved). RATIONALE: acute infection raises baseline inflammation, which amplifies VIP effects unpredictably.

### Drug interactions

Limited drug interaction data. VIP does not interact with CYP450 enzymes. Pharmacodynamic considerations: pairs with binders (CSM, Welchol) — no conflict; the CIRS patient is typically on multiple supportive agents during VIP. Coordination with thyroid medication may be needed — VIP can normalize HPT axis output and require dose adjustment. Coordination with sex hormone replacement — VIP often restores endogenous production, requiring HRT dose reduction. Bromocriptine or cabergoline (sometimes used in CIRS) — generally compatible. Statins — no interaction. Beta blockers, ACE inhibitors — no interaction. Caution with anything that affects pancreatic function (some atypical antipsychotics, certain HIV medications, GLP-1 agonists at high doses) — combination raises pancreatitis risk theoretically.

### Baseline labs & monitoring

- Baseline (BEFORE first dose): comprehensive Shoemaker panel — MSH, VEGF, TGF-β1, MMP-9, C4a, ADH/osmolality pair, ACTH/cortisol, ACLA antibodies, anti-gliadin antibodies, leptin, HLA-DR for biotoxin susceptibility

- Baseline lipase AND amylase — both must be normal. RATIONALE: establishes that pancreatic exocrine function is at baseline before introducing a peptide that stimulates acinar secretion. Either elevation defers VIP.

- MONTHLY LIPASE throughout VIP therapy — non-negotiable per Shoemaker protocol. RATIONALE: subclinical pancreatic stimulation precedes overt pancreatitis. A rising lipase trend (even within reference range) is the early warning sign that mandates dose reduction or discontinuation BEFORE clinical pancreatitis develops. This is the single most important safety lab in VIP therapy.

- Baseline echocardiogram with pulmonary artery pressure assessment (BNP and direct PA pressure if echo concerning). RATIONALE: VIP affects pulmonary vasodilation via VPAC2 receptors; baseline PA pressures must be known to interpret response and to flag undiagnosed pulmonary hypertension that VIP can both treat AND mask.

- Baseline VCS test (Visual Contrast Sensitivity). RATIONALE: VCS is the Shoemaker-validated screening tool for biotoxin exposure status; deficits at baseline confirm CIRS diagnosis and provide a marker for treatment response.

- Baseline neurocognitive testing (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsych testing if available). RATIONALE: VIP's most clinically valuable effects are cognitive — restored executive function, processing speed, memory. Documenting baseline is essential to demonstrate response and justify continued treatment.

- Document MARCoNS cleared (negative culture). RATIONALE: persistent MARCoNS sustains inflammatory state that amplifies VIP pancreatic effects.

- Document exposure resolved (mold remediation complete, ERMI testing acceptable, environmental assessment confirms low biotoxin burden). RATIONALE: VIP cannot work in a patient still being exposed; the inflammatory load overwhelms the peptide's regulatory capacity.

- Mid-titration (weeks 2, 4, 6 of QID phase): symptom check, MONTHLY lipase repeat, abdominal pain assessment, BP check (rare hypotension), olfactory recovery as early efficacy marker.

- Quarterly through first year: full Shoemaker panel, lipase, VCS, MoCA. RATIONALE: tracking biomarker normalization (TGF-β1, MMP-9, C4a falling toward normal; MSH and VEGF rising toward normal) confirms response and justifies continued therapy.

- Annually thereafter: full Shoemaker panel, echocardiogram, lipase. RATIONALE: long-term VIP use requires ongoing surveillance even after stable response.

### Side effects

*Common (mild, dose-limiting only if severe):*

- Mild nasal irritation or transient stinging — usually resolves

- Transient headache during titration — typically resolves within days

- Vivid dreams initially — often subsides

- Transient lightheadedness with first dose — should not persist

- Mild GI upset — flag for pancreatic monitoring if persistent

*Serious (stop and reassess):*

- PANCREATITIS — the most important serious AE. Signs: epigastric or back pain, persistent nausea/vomiting, elevated lipase. STOP immediately and evaluate. RATIONALE: VIP stimulates pancreatic acinar cells via VPAC1 → cAMP → exocrine secretion. In an inflammatorily-amplified state (active exposure, MARCoNS, unresolved CIRS), this physiologic stimulation can become pathologic. The Shoemaker protocol's monthly lipase monitoring is designed to catch subclinical elevation BEFORE clinical pancreatitis. The risk is meaningfully reduced — but not eliminated — when the prerequisite sequence is followed. Practitioners deviating from sequence are operating outside the validated protocol.

- Severe hypotension (rare; intranasal is much safer than systemic). RATIONALE: VIP is a potent vasodilator via VPAC1/VPAC2 on vascular smooth muscle; intranasal CNS-targeted delivery limits systemic exposure but does not eliminate it.

- Worsening pulmonary symptoms — should not occur if baseline echo cleared; may indicate undiagnosed pulmonary hypertension or pulmonary embolus. RATIONALE: VIP affects pulmonary vascular tone; in patients with right heart strain, the vasodilatory effect can produce paradoxical worsening.

- Severe Herx-like reaction — typically indicates incomplete CIRS treatment sequence; pause and reassess. RATIONALE: introducing immune modulation in a patient with persistent biotoxin or microbial burden can release inflammatory mediators faster than the patient can clear them.

- Anaphylaxis (rare; any peptide).

### Stacking & synergy

VIP is the FINAL phase of the Shoemaker CIRS sequence — it stacks WITH the supportive elements of CIRS treatment, not against them. Pairs with: (1) Continued binders if needed (CSM, Welchol) — no conflict; (2) Mast cell stabilization (cromolyn, ketotifen, quercetin, LDN) — synergistic for the residual mast cell component of CIRS; (3) Mitochondrial support (SS-31, MOTS-c, NAD⁺ — usually started in earlier phases and continued); (4) Thymic peptides (Thymalin, Thymagen) for residual immune dysregulation; (5) Limbic retraining programs (DNRS, Primal Trust, Gupta) — VIP works at neuroinflammation level; limbic retraining works at neuroplasticity level; powerful combination; (6) HBOT — synergistic for cerebral perfusion restoration; (7) Targeted nutrient repletion (B vitamins, magnesium, vitamin D, omega-3); (8) Sleep optimization (Seriphos, magnesium glycinate, glycine). DO NOT start VIP if: MARCoNS still positive; ongoing biotoxin exposure; ADH/osmolality not stabilized; lipase elevated; baseline pancreatitis history.

### Clinical pearls

- VIP is the final phase of Shoemaker's CIRS sequence. The sequence matters: (1) remove from exposure, (2) cholestyramine or Welchol binders, (3) MARCoNS treatment if positive (BEG spray), (4) reduce gluten if indicated, (5) correct androgens if needed, (6) ADH/osmolality balance, (7) treat MMP-9, (8) treat VEGF, (9) treat C3a, (10) treat C4a, (11) treat TGF-β1, (12) FINALLY VIP. RATIONALE: each step reduces the inflammatory amplification that would otherwise potentiate VIP's pancreatic and vascular effects. The sequence is not arbitrary — it is risk-reduction.

- The pancreatitis warning is real and is in the published Shoemaker protocol. Rationale: VIP stimulates pancreatic acinar cells via VPAC1/cAMP; persistent inflammation amplifies this effect. Monthly lipase is the early warning system. This is why the Shoemaker protocol mandates monthly lipase — not as defensive medicine but because subclinical elevation precedes overt pancreatitis.

- If you've completed the Shoemaker sequence and the patient's baseline lipase is normal, the published Shoemaker safety data is reassuring (>300 prescribing physicians, >90% reporting symptom reduction, no significant adverse events in published cohort). The protocol works when followed.

- Patients on VIP often have profound subjective improvement — restored cognition, energy, sense of smell, hormonal function. RATIONALE: VIP normalizes capillary perfusion in atrophied gray matter (Shoemaker 2017 paper documented restoration of gray matter volume). The clinical effect tracks with structural brain change. Counsel that the response timeline is months, not weeks.

- Re-exposure is a treatment-failure event. If a VIP patient relapses, look for new mold exposure, water damage at home/work, contaminated food, or travel exposure. RATIONALE: continued biotoxin exposure overwhelms VIP's regulatory capacity AND raises pancreatitis risk. ERMI testing of home is the first investigation.

- The intranasal route is essential. RATIONALE: VIP serum half-life is 1–2 minutes — too short for systemic dosing. Intranasal delivery exploits the olfactory and trigeminal nerve pathways for direct CNS uptake. Subcutaneous or IV VIP for CIRS is not standard and carries higher pancreatic exposure risk.

- VIP can normalize the HPA-thyroid-gonadal axes — patients on T3/T4 or HRT may need dose reductions over time as endogenous production recovers. RATIONALE: VIP restores hypothalamic-pituitary signaling that biotoxins had suppressed. Monitor TSH, free T3/T4, sex hormones every 3 months in the first year.

- Pulmonary hypertension is a Shoemaker-validated indication that often resolves on VIP. RATIONALE: VIP via VPAC2 receptors causes pulmonary vasodilation (the basis for aviptadil's investigational use in PAH and ARDS). Always get baseline echo before starting — many CIRS patients have subclinical PH that VIP can fix, but the diagnosis must be documented before treatment.

- MoCA scores often improve dramatically (5+ points) over 3–6 months of VIP. RATIONALE: VIP restores anterior cingulate, hippocampal, and brainstem function — the regions where biotoxin-driven neuroinflammation produced cognitive deficits. Document baseline and re-test periodically.

- Practitioners using VIP outside the validated Shoemaker sequence are operating outside the protocol. RATIONALE: the sequence requirement is mechanistic, not regulatory — it reduces the inflammatory amplification that potentiates pancreatitis risk. Practitioners new to VIP should consult a Shoemaker-certified physician for their first patient.

- Compounding pharmacies that supply CIRS-trained physicians (Hopkinton Drug, Belmar Pharmacy, others) understand the formulation requirements. Verify the compound matches Shoemaker specifications: 50 mcg per spray, isotonic, preservative considerations. RATIONALE: VIP is unstable in standard saline; the formulation matters for both efficacy and safety.

- Long-term VIP use (years) appears safe based on Shoemaker cohort follow-up. Some patients are able to taper off after sustained recovery; others remain on maintenance indefinitely. RATIONALE: VIP-deficient CIRS patients have chronic loss of upstream regulation; some recover endogenous production, others require ongoing replacement.

- The VIP patient typically has had a multi-year illness journey before reaching this peptide. Set expectations that it is a final-phase tool, not a magic bullet, and only works in patients whose CIRS has been properly sequenced.

- If the patient's MSH does not rise on VIP after 3–6 months, suspect ongoing exposure or incomplete earlier-phase treatment. RATIONALE: VIP is the upstream regulator of MSH production from the hypothalamus. Failure to rise indicates the hypothalamic-pituitary axis is still being suppressed by ongoing inflammation. The MSH response is a key biomarker of treatment success.

- Olfactory recovery is often the first noticeable improvement — patients regain sense of smell within weeks. RATIONALE: VIP's intranasal delivery directly bathes the olfactory epithelium; restoration of olfactory bulb function is rapid relative to deeper CNS recovery. This is a useful early efficacy marker.

- The Shoemaker QID loading dose (50 mcg × 4/day for 1 month) is more aggressive than many practitioners use today. RATIONALE: the published biomarker normalization (TGF-β1, C4a) was achieved at this dose. Lower-frequency dosing produces incomplete biomarker response. If using gentler titration, expect slower biomarker normalization.

- Storage: keep refrigerated; protect from light. Standard expiration 30–60 days post-compounding. RATIONALE: VIP is a labile peptide that degrades rapidly at room temperature and with UV exposure. Patients should be educated on storage and travel handling.

# Antimicrobial Peptides — Category Overview

This category contains two peptides with distinct mechanisms but overlapping clinical applications. Understanding the difference is essential — they are not interchangeable, and many complex patients benefit from BOTH but in sequence rather than simultaneously.

LL-37 is the human cathelicidin — our endogenous antimicrobial peptide. Its primary value is in CHRONIC infection, particularly biofilm-protected pathogens that resist standard antibiotic therapy. The clinical archetype: a CIRS patient with persistent MARCoNS, a Lyme patient with refractory co-infection symptoms, a chronic sinusitis patient who has failed multiple antibiotic courses. LL-37 disrupts the biofilm matrix that protects these pathogens, exposes them to immune clearance and antibiotic activity, and modulates innate immunity. RATIONALE for its unique value: classical antibiotics target enzymatic processes in bacteria, and resistance evolves through enzyme mutations. LL-37 disrupts bacterial membranes physically — bacteria cannot easily mutate around membrane lysis. This is why LL-37 is uniquely valuable in MRSA, MARCoNS, and other resistant infections.

ARA-290 is fundamentally different. It is a tissue-protective and neurotrophic peptide derived from erythropoietin's structure — but lacking the hematopoietic activity that drives EPO's cardiovascular risks. ARA-290 binds the innate repair receptor (IRR) on injured and inflamed tissues and produces three major effects: anti-inflammation, mitochondrial endothelial repair, and small fiber nerve regeneration. The clinical archetype: a CIRS or post-COVID patient with burning feet, dysautonomia, and exercise intolerance; a sarcoidosis patient with small fiber neuropathy; a chemotherapy patient with persistent neuropathic symptoms. ARA-290 has some of the strongest human clinical trial evidence of any peptide currently in functional medicine use — uncommon for compounded peptides outside pharmaceutical development.

| **The category decision tree** **Question 1: Is the dominant problem chronic infection or biofilm-protected pathogen colonization?** → YES (MARCoNS, chronic sinusitis, recurrent UTI, chronic wound, Lyme biofilm): LL-37 is first-line. → NO: continue to Question 2. **Question 2: Does the patient have small fiber neuropathy, dysautonomia, POTS, or persistent neuropathic features?** → YES: ARA-290 is first-line. Order skin biopsy for IENFD if available; document baseline. → NO: probably neither peptide is the primary intervention; reassess clinical phenotype. **Question 3: Does the patient have BOTH chronic infection AND neuropathic/dysautonomic features?** → YES (common in chronic Lyme + CIRS + post-COVID overlap): Sequence them. Address infection FIRST with LL-37 (disrupt biofilm, clear pathogen, allow Herx-and-recovery). Then add ARA-290 to repair the nerve and endothelial damage that infection caused. RATIONALE: neuropathy regeneration is slow and energy-demanding; doing it during active infection wastes the peptide. |
| --- |

Adjuncts to ALWAYS support this category: vitamin D titrated to 60–80 ng/mL (essential for endogenous LL-37 production), zinc 30–50 mg/day (innate immunity cofactor), omega-3 EPA/DHA 2–4 g/day (resolution of inflammation), B-complex with methylated forms (especially methylcobalamin 1000–5000 mcg/day for nerve regeneration), alpha-lipoic acid 300–600 mg/day, methylfolate 1–5 mg/day, benfotiamine 300–600 mg/day for diabetic neuropathy patients, adequate protein (1.0–1.5 g/kg) for tissue repair substrate. Without these, the peptides cannot deliver their full effect.

Severe Herx is not a treatment failure — it is the response to treatment exceeding clearance capacity. Slow down, support clearance, do not stop unless prolonged or severe enough to require medical intervention. |
