### What it is

LL-37 is the only human cathelicidin — a 37-amino-acid peptide cleaved from the precursor hCAP-18 (human cationic antimicrobial protein, 18 kDa). It is produced by neutrophils, macrophages, epithelial cells of skin, lung, and gut, and is a fundamental component of innate immunity. Discovered in the 1990s, LL-37 evolved over millions of years as the human body's own antimicrobial peptide — vitamin D upregulates its production via the VDR (vitamin D receptor), which is one of the mechanisms underlying vitamin D's immune effects. Synthetic LL-37 reproduces the natural sequence and is among the most clinically valuable peptides for chronic infection, biofilm-driven illness, and CIRS-associated mucosal colonization. Unlike pharmaceutical antibiotics, LL-37 acts on multiple targets simultaneously and does not generate classical antimicrobial resistance — making it particularly valuable in resistant infections and biofilm states.

### Mechanism of action

- Direct antimicrobial action against Gram-positive bacteria (including MRSA), Gram-negative bacteria, fungi (especially Candida), and enveloped viruses (including HIV) — broad-spectrum activity via membrane disruption.

- Mechanism of bacterial killing: cationic LL-37 binds to negatively charged bacterial membranes, inserts into the lipid bilayer, and forms transmembrane pores → osmotic lysis. This 'physical' membrane-disruptive mechanism is why classical antibiotic resistance does not develop.

- Biofilm disruption — penetrates and breaks down extracellular polymeric matrix that protects pathogens from antibiotics and immune cells. This is its most clinically valuable mechanism in chronic infection.

- Neutralizes lipopolysaccharide (LPS) endotoxin — reduces sepsis-driven inflammation and Gram-negative bacterial toxic effects.

- Modulates innate immunity: chemoattractant for neutrophils, monocytes, and T cells; bridges innate to adaptive immunity.

- Promotes wound healing — stimulates keratinocyte migration, angiogenesis, and re-epithelialization. The basis for chronic wound applications.

- Anti-inflammatory in chronic exposure (paradoxically — acutely pro-inflammatory, chronically anti-inflammatory through receptor desensitization and cytokine modulation).

- Enhances autophagy in macrophages — improves intracellular pathogen clearance (relevant to mycobacteria, intracellular Lyme).

- Vitamin D-dependent endogenous production — explains why vitamin D deficiency predisposes to chronic infection and why LL-37 supplementation is more effective in vitamin D-replete patients.

- Modulates the microbiome — selective antimicrobial activity that preserves commensals while targeting pathogens.

### Clinical indications

- Mold/mycotoxin illness (CIRS) with biofilm-protected colonization

- MARCoNS (Multiple Antibiotic Resistant Coagulase Negative Staphylococci) — addressed in Shoemaker CIRS sequence

- Chronic Lyme disease and tick-borne co-infections (Bartonella, Babesia, Borrelia biofilms)

- Chronic sinusitis with biofilm component

- Recurrent Candida (gut, vaginal, skin, oral)

- Chronic urinary tract infections, especially biofilm-protected

- Inflammatory bowel disease with dysbiosis component

- Chronic wound healing (chronic venous leg ulcers, diabetic ulcers, polymicrobial wounds)

- MRSA decolonization (off-label, growing use)

- Chronic dental and periodontal infection

- Oral aphthous ulcers (recurrent)

- Antiviral support — herpesvirus reactivation, chronic post-viral syndromes

- Post-COVID inflammation with persistent microbial driver

- Antifungal support in immunocompromised patients (with appropriate medical supervision)

### Dosing rationale & timing

The 200–500 mcg subcutaneous dose 2–3 times weekly is the standard maintenance protocol for chronic infection and biofilm disruption — sufficient to maintain antimicrobial activity without overwhelming inflammatory response. RATIONALE: LL-37 has a relatively short half-life (~2–4 hours), but its biological effects persist longer due to receptor signaling and biofilm penetration. Less frequent dosing (twice weekly) may be insufficient for biofilm-heavy infections; more frequent dosing (daily) is reserved for acute states. The 300–1000 mcg/day dose is for ACUTE infection — used during active flare or as part of MARCoNS treatment, typically for 5–14 days before tapering to maintenance. The 6–8 week course duration reflects the time required for biofilm disruption + pathogen clearance + immune normalization. Some patients require 12–16 week courses for refractory chronic infection. RATIONALE FOR ROUTE: Subcutaneous delivers consistent systemic levels for chronic infection. Intranasal compounded LL-37 is used specifically for chronic sinusitis and MARCoNS — direct mucosal application in the affected anatomy. RATIONALE FOR CYCLING: Many practitioners cycle 6 weeks on / 2 weeks off to prevent receptor desensitization and to give the immune system time to consolidate gains. Acute illness rescue dosing (days 1, 3, 5, 7) is appropriate for vulnerable patients. RECONSTITUTION: 5 mg / 2 mL = 2.5 mg/mL = 25 mcg per unit; 200 mcg = 8 units, 500 mcg = 20 units. Refrigerated stability 14–28 days post-reconstitution.

### Evidence base

Strong mechanistic foundation — LL-37 has been characterized at the molecular level since the 1990s. Robust antimicrobial activity demonstrated against MRSA, MRSE, Pseudomonas, E. coli, Candida albicans, HIV, HSV, influenza in laboratory studies. Animal models support antimicrobial, wound healing, and anti-biofilm effects. Human clinical trials are limited compared to pharmaceutical antibiotics — most clinical use is observational and case-series based. LL-37 has been investigated for chronic wounds, atopic dermatitis, oral candidiasis, and inflammatory bowel disease in small human studies. The Shoemaker MARCoNS protocol (BEG spray + LL-37) has substantial clinical track record in the CIRS community. The vitamin D-LL-37 axis is well-established in immunology — a key mechanism by which vitamin D affects infection susceptibility.

### Contraindications

- Pregnancy and lactation — limited human data; precautionary.

- Severe MCAS without pre-stabilization. RATIONALE: LL-37 is acutely pro-inflammatory and can trigger mast cell degranulation in unstable patients. Pre-treat with cromolyn, ketotifen, or quercetin and start at 1/4 dose.

- Active rosacea or atopic flare. RATIONALE: LL-37 is paradoxically elevated in rosacea pathogenesis; supplementation may worsen symptoms. Use cautiously and at reduced dose.

- Known peptide hypersensitivity.

- Severe Herx-prone patients without binders ready. RATIONALE: rapid biofilm disruption releases pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and endotoxins; these must be bound (CSM, charcoal, chlorella) and excreted to prevent severe Herx.

- Active autoimmune flare without immune monitoring. RATIONALE: LL-37 is a known autoantigen in some autoimmune conditions (psoriasis, lupus); use with caution in active autoimmune disease.

### Drug interactions

Pharmacodynamic synergy with: vitamin D (the upstream regulator of endogenous LL-37 production — repletion to ≥60 ng/mL augments effect); omega-3 fatty acids (resolve inflammation while LL-37 disrupts biofilm); zinc (cofactor for innate immunity and LL-37 activity); pharmaceutical antibiotics (LL-37 disrupts biofilms, exposing pathogens to antibiotics — synergistic in resistant infections, including MARCoNS). RATIONALE FOR ANTIBIOTIC PAIRING: Biofilms reduce antibiotic effective concentration by 100-1000×; LL-37 destruction of biofilm restores antibiotic susceptibility. This is the basis of combined LL-37 + BEG spray for MARCoNS. Compatible with most pharmaceuticals — no CYP450 interactions. Caution with high-dose corticosteroids (suppress endogenous LL-37 production and may blunt response). Caution combining with TA-1 in already-Herx-ing patient — additive immune activation; sequence them rather than combining acutely.

### Baseline labs & monitoring

- Baseline: CBC with differential (track WBC, eosinophils), hs-CRP, ESR, vitamin D (25-OH-D should be ≥60 ng/mL before starting for full effect).

- Infection-specific: MARCoNS culture (if CIRS), urine culture (if recurrent UTI), oral fungal culture (if oral candidiasis), wound culture (if chronic wound).

- Biotoxin/CIRS workup if relevant: full Shoemaker panel before starting MARCoNS treatment phase.

- Cytokine panel optional — useful for tracking immune normalization in chronic infection states.

- Mid-cycle (week 3–4): symptom check, Herx severity assessment, binder adequacy, abdominal symptoms, energy.

- Post-cycle (week 6–8): repeat infection-specific cultures or biomarkers, hs-CRP, CBC.

- Long-term users: annual CBC, vitamin D, hs-CRP, infection-specific markers as relevant.

### Side effects

*Common (mild, dose-limiting only if severe):*

- Mild injection site reaction — redness, transient nodule.

- Herx (Jarisch-Herxheimer-like) reaction in first 1–2 weeks — fatigue, low-grade fever, body aches, headache, brain fog. RATIONALE: rapid biofilm disruption releases pathogen toxins and PAMPs; this is the response to treatment, not failure. Manage with binders, hydration, rest.

- Mild GI upset, especially if treating gut biofilm — usually transient.

- Mild flu-like symptoms in week 1 — typically resolves.

- Transient histamine-like symptoms (flushing, mild itching) in first few doses, especially in mast cell-prone patients.

*Serious (stop and reassess):*

- Severe Herx reaction in heavy biofilm or pathogen burden — can be debilitating; manage with dose reduction, binders, hydration, rest. NOT a reason to stop unless prolonged. RATIONALE: severe Herx indicates large pathogen load being released; the treatment is working but exceeding clearance capacity.

- Severe MCAS flare in unstable patients — manage with mast cell stabilization and dose reduction.

- Worsening of psoriasis or lupus-spectrum autoimmunity (rare). RATIONALE: LL-37 is an autoantigen in these conditions.

- Anaphylaxis (rare; any peptide).

- Severe injection site abscess — rare but reported; may indicate sourcing/sterility issue.

### Stacking & synergy

LL-37 is the cornerstone antimicrobial peptide and is foundational to chronic infection protocols. Pairs especially well with: (1) Thymalin or Thymagen — restore adaptive immunity that biofilm-protected pathogens have suppressed; sequence Thymalin first to normalize T-cell function, then add LL-37 to disrupt biofilm; (2) BEG spray (Bactroban + EDTA + Gentamicin) for MARCoNS — LL-37 disrupts biofilm, BEG kills exposed bacteria; this is the Shoemaker protocol; (3) BPC-157 — gut barrier repair while LL-37 addresses gut pathogen load; (4) KPV — anti-inflammatory protection during Herx; (5) Binders (CSM, Welchol, charcoal, chlorella) — essential to prevent severe Herx; (6) Vitamin D (target ≥60 ng/mL) — augments endogenous LL-37 production; (7) Zinc 30–50 mg/day — innate immunity cofactor; (8) Pharmaceutical antibiotics in combination protocols — synergistic via biofilm disruption. AVOID stacking concerns: avoid combining with TA-1 acutely in Herx-prone patients (additive immune activation); avoid in unstable MCAS without pre-stabilization; coordinate with prescriber if using alongside high-dose pharmaceutical antibiotics for resistant infections.

### Clinical pearls

- LL-37 is the antimicrobial peptide that practitioners reach for in CHRONIC infection. Acute uncomplicated infection typically responds to standard antibiotics; LL-37 shines in biofilm-protected, chronic, recurrent, or resistant cases. Set patient expectations accordingly.

- Vitamin D status matters enormously. RATIONALE: vitamin D is the upstream regulator of endogenous LL-37 production via VDR. Patients with 25-OH-D <30 ng/mL have impaired innate immunity AND blunted response to exogenous LL-37. Replete D to ≥60 ng/mL before starting LL-37 protocol.

- The Herx reaction is the most common clinical issue. Counsel patients in advance: 'You may feel worse before you feel better in the first 1–2 weeks. This is the treatment working, not failing.' RATIONALE: biofilm disruption releases endotoxin and PAMPs; clearance capacity matters. Pre-load binders, hydrate, rest. If Herx is severe, drop to 1/4 dose and titrate up.

- MARCoNS treatment is the canonical clinical use in CIRS. Protocol: confirm MARCoNS by deep nasal culture; treat with intranasal BEG spray + LL-37 SQ; re-culture at 4–6 weeks. RATIONALE: MARCoNS is biofilm-protected staphylococcal colonization that prevents MSH normalization in CIRS; clearing it is essential before VIP can be used.

- Mast cell-prone patients require pre-stabilization. RATIONALE: LL-37 is acutely pro-inflammatory and can trigger mast cell degranulation. Pre-treat with cromolyn 200 mg QID × 1 week before starting, plus quercetin and ketotifen as needed. Start LL-37 at 1/4 dose and titrate over 2–4 weeks.

- Sinus indications use intranasal compounded LL-37 directly to the affected mucosa. Combine with BEG spray for MARCoNS. RATIONALE: mucosal application achieves higher local concentration than systemic; sinus biofilms are notoriously refractory.

- Wound healing is an underused indication. Topical LL-37 on chronic non-healing wounds — including diabetic ulcers and venous stasis ulcers — has substantial mechanistic and emerging clinical support. RATIONALE: combines antimicrobial effect with direct stimulation of keratinocyte migration and angiogenesis.

- LL-37 does NOT replace pharmaceutical antibiotics for acute infection. Pneumonia, cellulitis, pyelonephritis, sepsis — these require antibiotics. LL-37 is adjunctive in chronic, recurrent, or biofilm-protected infections.

- Antibiotic resistance is much less of a concern with LL-37 than with classical antibiotics. RATIONALE: LL-37 disrupts membranes physically rather than blocking specific enzymatic targets; bacteria cannot mutate around membrane-disruptive mechanisms in the same way they evolve enzymatic resistance. This is why LL-37 is uniquely valuable in MRSA and resistant Candida.

- In Lyme + biofilm coinfections, LL-37 is particularly valuable. Borrelia, Bartonella, and Babesia all form biofilm-protected reservoirs. RATIONALE: traditional antibiotic protocols often fail in chronic Lyme due to biofilm protection; LL-37 disruption of these structures restores antibiotic effectiveness.

- Counsel on sourcing. RATIONALE: LL-37 is sensitive to oxidation and degradation; quality varies between manufacturers. Verify COA, ≥99% purity, lyophilized form, and refrigerated shipping.

- Recurrent UTI in postmenopausal women is often biofilm-related. LL-37 SQ + topical estrogen + D-mannose + vitamin D repletion is a useful combination for refractory cases.

- If you see a paradoxical worsening of skin symptoms (especially rosacea pattern) after starting LL-37, suspect rosacea-pathway involvement. RATIONALE: LL-37 is elevated in rosacea pathogenesis; supplementation can worsen.

- LL-37 Complex (the blend formulation) is essentially LL-37 with stabilizers and sometimes additional antimicrobial peptide fragments. Clinical effects are similar to standard LL-37; use is interchangeable in most protocols.

- Herx severity correlates with pathogen burden. Severe Herx = large clearance challenge but also = treatment is working. Mild or absent Herx in a patient with documented heavy infection = consider whether the dose is sufficient.

- Reconstitution: 5 mg / 2 mL vial = 2.5 mg/mL = 25 mcg per unit. Most practitioners use 8–20 units (200–500 mcg) per dose. Easy to dose accurately with insulin syringe.

| **ARA-290 (Cibinetide)**  —  *Erythropoietin-derived 11-amino-acid peptide — small fiber neuropathy, dysautonomia, mitochondrial endothelial repair* |
| --- |
| **Vial** | **Dose** | **Route** | **Cycle** |
| 14 mg / 2 mL  (also 16 mg / 2 mL) | 4 mg/day SQ × 4 weeks (most conditions); some protocols use 4 mg TID × 4–5 weeks | Subcutaneous | 8-week course (~14 vials, 50 units daily) for typical neuropathy/inflammation; 12-week course for refractory; 4-week course for metabolic improvement |

### What it is

ARA-290 (international nonproprietary name: cibinetide) is an 11-amino-acid synthetic peptide derived from the structure of erythropoietin (EPO) — but lacking EPO's hematopoietic (red-blood-cell-stimulating) activity. It was developed by Anthony Cerami and Lutz Brines at the Araim Pharmaceuticals research program after the discovery that EPO has tissue-protective and anti-inflammatory effects independent of its erythropoietic effects. ARA-290 binds the innate repair receptor (IRR) — a tissue-protective receptor complex composed of the EPO receptor (EpoR) and the common β-chain (CD131) — without binding the homodimeric EPO receptor that drives red blood cell production. The result is a peptide that delivers EPO's tissue-protective effects (mitochondrial preservation, endothelial healing, anti-inflammatory action, and neurotrophic support) without the cardiovascular and thrombotic risks of EPO. ARA-290 has emerged as one of the most clinically valuable peptides for small fiber neuropathy, dysautonomia, persistent inflammation in CIRS and post-viral states, and refractory neuropathic pain.

### Mechanism of action

- Binds the innate repair receptor (IRR) — a heterodimer of EPO receptor + common β-chain (CD131) — expressed on stressed, injured, and inflamed tissues.

- RATIONALE FOR TISSUE SELECTIVITY: the IRR is upregulated specifically in injured tissues; ARA-290 binds preferentially where it's needed and minimally in healthy tissue. This explains the wide therapeutic window.

- Does NOT bind the EpoR homodimer — therefore does NOT stimulate erythropoiesis; no rise in hematocrit, no thrombotic risk, no cardiovascular concern that limits therapeutic EPO use.

- Restores mitochondrial function in endothelial cells — addresses the small vessel disease underlying many chronic illness phenotypes.

- Strong anti-inflammatory effects via downregulation of TNF-α, IL-6, and inflammatory pathways in tissue.

- Neurotrophic effects — promotes peripheral nerve regeneration, especially small unmyelinated fibers (C-fibers and Aδ-fibers).

- Restores autonomic function — particularly vagal tone and small-fiber autonomic innervation; this is why it works in dysautonomia.

- Reduces oxidative stress in endothelial and neural tissues.

- Modulates microglial activation — reduces neuroinflammation in CNS.

- Promotes wound healing and tissue repair via stem cell activation.

- Improves thermoregulation in patients with small fiber neuropathy.

- Modulates immune function gently — reduces excess inflammation without immunosuppression.

### Clinical indications

- Small fiber neuropathy — burning, tingling, numbness in extremities; the canonical ARA-290 indication with the strongest evidence

- Sarcoidosis-associated neuropathy (the original ARA-290 trial population)

- Diabetic neuropathy

- Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy

- Post-COVID dysautonomia and small fiber neuropathy

- Long COVID with autonomic features

- POTS (Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome)

- ME/CFS with autonomic component

- CIRS-driven small fiber neuropathy and dysautonomia

- Chronic inflammatory states with persistent neuropathic features

- Mast cell activation syndrome with neuropathic component

- Burning mouth syndrome

- Fibromyalgia (subset with small fiber findings)

- Erythromelalgia

- Persistent post-injury neuropathic pain

- Diabetic foot ulcer / chronic wound healing

- Kidney disease — anti-inflammatory and tissue-protective effects (research stage)

### Dosing rationale & timing

The 4 mg/day SQ dose comes from the original Araim Pharmaceuticals clinical trials in sarcoidosis-associated small fiber neuropathy — this dose produced consistent symptom improvement and small fiber regeneration on skin biopsy. RATIONALE FOR DOSE: ARA-290 saturates the innate repair receptor at this dose; higher doses do not produce additional benefit. Lower doses (1–2 mg) may be insufficient for tissue repair effects. The 4 mg TID protocol (some practitioners) is used for severe neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction, or persistent inflammation — this delivers more sustained receptor engagement. RATIONALE FOR DURATION: The 8-week course is the minimum for measurable clinical improvement in neuropathy; 12-week courses are used for long-standing disease. The 4-week course is for metabolic/inflammatory indications without neuropathic component. RATIONALE FOR MAINTENANCE DOSING: After initial 8-week course, many patients transition to 3 doses per week if symptoms partially improved but not fully resolved — this maintains receptor engagement at lower cost. RATIONALE FOR SQ ROUTE: Subcutaneous absorption is reliable; the peptide reaches systemic circulation and accumulates in IRR-expressing injured tissues. IM offers no advantage. Empty stomach is unnecessary. Morning dosing is generally preferred but timing flexibility is acceptable. RECONSTITUTION: 14 mg / 2 mL = 7 mg/mL = 70 mcg/U; 4 mg = ~57 units. 16 mg / 2 mL = 8 mg/mL = 80 mcg/U; 4 mg = 50 units. Refrigerated stability 28 days post-reconstitution.

### Evidence base

Strong human clinical trial data — uncommon for peptides outside pharmaceutical development. Original Araim Pharmaceuticals trials in sarcoidosis-associated small fiber neuropathy demonstrated improved corneal nerve fiber density, improved Patient-Reported Outcomes, and improved autonomic function. Phase 2 data in diabetic neuropathy and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy are positive. Published case series and observational data in CIRS-associated small fiber neuropathy and post-COVID dysautonomia demonstrate symptomatic and functional improvement. Mechanistic foundation in IRR signaling is well-validated. The peptide has been investigated in over 1,000 patients in formal trials. Although not FDA-approved, the evidence base for ARA-290 in small fiber neuropathy is among the strongest of any compounded peptide currently in clinical use.

### Contraindications

- Active malignancy. RATIONALE: although ARA-290 lacks EPO's erythropoietic and angiogenic effects, the IRR is expressed on some tumor cells; theoretical concern for tumor tissue protection. Coordinate with oncology in cancer survivors.

- Pregnancy and lactation — limited human data; precautionary.

- Known peptide hypersensitivity.

- Active uncontrolled hypertension. RATIONALE: although ARA-290 lacks EPO's pressor effects, vascular endothelial effects are not fully characterized in severe HTN.

- Recent thromboembolic event (within 3 months). RATIONALE: although ARA-290 does not raise hematocrit (the main thrombotic mechanism of EPO), endothelial repair effects are not fully characterized in acute post-thrombotic states.

- Unstable cardiac disease — relative; coordinate with cardiology.

### Drug interactions

Pharmacodynamic considerations: ARA-290 does NOT have EPO-like hematologic effects, so the cardiovascular and thrombotic concerns of EPO do not apply. Pairs favorably with: BPC-157 (additive endothelial and tissue repair); SS-31 (mitochondrial repair from complementary angles); VIP in CIRS final phase (both restore neuroimmune regulation); LL-37 (when treating chronic infection-driven neuropathy); KPV (anti-inflammatory adjunct). Compatible with most pharmaceuticals. Caution with high-dose corticosteroids — opposing tissue effects in some regards. No CYP450 interactions. No interaction with anticoagulants. Compatible with neuropathic pain medications (gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine, tricyclics). Often allows reduction of these medications over time as nerve regeneration occurs.

### Baseline labs & monitoring

- Baseline: skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) — gold standard for small fiber neuropathy diagnosis. RATIONALE: documents pre-treatment nerve fiber loss objectively; allows tracking of regeneration.

- Baseline autonomic testing if dysautonomia component: tilt table, QSART, HRV analysis. RATIONALE: provides objective measures of autonomic function for tracking response.

- Baseline patient-reported outcome measures: SF-NDS (Small Fiber Neuropathy Disability Score), neuropathic pain scale, autonomic symptom checklist.

- Baseline labs: CBC (verify normal — confirm no EPO-like effect), comprehensive metabolic panel, hs-CRP, vitamin B12 + methylmalonic acid, fasting glucose + A1c, TSH, Lyme/EBV/HHV-6 screen if relevant.

- Mid-cycle (week 3–4): symptom check, side effect review.

- Post-cycle (week 8): repeat patient-reported outcomes; consider repeat IENFD biopsy at 12–16 weeks (regeneration is slow).

- Long-term users: every 3–6 months CBC (confirm no hematocrit rise), CMP, hs-CRP, symptom-based monitoring.

- RATIONALE FOR CBC MONITORING: although ARA-290 does not bind the homodimeric EpoR and should not raise hematocrit, periodic CBC confirms this in clinical use — defensive practice given the EPO derivation.

### Side effects

*Common (mild, dose-limiting only if severe):*

- Mild injection site reaction.

- Transient mild headache in first week.

- Mild fatigue first 1–2 weeks (immune and tissue activation requires energy).

- Mild GI upset uncommon.

- Most patients report no acute side effects — ARA-290 is among the better-tolerated peptides.

*Serious (stop and reassess):*

- No serious adverse events reported in published clinical trials at therapeutic doses.

- Rare anaphylaxis (any peptide).

- Theoretical: tumor tissue protection in undiagnosed malignancy — basis for malignancy contraindication.

- If hematocrit rises during therapy (very rare), discontinue and reassess; this would suggest contamination or formulation issue.

### Stacking & synergy

ARA-290 is a foundational peptide for small fiber neuropathy and dysautonomia, and pairs naturally with other peptides in chronic illness protocols. Pairs especially well with: (1) BPC-157 — additive endothelial and microvascular repair; (2) SS-31 — mitochondrial repair from complementary angles (SS-31 inside the cell, ARA-290 at the IRR); (3) VIP for CIRS in patients with autonomic features (after Shoemaker sequence); (4) Thymalin or Thymagen — restore adaptive immune function in chronic illness states; (5) LL-37 if infection-driven neuropathy is suspected; (6) KPV for ongoing inflammation reduction; (7) Standard neuropathic pain medications (gabapentin, pregabalin, low-dose naltrexone) — synergistic; ARA-290 addresses the underlying pathology while these address symptoms; (8) Peripheral nerve nutrient support — alpha-lipoic acid 600 mg/day, methylcobalamin 1000–5000 mcg/day, methylfolate 1–5 mg/day, benfotiamine 300–600 mg/day. AVOID stacking concerns: avoid in active malignancy without oncology coordination; avoid in acute thromboembolic state.

### Clinical pearls

- ARA-290 has the strongest human trial evidence of nearly any compounded peptide currently in functional medicine use. RATIONALE: its development pathway through Araim Pharmaceuticals included formal Phase 2 trials. When patients ask 'is this proven?' — this is one of the strongest answers.

- The canonical indication is small fiber neuropathy. Look for: burning/tingling/numbness (especially feet and hands), heat/cold intolerance, autonomic symptoms (dry eyes/mouth, GI dysmotility, orthostatic intolerance), exercise intolerance with post-exertional crashes. Skin biopsy with IENFD is the diagnostic standard.

- ARA-290 is fundamentally different from EPO. Counsel patients clearly: 'This is derived from EPO but does NOT raise red blood cell counts, does NOT carry the cardiovascular risks of EPO, and works through a different receptor.' RATIONALE: many patients (and some clinicians) confuse the two; the IRR vs. EpoR distinction is essential.

- The 8-week course is the foundation. Set expectations: improvement is gradual and may not be obvious until week 4–6. Nerve regeneration is slow — full effect may take 3–6 months. Biopsy confirmation of nerve fiber density restoration may take 12+ weeks.

- POTS and dysautonomia patients respond well — particularly those with small fiber findings. RATIONALE: POTS is increasingly understood as a small fiber autonomic neuropathy in many cases; ARA-290 addresses the underlying nerve pathology rather than just the heart rate.

- Long COVID with neuropathic and autonomic features is a major emerging indication. RATIONALE: COVID-driven small fiber neuropathy has been documented in skin biopsy studies; ARA-290 addresses the same pathology that worked in sarcoidosis-associated small fiber neuropathy.

- ARA-290 does not directly suppress the immune system — it modulates inflammation while supporting tissue repair. RATIONALE: this is why it can be used alongside pharmaceutical immunosuppression in some autoimmune contexts (with rheumatology coordination).

- Combination with IVIG (in autoimmune small fiber neuropathy) is favored by some neurologists — they target different aspects of the same pathology.

- Maintenance dosing (3 doses/week) after the initial 8-week course is appropriate when symptoms partially improve but don't fully resolve. RATIONALE: ongoing receptor engagement maintains tissue protection and may allow continued slow regeneration.

- The CIRS overlap is significant. Many CIRS patients have small fiber neuropathy as part of their presentation; ARA-290 is a useful addition to the CIRS protocol AFTER the Shoemaker sequence stabilizes inflammation.

- Cost is a real consideration. The 8-week course requires ~14 vials. Counsel patients on cost-benefit; for severe disabling neuropathy, the value is clear, but for mild symptoms, alternatives may be more cost-effective.

- Diabetic neuropathy responds, but glycemic control must be optimized in parallel. RATIONALE: continued hyperglycemia drives ongoing nerve damage; ARA-290 cannot regenerate faster than diabetes is destroying.

- Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy is an important indication — coordinate with oncology, especially during active chemo cycles. RATIONALE: emerging evidence suggests ARA-290 can be used during chemotherapy to prevent neuropathy progression.

- Burning mouth syndrome is a small fiber neuropathy of the oral mucosa — under-recognized but ARA-290 can produce dramatic improvement.

- If ARA-290 has not produced improvement by week 6 of the 8-week course, reassess. Possibilities: incorrect diagnosis (neuropathy from non-IRR-mediated pathology), inadequate dose, ongoing driver (uncontrolled diabetes, ongoing biotoxin exposure, untreated nutrient deficiency), or sourcing issue.

- ALA, methylcobalamin, methylfolate, benfotiamine, and alpha-lipoic acid should ALWAYS run alongside ARA-290 in neuropathy protocols. RATIONALE: these are the substrates and cofactors for nerve regeneration; ARA-290 stimulates the process but the building blocks must be available.

- Reconstitution: 14 mg / 2 mL = 7 mg/mL = 70 mcg per unit; 4 mg dose = 57 units (round to 50 units for ease). 16 mg / 2 mL = 8 mg/mL = 80 mcg per unit; 4 mg dose = 50 units exactly. Most practitioners prefer the 16 mg vial for cleaner dosing math.

- Vial cost-effectiveness: an 8-week course at 4 mg/day requires ~225 mg total = ~14 vials of 16 mg formulation. Plan dispensing accordingly.

- Chronic non-healing wound: topical LL-37 application + SQ LL-37 200–500 mcg 2–3×/wk + standard wound care + nutritional optimization

- Combined infection + neuropathy (chronic Lyme + dysautonomia): SEQUENCE — LL-37 first × 6–8 weeks to address infection, allow Herx and recovery, then ARA-290 × 8 weeks for nerve repair

- Sarcoidosis-associated SFN: ARA-290 4 mg/day × 8–12 weeks + sarcoidosis-specific therapy per pulm/rheum + B-complex

## Required adjunct supplements

- Vitamin D₃ titrated to 60–80 ng/mL serum (essential for endogenous LL-37; supports IRR signaling)

- Zinc 30–50 mg/day with food (innate immunity cofactor)

- Omega-3 EPA/DHA 2–4 g/day (resolution of inflammation)

- Methylcobalamin (B12) 1000–5000 mcg/day for neuropathy patients

- Methylfolate 1–5 mg/day

- Alpha-lipoic acid 300–600 mg/day (nerve regeneration substrate)

- Benfotiamine 300–600 mg/day for diabetic or alcohol-related neuropathy

- Selenium 200 mcg/day (immune cofactor)

- Adequate protein (1.0–1.5 g/kg) for nerve and tissue repair substrate

- Binders for LL-37 protocols: CSM 1 g QID, charcoal, chlorella, zeolite — patient-specific selection

- Mast cell stabilization (cromolyn, ketotifen, quercetin) BEFORE starting LL-37 in MCAS-prone patients

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Starting LL-37 in unstable MCAS without pre-stabilization — predictable mast cell flare

- Starting LL-37 without binders ready in heavy biofilm/pathogen burden — severe Herx

- Treating an acute uncomplicated infection with LL-37 instead of antibiotics — wrong tool, wastes time and money

- Not optimizing vitamin D before starting LL-37 — endogenous LL-37 production depends on D-VDR-LL37 axis; supplementing exogenous LL-37 in a D-deficient patient is suboptimal

- Continuing LL-37 through severe Herx without modification — drop dose, increase binders, slow titration

- Confusing ARA-290 with EPO — different receptor, different effects, different risk profile; counsel patients clearly

- Underdosing ARA-290 — 1–2 mg is insufficient for IRR saturation; 4 mg is the established dose

- Stopping ARA-290 at week 4 without giving full 8-week course time to work — nerve regeneration is slow

- Not optimizing diabetes control before ARA-290 in diabetic neuropathy — ongoing hyperglycemia destroys nerves faster than ARA-290 regenerates

- Ignoring B-complex, methylcobalamin, ALA, benfotiamine in neuropathy protocols — peptides need substrates

- Using ARA-290 simultaneously with LL-37 in patient with both infection and neuropathy — sequence them: address infection first, then repair nerves

- Not getting baseline IENFD biopsy in suspected SFN — without baseline, treatment response cannot be objectively documented

# GH Axis Peptides — Category Overview

The growth hormone axis is one of the most clinically important systems in age-management and chronic-illness recovery. Endogenous GH production peaks in adolescence and declines progressively from the third decade onward — by age 60, most adults have only 25-50% of their peak GH output. This decline is not benign: it correlates with sarcopenia, visceral fat accumulation, declining bone density, deteriorating sleep architecture, slower wound healing, decreased exercise tolerance, mood changes, and accelerated aging in general.

The clinical question is not WHETHER to support the GH axis in declining patients — it is HOW. Three approaches exist: (1) exogenous human growth hormone (HGH) replacement; (2) GHRH analog peptides (Sermorelin, CJC-1295, Tesamorelin); (3) ghrelin mimetic peptides (Ipamorelin, hexarelin). Functional medicine has overwhelmingly chosen the peptide approaches over HGH. RATIONALE: GHRH analogs and ghrelin mimetics PRESERVE the body's negative feedback system — high IGF-1 levels suppress further GH release. This means the patient cannot be 'overdosed' the way HGH replacement allows. Exogenous HGH bypasses all regulatory feedback and can drive supraphysiologic IGF-1 levels, with associated risks: insulin resistance, fluid retention, joint problems, theoretical malignancy concerns, and acromegaly-like features.

Choosing among the three GH peptides depends on the patient's clinical phenotype:

### What it is

Sermorelin is a synthetic 29-amino-acid peptide identical to the first 29 amino acids of endogenous growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) — also known as GRF 1-29 (Growth Hormone Releasing Factor, residues 1-29). The full-length endogenous GHRH is 44 amino acids, but the first 29 residues contain the entire receptor-binding and biological activity. Sermorelin was developed in the 1980s and was briefly available as an FDA-approved diagnostic agent (Geref) for evaluating pituitary GH secretion before being withdrawn from the commercial market for non-safety reasons. It remains widely used in compounded form. Unlike exogenous human growth hormone (HGH), Sermorelin works by stimulating the patient's OWN pituitary to produce GH in physiologic pulses — preserving the negative feedback loop, the natural circadian rhythm, and the body's ability to titrate GH output to actual need. This is fundamentally safer than exogenous HGH, which bypasses all regulatory feedback and can produce supraphysiologic levels that drive insulin resistance, edema, and theoretical malignancy concerns.

### Mechanism of action

- Binds the GHRH receptor (GHRHR) on anterior pituitary somatotrophs.

- Stimulates intracellular cAMP and calcium signaling → release of stored GH from secretory granules.

- Restores rhythmic, pulsatile GH release patterns — the physiologic mode of GH secretion that decreases with age.

- PRESERVES negative feedback: high GH and IGF-1 levels suppress further GH release via somatostatin and IGF-1 negative feedback. This is why Sermorelin cannot drive supraphysiologic GH levels the way exogenous HGH can.

- RATIONALE FOR PHYSIOLOGIC SAFETY: because the pituitary itself controls how much GH is released in response to Sermorelin, the body cannot be 'overdosed' in the same way as exogenous HGH. Sermorelin amplifies the natural system rather than replacing it.

- Anchors the natural circadian GH pulse at ~11 PM — restoring sleep architecture and deep slow-wave sleep.

- Increases IGF-1 production by the liver — IGF-1 mediates many of GH's tissue effects (muscle protein synthesis, bone density, connective tissue repair, metabolic effects).

- Improves body composition gradually: increases lean mass, decreases visceral fat, improves bone density.

- Restores GH-dependent immune function and tissue repair capacity that decline with age.

- Modulates the hypothalamic-pituitary axis — restores upstream signaling that becomes dysregulated in chronic illness, mold/CIRS, and aging.

### Clinical indications

- Adult growth hormone deficiency (clinically defined or functional/relative)

- Age-related GH decline ('somatopause') — typically beginning in 40s

- Body composition optimization in middle-aged and older adults

- Sleep architecture restoration — particularly in flat-cortisol-curve patients

- Recovery support in chronic illness — mold/CIRS, post-viral, post-Lyme

- Bone density support in osteopenia/osteoporosis (adjunct to standard care)

- Connective tissue and tendon repair in aging athletes

- Cognitive support in age-related decline

- Mood and quality of life improvement in age-related GH decline

- Post-surgical recovery

- Adjunct to BHRT in comprehensive aging-medicine protocols

- Visceral adiposity reduction (less potent than Tesamorelin for this indication)

### Dosing rationale & timing

The 300 mcg–2 mg bedtime dose range reflects the wide individual variability in GHRH receptor sensitivity. Most patients start at 300–500 mcg QHS and titrate based on IGF-1 response. RATIONALE FOR BEDTIME DOSING: the natural GH pulse occurs at approximately 11 PM during the first phase of slow-wave sleep. Sermorelin given at bedtime amplifies this physiologic pulse rather than creating an artificial pulse at the wrong time. This is also why Sermorelin improves sleep — it works WITH the body's circadian rhythm. RATIONALE FOR EMPTY STOMACH: meals (especially carbohydrate and fat) trigger somatostatin release, which is the brake on GH secretion. Eating within 2 hours of Sermorelin dosing blunts the GH pulse — this is non-negotiable. Patients who 'don't feel anything' on Sermorelin are often eating too close to bedtime. RATIONALE FOR 5-ON-2-OFF CYCLING: continuous daily dosing leads to GHRH receptor desensitization and tachyphylaxis. Brief weekly washout maintains receptor sensitivity. RATIONALE FOR 6-WEEKS-ON / 6-WEEKS-OFF: longer cycling with extended washout produces sustained response without progressive desensitization; this is the longevity-medicine standard. RATIONALE FOR IGF-1 TITRATION: target adult IGF-1 ≈180–200 ng/mL — the upper-mid normal range for young adults. Going higher does not produce better outcomes and increases theoretical risks (insulin resistance, malignancy concern). Going lower is undertreatment. Dose-titrate based on 8-week IGF-1.

### Evidence base

Strong mechanistic foundation — GHRH biology has been extensively characterized since the 1980s. Sermorelin was originally developed as a pharmaceutical (Geref) and has substantial human safety data from that era. The peptide was withdrawn from commercial sale for business rather than safety reasons. Compounded Sermorelin has decades of clinical use in age-management medicine; outcomes data is primarily observational and clinical-experience-based. IGF-1 normalization, body composition improvement, sleep quality improvement, and quality-of-life measures consistently respond. The peptide has a more conservative safety profile than exogenous HGH because of preserved negative feedback. Long-term safety data spans 20+ years of clinical use without major safety signals.

### Contraindications

- Active malignancy. RATIONALE: GH and IGF-1 are growth factors; theoretical concern that elevated levels could support tumor growth. Insufficient human data in active cancer to establish safety. Coordinate with oncology in cancer survivors (>5 years remission with normal IGF-1 may be appropriate candidates).

- Uncontrolled diabetes (HbA1c >8%). RATIONALE: GH antagonizes insulin action; in poorly controlled diabetes, Sermorelin can worsen glycemic control. Optimize diabetes management first.

- Severe diabetic retinopathy. RATIONALE: GH and IGF-1 promote retinal vascular proliferation; can worsen proliferative retinopathy.

- Pregnancy and lactation.

- Severe untreated obstructive sleep apnea. RATIONALE: GH affects soft tissue and airway; can worsen OSA in untreated patients. Treat OSA first, then introduce Sermorelin.

- Active pituitary tumor or recent pituitary surgery (within 6 months). RATIONALE: GHRH receptor activation in pituitary tumor tissue is unpredictable.

- Known peptide hypersensitivity.

### Drug interactions

Pharmacodynamic considerations: insulin and oral hypoglycemics — GH antagonizes insulin; monitor glucose and adjust diabetes meds as needed during Sermorelin therapy. Corticosteroids — chronic high-dose corticosteroids suppress GH/IGF-1 axis; the combination is suboptimal. Thyroid hormone — Sermorelin can increase peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion; monitor free T3, may allow thyroid medication reduction. Sex hormones (testosterone, estrogen) — synergistic for body composition and bone density; commonly co-administered in BHRT protocols. Statins — no significant interaction. Beta-blockers — propranolol can blunt GH response; monitor IGF-1 if patient is on beta-blockers. No CYP450 interactions. Compatible with most peptides — pairs especially well with Ipamorelin (combined product), BPC-157, GHK-Cu, and TB-500 for tissue repair synergy.

### Baseline labs & monitoring

- Baseline: IGF-1 (the master tracking lab — establishes pre-treatment level), fasting glucose, HbA1c, fasting insulin (assess insulin resistance baseline), comprehensive metabolic panel, lipid panel, TSH and free T3/T4.

- 6-month mark: repeat full metabolic panel, IGF-1, body composition.

- Annually: IGF-1, glucose/A1c, lipid panel, body composition, age-appropriate cancer screening.

- RATIONALE FOR IGF-1 AS PRIMARY MARKER: GH itself has a short half-life (minutes) and pulsatile secretion makes single GH measurements meaningless. IGF-1 has a long half-life and reflects integrated 24-hour GH activity. It is THE marker for both diagnosis and titration.

### Side effects

*Common (mild, dose-limiting only if severe):*

- Mild injection site reaction.

- Mild flushing or warmth in first few doses.

- Vivid dreams initially (improvement in slow-wave sleep architecture brings more dream recall).

- Mild morning fatigue in first 1–2 weeks as sleep architecture remodels.

- Mild fluid retention initially — usually transient.

- Mild joint stiffness or carpal tunnel-like symptoms — dose-dependent; reduce dose if persistent.

*Serious (stop and reassess):*

- Worsening glycemic control in diabetic or pre-diabetic patients — monitor and adjust as needed.

- Worsening OSA in untreated patients.

- Acromegaly-like features (rare; would require sustained supraphysiologic IGF-1 — unusual with Sermorelin alone). RATIONALE: Sermorelin's preserved negative feedback makes this uncommon, unlike exogenous HGH.

- Carpal tunnel syndrome with sustained high doses.

- Pseudotumor cerebri (very rare; reported with HGH more than Sermorelin).

- Anaphylaxis (rare; any peptide).

Sermorelin pairs naturally with multiple peptide categories. ### Clinical pearls

- Sermorelin is the 'older patient' GH peptide of choice. RATIONALE: the preserved negative feedback makes it safer than CJC-1295 + Ipamorelin in patients with cardiovascular risk, mild glucose dysregulation, or generally fragile baseline. In older patients with flat cortisol curves, Sermorelin at bedtime restores the missing 11 PM GH pulse — and much improves with it: sleep, mood, body composition, and cognition.

- The empty stomach rule is non-negotiable. RATIONALE: meals trigger somatostatin (the GH brake), which abolishes Sermorelin's effect. Patients eating within 2 hours of dosing get no benefit. Counsel explicitly: 'Last food at 6 PM, dose at 9 PM' for a typical 10–11 PM bedtime.

- IGF-1 is THE titration marker. RATIONALE: GH itself has a 20-minute half-life and pulsatile secretion — single GH measurements are clinically useless. IGF-1 has a 12-hour half-life and reflects integrated GH activity. Target 180–200 ng/mL adult; do not push above range.

- Sleep improvement is often the first noticeable effect — within 1–2 weeks. Patients report deeper sleep, more dream recall, and waking refreshed. RATIONALE: Sermorelin restores the natural 11 PM GH pulse that anchors slow-wave sleep architecture.

- The 6-weeks-on / 6-weeks-off cycling prevents progressive receptor desensitization. RATIONALE: continuous daily dosing produces declining response over months; cycling preserves long-term effectiveness. Some practitioners use 5-on / 2-off (week-by-week); both are valid.

- In flat cortisol curve patients (Pattern B in cortisol categorization — burnt-out HPA), Sermorelin at bedtime can dramatically improve overall recovery. RATIONALE: GH pulse is one of the major nocturnal anabolic signals; restoring it allows the body to repair instead of stay catabolic.

- Body composition changes are slow but durable — 6 months for clinically meaningful lean mass and visceral fat changes. RATIONALE: GH effects are mediated through IGF-1 and require sustained tissue exposure. Set patient expectations.

- Joint stiffness or fluid retention is dose-related and resolves with dose reduction. RATIONALE: GH affects sodium retention and connective tissue water content; supraphysiologic levels produce these effects. Drop by 200–300 mcg if persistent.

- Cancer history is the most common contraindication question. RATIONALE: GH/IGF-1 are growth factors; theoretical concern but limited human data showing actual harm. Most age-management physicians avoid in active cancer; many use cautiously in 5+ year remission patients with normal IGF-1 — coordinate with oncology.

- Sermorelin is significantly cheaper than CJC-1295 + Ipamorelin. RATIONALE: shorter peptide, simpler synthesis, broader availability. For cost-conscious patients with mild GH decline, Sermorelin alone is often sufficient.

- Diabetic patients require careful management. RATIONALE: GH antagonizes insulin; A1c may rise 0.3–0.5 points in early months. Monitor closely and adjust diabetic medications as needed. Consider Tesamorelin for diabetic patients with visceral adiposity (better metabolic profile than Sermorelin).

- Sermorelin is among the safest peptides for long-term use in age management. RATIONALE: preserved negative feedback prevents supraphysiologic levels; no major safety signals in 20+ years of compounded use. Many practitioners use it for years cycled.

- If a patient is not responding (IGF-1 not rising adequately at 8 weeks), check: empty stomach compliance, beta-blocker use, severe sleep deprivation, severe under-eating (calorie restriction blunts GH), severe stress (cortisol blunts GH), liver disease (impaired IGF-1 production), and sourcing quality.

- Reconstitution varies by vial size; verify with compounding pharmacy. Common: 5 mg / 1 mL = 5 mg/mL = 50 mcg per unit; 500 mcg = 10 units; 1 mg = 20 units.

### What it is

CJC-1295 + Ipamorelin is the current standard combination for GH axis stimulation in functional medicine. CJC-1295 is a 30-amino-acid synthetic peptide — a modified GHRH analog with extended half-life (12–24 hours for the no-DAC version, days for the DAC version) due to amino acid substitutions that resist enzymatic degradation. Ipamorelin is a 5-amino-acid synthetic peptide that is a selective ghrelin receptor agonist (GHS-R1a) — it stimulates GH release through a complementary pathway to GHRH, AND notably does NOT stimulate cortisol, ACTH, or prolactin (which earlier ghrelin mimetics did). The two peptides are typically combined because GHRH (CJC-1295) and ghrelin mimetics (Ipamorelin) act through different receptors on the same somatotroph cells, producing supra-additive GH release when used together. The combination has become more popular than Sermorelin alone in younger and middle-aged patients seeking body composition and recovery effects, because the combined GH pulses are larger and produce more pronounced clinical effects.

### Mechanism of action

- CJC-1295: Binds GHRH receptor (GHRHR) on anterior pituitary somatotrophs — stimulates GH release through cAMP-mediated pathway.

- Ipamorelin: Binds the ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a) on somatotrophs — stimulates GH release through phospholipase C and calcium signaling pathway.

- RATIONALE FOR SYNERGY: GHRH and ghrelin act through DIFFERENT intracellular pathways converging on the same GH-releasing cells. Combined activation produces supra-additive GH release — the two pathways amplify each other rather than competing.

- Ipamorelin's selective ghrelin receptor binding profile is the key advantage over older ghrelin mimetics (GHRP-2, GHRP-6, hexarelin): no cortisol elevation, no ACTH elevation, no prolactin elevation, no significant appetite stimulation.

- PRESERVES negative feedback similar to Sermorelin — high IGF-1 levels suppress further GH release.

- Increases IGF-1 production by the liver — mediates muscle protein synthesis, bone density, connective tissue repair, metabolic effects.

- Restores rhythmic, pulsatile GH release patterns.

- CJC-1295 (no DAC) version produces shorter, more physiologic pulses; CJC-1295 (DAC) produces sustained elevation that some practitioners avoid as 'less physiologic.'

- Improves body composition: lean mass gain, fat mass loss (especially visceral), bone density support.

- Improves sleep architecture and slow-wave sleep when dosed at bedtime.

- Restores GH-dependent immune function and tissue repair capacity.

### What it is

Tesamorelin is a 44-amino-acid synthetic peptide identical to natural endogenous GHRH but stabilized with a trans-3-hexenoyl group at the N-terminus to resist degradation by dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4). It was developed by Theratechnologies and approved by the FDA in 2010 as Egrifta for the reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-associated lipodystrophy — making it the only GHRH analog with formal FDA approval. The compounded version is widely available for off-label use in age-management, NAFLD, and visceral adiposity. Tesamorelin's distinctive clinical effect is its preferential reduction of visceral adipose tissue (VAT) — the metabolically dangerous fat surrounding internal organs — without significant effect on subcutaneous fat. This makes it qualitatively different from Sermorelin and CJC-1295 + Ipamorelin in its body composition effects. Tesamorelin also shows particular efficacy in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and has emerging cognitive applications.

### Mechanism of action

- Binds GHRH receptor (GHRHR) on anterior pituitary somatotrophs — same receptor as Sermorelin and CJC-1295.

- Extended half-life vs. Sermorelin due to N-terminal modification — produces stronger and longer GH pulses.

- RATIONALE FOR VISCERAL FAT SELECTIVITY: GH preferentially mobilizes visceral fat over subcutaneous fat — visceral adipocytes have higher GH receptor density and greater lipolytic response to GH. Tesamorelin's potent GH pulses exploit this differential effect.

- Increases IGF-1 production by the liver — mediates muscle protein synthesis, bone density, metabolic effects.

- PRESERVES negative feedback — IGF-1 suppresses further GH release.

- Reduces visceral adipose tissue (VAT) by 15–18% in HIV lipodystrophy trials over 6 months.

- Reduces hepatic fat content — primary mechanism of NAFLD benefit.

- Improves lipid profile — reduces triglycerides, increases HDL.

- Improves cognitive function in older adults (multiple trials including AD/MCI populations).

- Reduces inflammatory markers (CRP, fibrinogen) in HIV lipodystrophy.

- Modest improvement in insulin sensitivity in some patients — neutral or slightly worse in others (GH antagonizes insulin acutely but improves body composition over time).

### Clinical indications

- HIV-associated lipodystrophy (the FDA-approved indication)

- Visceral adiposity / metabolic syndrome

- Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) — emerging indication with strong support

- Age-related visceral fat accumulation

- Cognitive support in older adults (multiple positive trials)

- Post-bariatric surgery body composition optimization

- Adjunct in metabolic syndrome with visceral component

- Diabetes adjunct when CJC/Ipa is too aggressive (Tesamorelin has better metabolic profile)

- Patients with cardiovascular risk and visceral fat (where visceral fat reduction matters more than overall body composition)

- Mood and quality-of-life support in age-related decline

- Adjunct to BHRT in patients with prominent visceral adiposity

### Dosing rationale & timing

The 1–2 mg male dose comes from the FDA-approved HIV lipodystrophy trials, where 2 mg/day produced 15–18% VAT reduction over 6 months. RATIONALE FOR FEMALE DOSE REDUCTION (500 mcg–1 mg): women have lower GH receptor numbers and produce more IGF-1 per mg of GHRH stimulation; lower doses achieve similar IGF-1 responses with fewer side effects. RATIONALE FOR BEDTIME DOSING: amplifies the natural 11 PM GH pulse. RATIONALE FOR EMPTY STOMACH: same as other GHRH analogs — meals trigger somatostatin which abolishes GH pulse. RATIONALE FOR 5-ON / 2-OFF: prevents GHRH receptor desensitization. RATIONALE FOR 6-MONTH CONTINUOUS COURSE: visceral fat reduction is slow — pivotal trials demonstrated effect at 6 months, with continued benefit at 12 months. Patients should plan on a 6-month minimum commitment to see meaningful VAT reduction. RATIONALE FOR DOSE TITRATION: start at 1 mg (men) or 500 mcg (women), titrate up after 4–6 weeks if IGF-1 has not normalized to 180–200 ng/mL. RECONSTITUTION: 10 mg / 1 mL = 10 mg/mL = 100 mcg per unit. 1 mg = 10 units; 2 mg = 20 units. The 10 mg vial provides 5–10 doses depending on dosing.

### Evidence base

By far the strongest evidence base of any GH peptide. FDA approval as Egrifta required Phase 3 trials in HIV lipodystrophy. Multiple subsequent RCTs in NAFLD, cognitive function in older adults, AD/MCI populations. Visceral fat reduction has been demonstrated by abdominal CT measurement in pivotal trials. Cognitive trials have shown improvement in executive function and processing speed. NAFLD trials have shown reduction in hepatic fat fraction by MR spectroscopy. Cardiovascular safety has been established in HIV population (a population with elevated CV risk). Long-term follow-up in HIV lipodystrophy demonstrates sustained benefit and good tolerability. Tesamorelin has the most robust evidence base of any peptide we discuss in these volumes outside of TA-1.

### Contraindications

- Active malignancy. RATIONALE: GH and IGF-1 are growth factors. Important note — Tesamorelin has been studied in HIV patients with elevated cancer risk; safety in survivors is well-characterized. Coordinate with oncology in cancer survivors.

- Uncontrolled diabetes (HbA1c >8%). RATIONALE: GH antagonizes insulin acutely; visceral fat reduction improves insulin sensitivity over time. Net effect varies by patient.

- Severe diabetic retinopathy. RATIONALE: GH/IGF-1 promote retinal vascular proliferation.

- Pregnancy and lactation.

- Severe untreated obstructive sleep apnea. RATIONALE: GH affects soft tissue and airway.

- Active pituitary tumor or recent pituitary surgery.

- Known peptide hypersensitivity.

- Severe edema or congestive heart failure (NYHA Class III–IV).

### Drug interactions

Pharmacodynamic considerations: insulin and oral hypoglycemics — monitor glucose; acute insulin antagonism but long-term improvement via visceral fat reduction. Corticosteroids — chronic high-dose suppresses GH/IGF-1 axis. Thyroid hormone — may increase T4-to-T3 conversion. Sex hormones — synergistic for body composition. Statins — Tesamorelin's NAFLD benefit is complementary to statin therapy. Beta-blockers — may blunt GH response. GLP-1 agonists — synergistic and complementary; both target visceral fat from different angles; the combination is increasingly used in metabolic medicine. Compatible with most peptides. No CYP450 interactions.

### Baseline labs & monitoring

- Baseline: IGF-1, fasting glucose, HbA1c, fasting insulin, comprehensive metabolic panel, lipid panel, ALT/AST (liver function), TSH and free T3/T4.

- Body composition: DEXA scan or abdominal CT at baseline (CT measures visceral fat directly; DEXA approximates).

- NAFLD-specific: ALT, AST, GGT, triglycerides, HOMA-IR, FibroScan or MR spectroscopy if available.

- Cardiovascular: blood pressure, optional echo in cardiac risk patients.

- Cancer screening per age-appropriate guidelines BEFORE starting.

- 8-week mark: repeat IGF-1 — primary titration marker. Target 180–200 ng/mL.

- 3-month mark: repeat ALT/AST/GGT (NAFLD response), fasting glucose/A1c, lipid panel.

- 6-month mark: full metabolic panel, IGF-1, body composition (DEXA or repeat CT for visceral fat), repeat NAFLD assessment if applicable.

- Annually: IGF-1, A1c, lipid panel, body composition, age-appropriate cancer screening.

- RATIONALE FOR VISCERAL FAT MEASUREMENT: tracking the actual treatment target (VAT) by abdominal CT or DEXA visceral fat estimate provides objective documentation of response.

### Side effects

*Common (mild, dose-limiting only if severe):*

- Injection site reaction (more common with Tesamorelin than other GH peptides; rotate sites).

- Mild flushing in first few doses.

- Vivid dreams initially.

- Mild fluid retention — typically transient.

- Mild joint stiffness or arthralgia — dose-dependent.

- Mild peripheral edema.

- Carpal tunnel-like symptoms.

- Mild headache.

*Serious (stop and reassess):*

- Worsening glycemic control acutely (improvement over months).

- Pseudotumor cerebri (rare).

- Severe edema or worsening heart failure.

- Acromegaly-like features with sustained supraphysiologic IGF-1.

- Worsening OSA in untreated patients.

- Severe injection site reactions (more common with Tesamorelin than other GHRH analogs).

- Anaphylaxis (rare; any peptide).

### Stacking & synergy

Tesamorelin pairs naturally with metabolic and body composition protocols. Pairs especially well with: (1) GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, tirzepatide, retatrutide) — combination is increasingly used in metabolic medicine; both target visceral fat from different angles; particularly synergistic in NAFLD; (2) BPC-157 — gut and tissue repair adjunct; (3) MOTS-c — addresses mitochondrial component of metabolic disease; (4) SS-31 — protects mitochondria during metabolic transition; (5) Standard NAFLD therapy — Tesamorelin complements vitamin E, omega-3, dietary intervention, exercise; (6) BHRT — synergistic for body composition; (7) Resistance training and adequate protein (1.2–1.6 g/kg) — Tesamorelin preserves lean mass during fat loss; without resistance training, lean mass effects are blunted; (8) PE-22-28 — emerging combination for cognitive support in older adults with metabolic component. AVOID stacking concerns: monitor closely in diabetics; coordinate with oncology in cancer history; avoid simultaneous start with multiple peptides.

### Clinical pearls

- Tesamorelin is the GH peptide for VISCERAL fat reduction. RATIONALE: GH preferentially mobilizes visceral adipocytes; Tesamorelin's potent GH pulses exploit this differential effect. Subcutaneous fat is less affected. This makes Tesamorelin qualitatively different from Sermorelin and CJC/Ipa.

- The strongest evidence base of any GH peptide. RATIONALE: FDA approval required Phase 3 trials. Subsequent NAFLD and cognitive trials have built the evidence further. When patients ask 'is this proven?' — Tesamorelin has the strongest answer in the GH category.

- NAFLD is an underused indication. RATIONALE: Tesamorelin reduces hepatic fat content directly; trials have shown reduction in liver fat fraction by MR spectroscopy. For patients with NAFLD + visceral adiposity + insulin resistance, Tesamorelin addresses all three. Coordinate with hepatology if cirrhosis is present.

- Cognitive applications are increasingly recognized. RATIONALE: trials in older adults and MCI/AD populations have shown improvement in executive function and processing speed. Mechanism likely involves cerebrovascular and hippocampal effects of restored IGF-1 signaling.

- Diabetic patients tolerate Tesamorelin BETTER than CJC/Ipa. RATIONALE: Tesamorelin's visceral fat reduction improves insulin sensitivity over months; the acute GH-mediated insulin antagonism is offset by the body composition improvement. A1c often IMPROVES on Tesamorelin in diabetic patients with visceral adiposity.

- The injection site reaction is more common with Tesamorelin than other GH peptides. RATIONALE: the trans-3-hexenoyl modification can cause local irritation. Rotate injection sites systematically (abdomen quadrants, both thighs, both flanks). Severe persistent reaction warrants dose reduction or switching to a different GH peptide.

- Female dosing is HALF the male dose typically. RATIONALE: women have higher GH/IGF-1 responsiveness. Female 500 mcg often produces same IGF-1 response as male 1 mg. Avoid overdosing women.

- MUSCLE PRESERVATION DURING GLP-1 THERAPY: Tesamorelin is an excellent option. RATIONALE: combines visceral fat reduction (synergistic with GLP-1) with muscle preservation (counters GLP-1-driven lean mass loss). Specifically for patients with prominent visceral adiposity. CJC/Ipa is the alternative — see Volume 6 for the full muscle preservation stack.

- 6-month commitment: counsel patients explicitly. RATIONALE: visceral fat reduction is slow; pivotal trials demonstrated effect at 6 months. Patients expecting rapid changes will discontinue prematurely.

- DEXA scan or abdominal CT at baseline is worth the cost. RATIONALE: quantifies visceral fat objectively; allows tracking of response. Without baseline measurement, response cannot be objectively documented to justify continued treatment.

- Cardiovascular safety is well-established. RATIONALE: Phase 3 trials in HIV population (elevated CV risk baseline) showed neutral or favorable cardiovascular outcomes. Tesamorelin can be used in patients with cardiovascular risk who would not be candidates for HGH.

- Cost is higher than Sermorelin or CJC/Ipa. RATIONALE: more complex synthesis, FDA-approved pharmaceutical version drives compounded pricing. Patients should understand the cost/benefit — for visceral fat and NAFLD specifically, the unique efficacy may justify cost; for general age management, less expensive alternatives may suffice.

- Tesamorelin + GLP-1 + adequate protein + resistance training is becoming a standard metabolic medicine combination. RATIONALE: GLP-1 drives weight loss but causes lean mass loss; Tesamorelin preserves lean mass and accelerates visceral fat reduction; protein and resistance training provide substrate and stimulus for muscle. The four-legged stool.

- If a patient is not responding (no IGF-1 rise, no body composition change at 3 months), check: empty stomach compliance, sourcing quality, severe under-eating, severe stress (cortisol), liver dysfunction (impaired IGF-1 production), beta-blocker use.

- Reconstitution: 10 mg / 1 mL = 10 mg/mL = 100 mcg per unit. 1 mg = 10 units; 2 mg = 20 units. Standard pharmacy compounding.

## Common stacking patterns

- Age management — older patient (65+): Sermorelin 500 mcg–1 mg QHS + BPC-157 250 mcg/day if joint issues + GHK-Cu 1–2 mg 3×/wk for skin/connective tissue + adequate protein + resistance training 2-3×/wk

- Body composition — middle-aged: CJC-1295/Ipamorelin 200/200 QHS, 5 days/wk + adequate protein 1.2–1.6 g/kg + resistance training 3×/wk + BHRT optimized + cycle 6 weeks on / 6 weeks off

- Athletic recovery from injury: CJC-1295/Ipamorelin 200/200 QHS + BPC-157 500 mcg/day SQ regional + TB-500 2.5 mg 2×/wk + collagen peptides 20 g/day + adequate protein

- Visceral fat / NAFLD: Tesamorelin 1 mg (women) or 2 mg (men) QHS × 6 months + GLP-1 if appropriate + omega-3 + vitamin E + dietary intervention + exercise + serial DEXA/CT for visceral fat

- Diabetic + visceral adiposity: Tesamorelin 1–2 mg QHS (better than CJC/Ipa for diabetics) + glucose monitoring + diabetic medication titration + dietary intervention

- Cognitive support — older adults: Tesamorelin 1 mg QHS (women) or 1–2 mg (men) + omega-3 + B-complex + Selank/Semax intranasal + cognitive training

- Muscle preservation during GLP-1 therapy: see Volume 6 (GLP/Metabolic) for full protocol — typically CJC/Ipa or Tesamorelin + protein 1.2–1.6 g/kg + resistance training + creatine 5 g/day + appropriate adjuncts

- Post-surgical recovery: Sermorelin or CJC/Ipa (depending on age) + BPC-157 SQ + adequate protein + early mobilization + sleep optimization

## Required adjunct supplements and lifestyle

- Adequate protein: 1.2–1.6 g/kg total body weight for muscle preservation/gain (NOT lean body mass — total weight is the better target for older and metabolic patients)

- Resistance training 3×/week minimum — synergistic with GH peptides for muscle and bone effects

- Empty stomach dosing — ≥2 hours post-meal, 3 hours preferred. NON-NEGOTIABLE.

- Adequate sleep — protect 7-9 hours; the 11 PM GH pulse requires deep sleep architecture

- Vitamin D₃ titrated to 60–80 ng/mL

- Omega-3 EPA/DHA 2-4 g/day

- Magnesium glycinate 300-600 mg/day (bone health, sleep)

- Zinc 30-50 mg/day (cofactor for GH receptor function)

- Optional: collagen peptides 20 g/day for connective tissue support

- Optional: creatine monohydrate 5 g/day for muscle preservation, especially during caloric restriction or GLP-1 therapy

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Allowing patients to eat within 2 hours of dosing — abolishes the GH pulse via somatostatin; the most common reason for 'no response'

- Pushing IGF-1 above 200 ng/mL — does not produce better outcomes, increases theoretical risks; discontinue dose escalation at this target

- Using single GH measurements for monitoring — clinically useless due to pulsatile secretion and short half-life; use IGF-1 only

- Choosing CJC/Ipa for diabetic patients with visceral adiposity — Tesamorelin has better metabolic profile; switch peptide rather than accept worse glycemic control

- Choosing CJC/Ipa for older fragile patients — Sermorelin's gentler profile is better tolerated; less fluid retention and joint stiffness

- Skipping body composition baseline (DEXA, CT, or InBody) — without baseline, response cannot be objectively documented

- Skipping cancer screening before starting — age-appropriate screening should be current before initiating GH peptide protocols

- Continuous daily dosing without cycling — leads to receptor desensitization and progressive loss of effect

- Forgetting protein requirement — GH/IGF-1 cannot drive muscle protein synthesis without amino acid substrate; without adequate protein, body composition effects are blunted

- Forgetting resistance training — GH peptides without exercise produce far less body composition change; always pair

- Not monitoring glucose closely in pre-diabetic or diabetic patients — A1c may rise 0.3–0.5 points especially in early months

- Untreated severe OSA before starting — GH affects soft tissue and airway, can worsen OSA; treat OSA first

- Using exogenous HGH instead of GH peptides without specific medical indication — HGH bypasses negative feedback, increases risks; peptides are safer for most age-management indications

## FDA Compounding Categories — current status note

*As of recent reviews, peptides referenced in this volume have varying FDA compounding category status:*

- Sermorelin — generally Category 1 (acceptable for 503A compounding)

- CJC-1295 and Ipamorelin — historically on Category 2 review; status actively under reconsideration with possible reclassification

- Tesamorelin — pharmaceutical version (Egrifta) FDA-approved; compounded version available with appropriate prescriber relationships

*Verify current FDA compounding category status with your sourcing pharmacy at time of prescription. The categorizations have been actively under review and changes are possible. Categories should not affect clinical decision-making but DO affect sourcing reliability and provider access. Always have backup peptides identified if access becomes restricted.*

Always coordinate with oncology for cancer history. Always screen for contraindications including severe OSA, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.*

# GLP / Metabolic Peptides — Category Overview

The GLP-1 class has fundamentally changed metabolic medicine. Patients who have failed every previous intervention — diet, exercise, behavioral therapy, bariatric surgery in some cases — achieve and maintain meaningful weight loss with GLP-1s. Type 2 diabetes is now treatable to remission in many cases. NAFLD is reversible. Cardiovascular outcomes improve. The question facing the modern functional medicine practitioner is not whether GLP-1s should be used, but how to use them while preserving muscle, bone, skin, and hair.

This volume covers the GLP-class metabolic peptides plus complementary mechanisms. Four peptides anchor this category in mechanistic order: Tirzepatide (GIP + GLP-1, the workhorse), Survodutide (GLP-1 + glucagon, hepatic-fat-targeted), Retatrutide (GIP + GLP-1 + glucagon, triple agonist heavyweight), and Cagrilintide (amylin analog, complementary mechanism class). Semaglutide is mentioned briefly but not extensively covered — tirzepatide produces superior weight outcomes (22% vs 15%) with comparable or better tolerance, making it the preferred choice for most patients. Retatrutide is for patients requiring maximum effect. Survodutide fills the mechanistic gap between tirzepatide and retatrutide and is best-in-class for MASH. Cagrilintide is the third major axis (amylin) — distinct receptor class that combines mechanistically with GLP-class agents without same-class additive toxicity (CagriSema is the prototype combination).

| **The semaglutide note** Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) was the first GLP-1 to achieve mass adoption and remains widely prescribed.
