# The Muscle Preservation Stack on GLP-1 Therapy

***The most clinically important content in this volume. This stack is not optional — it is the difference between weight loss and sarcopenic obesity.***

## The four-legged stool framework

Muscle preservation on GLP-1s requires four simultaneous interventions. Missing any leg compromises outcomes:

### Leg 1 — Foundations (always required, regardless of peptide additions)

- Adequate protein: 1.2–1.6 g/kg of TOTAL body weight (NOT lean mass) on tirzepatide; 1.4–1.8 g/kg total weight on retatrutide. RATIONALE: appetite suppression reduces total intake; protein percentage of intake must INCREASE to maintain absolute protein adequacy. Most patients on GLP-1s default to inadequate protein.

- Resistance training 3×/week MINIMUM. RATIONALE: muscle protein synthesis requires mechanical loading. Without resistance training, muscle protein synthesis cannot keep up with the catabolic pressure of caloric deficit. This is the most underappreciated requirement.

- Slow titration: don't escalate dose faster than clinically necessary. RATIONALE: rapid weight loss (>2 lb/week sustained) accelerates lean mass and skin/hair loss disproportionate to body fat reduction. Slower is better for body composition outcomes.

- Adequate sleep: 7–9 hours minimum. RATIONALE: GH pulse anchors at 11 PM during slow-wave sleep; muscle repair requires this physiology. Sleep-deprived patients have markedly worse muscle preservation.

- Hydration: 2–3 L/day minimum. RATIONALE: GLP-1 side effects produce volume depletion; muscle metabolism requires adequate hydration; counsel proactively.

### Leg 2 — Injectable peptides (the GH axis stack)

*Choose ONE of the following based on patient phenotype:*

- CJC-1295 + Ipamorelin (the standard choice): 100-200 mcg of each, QHS, 5 days/week. RATIONALE: GH pulse-driven IGF-1 elevation maintains muscle protein synthesis during caloric deficit. The middle-aged body composition workhorse. See Volume 5 for full details.

- Tesamorelin (preferred when visceral adiposity prominent or NAFLD present): 1 mg (women) or 1-2 mg (men) QHS. RATIONALE: stronger visceral fat reduction synergizes with GLP-1; better metabolic profile in diabetic patients. Particularly indicated when NAFLD present. See Volume 5 for full details.

- Sermorelin (when fragile patient or older age): 500 mcg–1 mg QHS. RATIONALE: gentler GH effect; better tolerated in fragile or older patients. Less potent than CJC/Ipa or Tesamorelin but adequate for many patients with mild GH decline.

*ADD if microvascular or connective tissue support needed:*

- BPC-157: 250–500 mcg/day SQ. RATIONALE: gut healing during GLP-1 GI adaptation; microvascular support; collagen synthesis support for skin during weight loss. See Volume 3 for full details.

- MOTS-c: 5–10 mg SQ 2-3×/week. RATIONALE: additional AMPK activation; mitochondrial flexibility; addresses GLP-1 plateau patterns. See Volume 1 for full details.

### Leg 3 — Oral options (cost-effective adjuncts)

- Creatine monohydrate: 5 g/day. RATIONALE: cellular ATP buffer; muscle protein synthesis; one of the most cost-effective and evidence-based ergogenic aids. Particularly important during caloric deficit. Take with water; no loading dose needed; safe long-term.

- Leucine 2–3 g/day OR HMB 1.5-3 g/day. RATIONALE: leucine is the trigger amino acid for mTOR-mediated muscle protein synthesis; HMB is a leucine metabolite with anti-catabolic effects. Take with meals.

- OS-01 (oral pan-AMPK activator from PD Labs) — see featured entry below.

- 5-Amino-1MQ (alternative AMPK approach): 50–100 mg/day. RATIONALE: NNMT inhibitor → boosts NAD⁺ availability and supports muscle preservation; alternative to OS-01 for patients seeking different mechanism.

- Methyl B-complex with biotin (5-10 mg biotin), methylcobalamin (1000-5000 mcg), methylfolate (1-5 mg). RATIONALE: B-complex supports both muscle metabolism AND prevents the predictable hair loss with rapid weight loss.

## OS-01 — Featured Adjunct for GLP-1 Patients

| **OS-01 quick stats** Identity: small molecule pan-AMPK activator (formal designation ATX-304); molecular weight 380.25 g/mol; molecular formula C16H11Cl2N3O2S. Available as oral capsule (PD Labs systemic) and topical creams (O1 Skin face, body, eye formulations). Dose: 100 mg/day oral (capsule); 4 weeks on / 2-3 weeks off cycling. Topical applied per product directions for skin applications. *Mental model: 'Exercise in a capsule' via AMPK stimulation. Mimics MOTS-c / MOD-C action through AMPK pathway. Bridges GLP-1 metabolic effects and muscle preservation.* |
| --- |

### What it is and why it matters for GLP-1 patients

OS-01 (also known as ATX-304) is a small molecule pan-AMPK activator — not technically a peptide, but classified clinically alongside the peptide library because of its complementary mechanism and use patterns. Developed primarily by O1 Skin (originally for skin senotherapeutic applications) and now available as a systemic oral capsule through PD Labs. The compound has been characterized as a 'small molecule made to stimulate AMPK' that produces effects analogous to MOTS-c and MOD-C — but with the practical advantage of oral delivery. For GLP-1 patients, OS-01 addresses the residual mitochondrial inflexibility and AMPK-mediated muscle protection that GLP-1 alone cannot fully achieve.

### Mechanism — why OS-01 + GLP-1 is synergistic

- Direct pan-AMPK activation. RATIONALE: AMPK is the cellular energy sensor; activation drives glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, autophagy, and mitochondrial biogenesis.

- GLP-1 agonists work PARTLY through AMPK phosphorylation in muscle (Wu et al. 2022 mechanistic data). RATIONALE: OS-01 directly activates the same downstream pathway, addressing the residual signaling that GLP-1 alone produces incompletely. The combination amplifies the muscle-protective AMPK signaling.

- Increases fatty acid metabolism and lipolysis in adipose tissue and liver. RATIONALE: addresses the hepatic component of metabolic disease that GLP-1 partially addresses; particularly beneficial in NAFLD.

- Increases energy expenditure in animal studies — supports continued weight loss when GLP-1 plateau occurs.

- Increases glucose uptake in skeletal and cardiac muscle — improves cellular energy balance.

- Improves microvascular perfusion in skeletal muscle. RATIONALE: muscle that is well-perfused at the capillary level performs better and recovers faster; OS-01's microvascular effect is one of the underappreciated advantages.

- Renal protection — particularly important in diabetic GLP-1 patients with elevated CKD risk.

- Decreased oxidative stress in tissues.

- Pain and inflammation reduction at the cellular level.

- Improves cardiovascular performance — increases stroke volume and exercise endurance in animal studies.

### Clinical use in GLP-1 patients

- Primary indication: muscle preservation during GLP-1-driven weight loss. Particularly important in patients who cannot yet exercise extensively due to severe obesity or deconditioning.

- Secondary indication: insulin resistance / T2DM support — additive to GLP-1 effects on glucose.

- Tertiary indication: NAFLD — synergistic hepatic effects.

- Bridge for non-exercising patients: 'exercise in a capsule' — provides AMPK signaling that exercise would normally provide, as a bridge while patients build capacity to exercise.

- Plateau-breaking: when GLP-1 weight loss stalls, OS-01 addition often restores progress.

### OS-01 dosing rationale

Oral 100 mg/day standard, cycled 4 weeks on / 2-3 weeks off. RATIONALE FOR CYCLING: continuous activation produces AMPK desensitization; the on-off cycling preserves long-term effectiveness. RATIONALE FOR DAILY DOSING: the AMPK pathway responds best to consistent stimulation rather than intermittent; daily dosing during the 'on' weeks. RATIONALE FOR ORAL ROUTE: OS-01 has good oral bioavailability (small molecule, stable to digestion); injection unnecessary. Cycling pattern can be adapted: some practitioners use 6 weeks on / 2 weeks off for more aggressive protocols, or 3 weeks on / 1 week off for more conservative use.

### OS-01 contraindications and considerations

- Pregnancy and lactation — limited data.

- Severe liver disease — although primarily protective at standard doses, severe hepatic dysfunction warrants caution.

- Caution combining with metformin — both AMPK activators; monitor for additive effects (generally favorable but worth tracking).

- Caution combining with high-dose corticosteroids — opposing mechanisms.

- No major drug interactions identified.

- Monitor: glucose/A1c (may improve), liver function, body composition during use. Most patients tolerate well; mild GI symptoms in first week of dosing are most common minor effect.

### OS-01 also has skin applications — cross-reference

OS-01 is also available as topical creams (O1 Skin face, body, eye) for skin rejuvenation and senotherapeutic applications. Topical OS-01 reduces wrinkles, improves skin elasticity, enhances hydration, reduces DNA methylation age, and targets senescent cells. These applications are detailed in Volume 11 (Skin and Hair Synthesis). The systemic oral and topical can be combined — particularly relevant for GLP-1 patients with skin laxity concerns. The skin laxity from rapid weight loss responds to combined topical OS-01 + adequate protein + GHK-Cu (peptide), with consistent use over 45-60+ days.

### Leg 4 — Topical adjuncts (for skin and tissue specifically)

- OS-01 topical cream (O1 Skin) — for skin laxity, post-weight-loss skin firmness. See Volume 11.

- GHK-Cu — collagen and ECM synthesis; both injectable (1-2 mg SQ 3×/week) and topical applications. See Volume 7 (Tissue Repair) for full details.

- Topical retinoids — supportive for skin remodeling during weight loss. Standard dermatology guidelines apply.

## Decision tree for muscle preservation stack

*Match the stack to the patient — but individualize every GLP-1 dose to the patient in front of you, not to the weight-loss goal. Start low (often 2.5 mg/week; many sensitive or smaller patients should start at 1 mg or lower), hold at the lowest effective dose, and escalate ONLY when a patient has achieved benefit and then plateaued. The FDA titration schedule reflects the clinical trials, not a mandate — most patients never need to climb it. Note also that true microdosing (~0.25–1.5 mg tirzepatide) is a distinct strategy aimed primarily at the anti-inflammatory / metabolic effect; patients may lose weight on it, but a 2.5 mg starting dose is NOT a microdose.*

- Active, otherwise-healthy patient, smaller goal (ages ~30-55, no major comorbidities): start the GLP-1 at the lowest effective dose for that patient (often 1–2.5 mg/week; some lower) + protein 1.2 g/kg + resistance training 3×/wk + creatine 5 g/day + B-complex. Add CJC/Ipa only if body composition stalls. Raise the GLP-1 dose only if benefit plateaus.

- Middle-aged, possible insulin resistance: same start-low, individualize principle for the GLP-1 + protein 1.2-1.4 g/kg + resistance training + CJC/Ipa OR Tesamorelin (depending on visceral adiposity) + creatine + OS-01 oral cycle 4/2 + B-complex. Raise the GLP-1 dose only if benefit plateaus — the stack, not a higher dose, is what protects tissue.

- Insulin resistance / NAFLD: start low and individualize the GLP-1 + protein 1.2-1.6 g/kg + resistance training + Tesamorelin (preferred for the NAFLD/hepatic indication) + OS-01 oral 100 mg/day cycle 4/2 + creatine + B-complex + omega-3. Note: Tesamorelin is added for the hepatic-fat indication — not as a reason to push the GLP-1 dose higher.

- SEVERE sarcopenia risk (older, fragile, currently can't exercise much): Conservative tirzepatide titration + protein 1.4-1.6 g/kg + Tesamorelin + OS-01 oral (the 'exercise in a capsule') + 5-Amino-1MQ + creatine + early light resistance training as tolerated + careful body composition monitoring.

- MAXIMUM weight loss (severe obesity, NAFLD with significant hepatic fat): Retatrutide + protein 1.4-1.8 g/kg + resistance training MANDATORY + Tesamorelin + OS-01 oral + creatine + B-complex + heart rate monitoring during titration.

- Skin/hair concerns prominent: ANY of above stacks + GHK-Cu peptide + OS-01 topical + adequate protein + slower weight loss rate + B-complex with biotin. See Volume 11 for full skin protocol.

## The slow weight loss principle

Core clinical principle: it is better to lose the weight slowly, so the body can better protect all of its tissues — bone, muscle, and skin. RATIONALE: skin remodels at a finite rate; bone density adapts at a finite rate; muscle protein synthesis maximizes at certain caloric and protein conditions. Weight loss faster than these biological rates produces predictable losses in muscle, bone, skin, and hair. Target: 1-2 lb per week MAXIMUM during active weight loss phase. This is achieved with restrained, individualized dosing and slow titration — holding at the lowest effective dose rather than climbing a schedule — not by microdosing per se. Counsel patients explicitly: 'The scale moving 2 lb/week with preserved muscle and bone is far better than 4 lb/week with sarcopenic obesity.'

### What it is

Tirzepatide is a 39-amino-acid synthetic peptide that simultaneously activates two incretin receptors: glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIP-R) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R). Originally developed by Eli Lilly and approved by the FDA in 2022 as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes and in 2023 as Zepbound for chronic weight management, tirzepatide is now widely available in compounded form referred to as GLP-T or 'GLP-tirzepatide.' It produces the strongest weight loss outcomes of any GLP-1-class agent currently available outside of triple agonists (retatrutide). The dual receptor activation produces synergistic effects: GLP-1 component drives appetite suppression, gastric emptying delay, insulin sensitivity, and satiety; GIP component adds enhanced insulin secretion in response to glucose, improved fat metabolism, and additional appetite effects through hypothalamic GIP receptors. Combined effect produces consistently 20-22% weight loss in trials at maximum dose — significantly more than semaglutide (~15%). For complex chronic illness practitioners, tirzepatide-class is increasingly the GLP-1 of choice over semaglutide.

### Mechanism of action

- Binds GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) and GIP receptor (GIP-R) — dual agonism is the defining mechanistic feature.

- GLP-1R effects: stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells, suppresses inappropriate glucagon secretion from α-cells, slows gastric emptying, increases satiety via hypothalamic GLP-1R, reduces food reward signaling in mesolimbic pathways.

- GIP-R effects: enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion (additive to GLP-1), promotes fat metabolism in adipose tissue, modulates hypothalamic appetite circuits through different mechanisms than GLP-1, may protect against GLP-1 receptor desensitization over time.

- RATIONALE FOR DUAL AGONISM SYNERGY: GLP-1 and GIP receptors are co-expressed on β-cells, hypothalamic neurons, and adipocytes. Combined activation produces supra-additive effects — the two pathways amplify each other rather than competing. This is the basis for tirzepatide's superior weight outcomes vs. semaglutide.

- Reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis — improves fasting glucose.

- Improves insulin sensitivity over weeks to months — partly direct, partly via fat mass reduction.

- Reduces hepatic fat content — strong NAFLD effect (some practitioners now prescribe tirzepatide specifically for NAFLD with metabolic component).

- Anti-inflammatory effects — reduces hs-CRP, IL-6 in trials; mechanism partly weight-loss mediated, partly direct.

- Cardiovascular protective effects in trials — reduced MACE in SURMOUNT-MMO and other endpoints.

- Modulates GLP-1 effects on the gut-brain axis — improves cognitive flexibility, reduces food noise, and produces neuroprotective effects in animal models (relevant to the emerging cognitive applications).

- Suppresses MSTN (myostatin) and muscle atrophic factors via GLP-1R-AMPK signaling — actually somewhat protective of muscle when adequate protein and resistance training are provided. Without those supports, the catabolic effect of caloric restriction dominates and lean mass is lost.

### Clinical indications

- Type 2 diabetes mellitus — particularly with obesity component

- Chronic weight management in BMI ≥30, or BMI ≥27 with weight-related comorbidity

- Metabolic syndrome with visceral adiposity

- Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and metabolic-associated steatohepatitis (MASH)

- Cardiovascular risk reduction in T2DM and obesity

- Pre-diabetes with elevated HbA1c and weight component

- PCOS with insulin resistance and weight component

- Sleep apnea improvement (weight-mediated)

- Obesity-related joint disease (weight-mediated reduction)

- Chronic diarrhea (off-label — emerging use; GLP-1s have been observed to improve chronic functional diarrhea in some patients)

- ALS adjunct (research stage — misfolded protein clearance; emerging mechanistic interest)

- Severe binge eating disorder (off-label, food-noise reduction)

- Adjunct in some chronic inflammatory states with metabolic component

### Dosing rationale & timing

The FDA-approved Mounjaro/Zepbound label schedule is: start 2.5 mg/week × 4 weeks → 5 mg/week × 4 weeks → 7.5 mg/week × 4 weeks → 10 mg/week × 4 weeks → 12.5 mg/week × 4 weeks → 15 mg/week ongoing as tolerated. Understand this for what it is: the fixed-step protocol used in the registration trials — it jumps 2.5 mg every 4 weeks, which is a relatively aggressive escalation, NOT a gentle or individualized approach. It is a reference point, not a mandate. RATIONALE FOR INDIVIDUALIZED TITRATION (how this is actually done in complex-patient practice): start low and increase in small increments — typically 0.5–1 mg at a time — and only when clinically warranted (benefit achieved, then a true plateau, with confounders addressed). Many complex or sensitive patients never approach the label's step sizes or its ceiling. Some practitioners also split the weekly dose into smaller twice-weekly dosing to smooth tolerability and steady levels. The goal is the lowest effective dose for that patient, reached gently — not adherence to a trial schedule. RATIONALE FOR GOING SLOWLY: GI side effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation) are dose-related; small increments and unhurried timing minimize them, protect adherence, and slow fat-loss velocity to preserve lean mass, bone, and skin. RATIONALE FOR LOW-DOSE / MICRODOSE USE: dosing below the standard 2.5 mg start falls into two bands with different intents. True microdosing (~0.25–1.5 mg/week) is aimed primarily at the metabolic and anti-inflammatory benefit — patients may also lose some weight, but that is not its purpose. Low-dose use (~1.5–2.5 mg/week) suits patients with milder weight-loss goals or insulin resistance without obesity, preserving metabolic and anti-inflammatory benefit while minimizing catabolic effects on muscle, bone, and skin. Note that 2.5 mg is the standard STARTING dose, not a microdose. These lower-dose strategies are increasingly preferred where preservation of muscle and skin is paramount. RATIONALE FOR WEEKLY DOSING: tirzepatide has a half-life of approximately 5 days; weekly dosing produces sustained therapeutic levels with stable receptor occupancy (some practitioners divide this into smaller twice-weekly doses for smoother tolerability). RATIONALE FOR DOSE PLATEAU: many patients reach effective weight loss at lower doses and never need to climb the schedule. 15 mg is the studied maximum, not a target. When a patient plateaus, do NOT reflexively increase the dose — first investigate why: adherence, protein intake and resistance training, sleep, thyroid and other endocrine confounders, alcohol, medications, and whether weight loss has simply reached an appropriate set point. Only after benefit was achieved and genuine plateau is confirmed — with confounders addressed — consider a measured dose increase of 0.5–1 mg. Individualize; higher is not automatically better and increases side-effect risk. RECONSTITUTION VARIES BY VIAL SIZE: 10 mg/1 mL = 10 mg/mL (10 mg = 100 units, 5 mg = 50 units, 2.5 mg = 25 units); 30 mg/3 mL = 10 mg/mL (same calculations); 50 mg/3 mL = 16.67 mg/mL (5 mg = 30 units, 10 mg = 60 units); 60 mg/3 mL = 20 mg/mL (5 mg = 25 units, 10 mg = 50 units). The 60 mg/3 mL provides the most efficient dosing for weekly maintenance.

### Evidence base

Strongest evidence base of any GLP-1-class agent. SURMOUNT-1 trial: 22.5% weight loss at 15 mg vs. 2.4% placebo over 72 weeks. SURPASS series: superior A1c and weight outcomes vs. semaglutide. SURMOUNT-MMO: cardiovascular event reduction. Pharmaceutical version FDA-approved with comprehensive safety database. Compounded tirzepatide has become widely available since 2023 due to drug shortages and patient access concerns. Mechanism is well-validated at receptor and downstream signaling levels. Long-term safety data (5+ years) accumulating; appears favorable. Cardiovascular outcome trials ongoing.

### Contraindications

- Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). RATIONALE: GLP-1 agonists cause thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents; relevance to humans is debated but precaution maintained. MTC is rare but the precaution is absolute.

- Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN-2). RATIONALE: increased baseline MTC risk.

- Active pancreatitis or recent (within 6 months) pancreatitis. RATIONALE: GLP-1 agonists have been associated with pancreatitis; the mechanism may relate to GLP-1's effects on pancreatic acinar cells.

- Severe gastroparesis. RATIONALE: tirzepatide significantly delays gastric emptying — in patients with pre-existing severe gastroparesis, this can produce intractable symptoms or bezoar formation.

- Pregnancy and lactation. RATIONALE: animal data shows effects on fetal weight; insufficient human data.

- Severe hypoglycemia history with insulin use. RATIONALE: GLP-1 agonists potentiate insulin's hypoglycemic effect; requires insulin dose reduction.

- Severe diabetic retinopathy with recent rapid glucose change. RATIONALE: rapid normalization of glucose can transiently worsen retinopathy.

- Known hypersensitivity to tirzepatide or other GLP-1 agonists.

- Severe psychiatric history with food-related issues — relative; coordinate with mental health if anorexia history.

### Drug interactions

Pharmacodynamic considerations: insulin and sulfonylureas — additive hypoglycemic effect; reduce dose of these by 30-50% when starting GLP-1 to prevent hypoglycemia. Other diabetes medications (metformin, SGLT2i, DPP-4i) — generally compatible and synergistic. Oral contraceptives — delayed gastric emptying may reduce absorption; use additional contraception or prefer non-oral forms. Warfarin — monitor INR more frequently as appetite and absorption changes can affect levels. Thyroid medication (levothyroxine) — delayed gastric emptying may delay absorption; take 4 hours before tirzepatide dose; monitor TSH. PPIs and H2 blockers — no significant interaction. Most antibiotics — generally compatible. Compatible with most peptides — pairs especially well with CJC/Ipa, Tesamorelin, OS-01, MOTS-c, BPC-157 (see muscle preservation section). No CYP450 interactions. Caution with anticoagulants — appetite changes may affect absorption.

### Baseline labs & monitoring

- Baseline: comprehensive metabolic panel, HbA1c, fasting insulin, fasting glucose, lipid panel, ALT/AST/GGT (liver function), TSH, lipase + amylase, vitamin D, B12, ferritin, comprehensive nutritional status.

- Body composition baseline: DEXA scan or InBody analysis (lean mass, fat mass, visceral adiposity, bone density). RATIONALE: tracking body composition rather than scale weight reveals lean mass loss and informs muscle preservation strategy.

- Cardiovascular: blood pressure, optional echo in cardiac risk patients.

- Cancer screening per age-appropriate guidelines.

- Mid-titration (every 4 weeks during dose escalation): symptom check (especially GI), pulse rate, BP, side effect tolerance.

- 3-month mark: HbA1c, fasting glucose, weight, body composition, lipid panel, ALT/AST/GGT, repeat lipase if any GI symptoms.

- 6-month mark: full metabolic panel, body composition (repeat DEXA), assess muscle/bone/skin/hair status, vitamin/mineral status (B12, iron, calcium, magnesium, zinc, selenium), screen for nutritional deficiencies.

- Annually: cardiovascular assessment, full metabolic panel, body composition, age-appropriate cancer screening.

- RATIONALE FOR REGULAR BODY COMPOSITION MONITORING: scale weight loss conceals lean mass loss. Patients losing 30 lb may be losing 7-12 lb of muscle without intervention. DEXA tracking allows early detection and protocol adjustment.

- RATIONALE FOR MICRONUTRIENT MONITORING: appetite suppression and reduced food intake leads to predictable deficiencies (B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D) over months. Monitor and supplement preventively.

### Side effects

*Common (mild, dose-limiting only if severe):*

- Nausea (most common; especially during titration; usually decreases over weeks at stable dose).

- Vomiting — typically mild but can be severe; reduce dose if interferes with hydration/nutrition.

- Diarrhea or constipation — varies by patient.

- Decreased appetite — primary intended effect, but counsel patients on adequate protein intake.

- Indigestion, eructation, abdominal pain.

- Injection site reactions.

- Fatigue (especially during initial titration).

- Dysgeusia (altered taste — common, often distinctive).

- Hair loss (telogen effluvium; predictable with rapid weight loss, largely reversible and self-limited once the trigger is corrected — roughly 95% recover within 2–3 months of correcting the stressor). The signal is strongest with the once-weekly agents (semaglutide, tirzepatide); the mechanism is mostly indirect — rapid weight loss and the nutrient shortfalls it drives — rather than direct drug toxicity. When it appears, check: ferritin (target >70 ng/mL; note a normal CBC/hemoglobin can still hide low ferritin, so screen ferritin specifically), zinc, vitamin D (target ~50–60 ng/mL), thyroid (TSH, free T3), protein intake (1.2–1.6 g/kg), B12/folate, biotin, selenium, and the rate of weight loss itself. Manage by correcting the deficiencies found, ensuring adequate protein, slowing the weight-loss rate, and B-complex with biotin. Adjunct where ferritin stays low despite iron: L-lysine 1–1.5 g/day added to iron has been shown to raise ferritin better than iron alone. Reassure patients — this is usually temporary.

- Skin laxity / loose skin (predictable with rapid weight loss; see muscle preservation section).

*Serious (stop and reassess):*

- Pancreatitis — uncommon but documented. RATIONALE: GLP-1 effects on pancreatic acinar cells may potentiate pancreatic stress; persistent abdominal pain, especially radiating to back, requires evaluation. Discontinue if confirmed.

- Severe gastroparesis or intractable nausea/vomiting — may require permanent discontinuation in some patients.

- Acute kidney injury from severe dehydration — RATIONALE: severe vomiting/diarrhea can cause volume depletion; ensure adequate hydration during titration.

- Cholelithiasis / cholecystitis — rapid weight loss is a known risk factor for gallstones; monitor for symptoms.

- Hypoglycemia (when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas) — preventable with proactive medication adjustment.

- Severe hair loss / sarcopenic malnutrition — addressable with intervention but indicates the muscle preservation stack was not implemented.

- Diabetic retinopathy worsening with rapid glucose normalization (rare).

- Anaphylaxis (rare; any peptide).

- Suicidal ideation — recent FDA warning consideration; rare but monitor mood.

### Stacking & synergy

Tirzepatide-class is the cornerstone of metabolic medicine and pairs with multiple peptide categories. Pairs especially well with: (1) CJC-1295 + Ipamorelin OR Tesamorelin — for muscle preservation during weight loss (see dedicated section); (2) BPC-157 — gut healing during GI adaptation, microvascular support; (3) OS-01 (oral pan-AMPK activator) — synergistic AMPK activation, muscle preservation, NAFLD support, microvascular perfusion. RATIONALE FOR OS-01 SYNERGY: GLP-1 agonists work partly through AMPK phosphorylation in muscle (Wu et al. 2022 mechanistic data); OS-01 is a direct AMPK activator that adds to this signaling at the muscle level — addresses the residual muscle catabolism that GLP-1 alone produces; (4) MOTS-c — additional mitochondrial AMPK activation for stuck weight loss; (5) Cagrilintide — amylin analog; further appetite control, often used in combination protocols; (6) Adequate protein (1.2–1.6 g/kg total weight); (7) Resistance training 3×/week minimum; (8) Comprehensive multivitamin/mineral; (9) Creatine 5 g/day for muscle preservation; (10) Methyl B-complex; (11) For NAFLD: vitamin E 800 IU/day, omega-3 EPA/DHA 2-4 g/day. AVOID stacking concerns: avoid in active pancreatitis or pancreatitis history; coordinate insulin/sulfonylurea doses to prevent hypoglycemia; avoid in severe gastroparesis.

### Clinical pearls

- Tirzepatide-class is the GLP-1 of choice over semaglutide in most current functional medicine practice. RATIONALE: superior weight outcomes (22% vs 15%), better metabolic profile, often better tolerated. Semaglutide remains useful in some specific contexts but tirzepatide produces better outcomes in most patients.

- Low-dose and microdose strategies are a quiet advantage. RATIONALE: many practitioners now use sub-standard doses for patients with metabolic dysfunction without severe obesity — true microdosing (~0.25–1.5 mg/week) primarily for the metabolic and anti-inflammatory effect, and low-dose (~1.5–2.5 mg/week) for milder weight goals. Both preserve metabolic and anti-inflammatory benefit, minimize catabolic effects on muscle/bone/skin, and improve long-term tolerance. Counsel patients that 'less may be enough' — especially where muscle/skin preservation is a priority. Remember: 2.5 mg is the standard starting dose, not a microdose.

- Going slowly produces better long-term outcomes. RATIONALE: rapid escalation produces severe GI symptoms that hurt tolerability and adherence. Small, unhurried increments (0.5–1 mg at a time, with several weeks to assess each step) keep patients comfortable and let you find the lowest dose that delivers benefit — the goal is the right dose for that patient, not a higher one.

- Body composition monitoring is essential — not optional. RATIONALE: scale weight conceals lean mass loss. A patient losing 30 lb of total weight may have lost 8-12 lb of muscle without intervention. DEXA every 6 months at minimum reveals this and allows protocol adjustment. The scale alone produces sarcopenic obesity — metabolically worse outcomes hidden by the scale.

- The MUSCLE PRESERVATION STACK is non-negotiable for any patient on GLP-1s. See dedicated section in this volume. The four-legged stool: protein + resistance training + GH peptides (CJC/Ipa or Tesamorelin) + AMPK support (OS-01 oral or MOTS-c).

- Patients on tirzepatide need MORE protein, not less. Counsel: 1.2–1.6 g/kg of TOTAL body weight (NOT lean mass). RATIONALE: appetite suppression reduces total intake; the percentage of intake that is protein must increase to maintain absolute protein adequacy. Patients who 'eat what they feel like' on GLP-1s typically eat far too little protein.

- GLP-1s actually have anti-myostatin effects via GLP-1R-AMPK signaling. RATIONALE: Wu et al. 2022 and Fan et al. 2023 demonstrated that GLP-1 agonists suppress MSTN and atrophic factors AND enhance myogenic factors. The catabolic effect is from caloric restriction, not GLP-1 itself. With proper protein and resistance training, GLP-1s can actually be muscle-protective.

- OS-01 oral capsule is the perfect AMPK adjunct for tirzepatide patients. RATIONALE: GLP-1s work partly through AMPK; OS-01 is a direct pan-AMPK activator. The combination addresses muscle preservation, microvascular perfusion in skeletal muscle, renal protection, insulin resistance, and NAFLD from complementary angles. PD Labs sources the systemic oral. Cycle 4 weeks on / 2-3 weeks off.

- Hair loss is predictable with rapid weight loss but is reversible. RATIONALE: telogen effluvium (stress-induced hair shedding) follows any rapid weight loss. Prevention: slower weight loss rate, adequate protein, B-complex with biotin, vitamin D, zinc, ferritin >70 ng/mL. Reassure patients that hair regrows within 6-12 months with adequate nutrition.

- Skin laxity is partly preventable with proper rate and adjuncts. RATIONALE: skin remodels at a finite rate; weight loss faster than skin remodeling produces laxity. Prevention: slower weight loss rate (1–2 lb/week target rather than maximum), adequate protein (collagen synthesis substrate), GHK-Cu peptide, OS-01 topical cream, hydration. See Volume 11 for full skin protocols.

- NAFLD is an increasingly important indication. RATIONALE: tirzepatide reduces hepatic fat content significantly; for patients with metabolic syndrome + NAFLD + visceral adiposity, this is among the most powerful single interventions available. Coordinate with hepatology if cirrhosis is present.

- Patients describing 'food noise reduction' or 'I can think about other things' are reporting a real neurological effect. RATIONALE: GLP-1Rs in mesolimbic reward pathways modulate food reward signaling. This is one of the most appreciated subjective effects.

- Hydration is critical during titration. RATIONALE: vomiting and diarrhea risk volume depletion; combined with reduced appetite/intake, dehydration can produce kidney injury. Counsel: 'When in doubt, drink water and electrolytes.'

- If a patient develops persistent severe nausea at any dose, drop back one level. RATIONALE: pushing through severe nausea produces malnutrition, dehydration, gallstones, and adherence failure. Slower is better.

- Don't combine tirzepatide initiation with multiple new peptides simultaneously. RATIONALE: GLP-1 side effects are common enough that adding new peptides at the same time confounds tolerance assessment. Establish tirzepatide stability for 2-3 months, then layer adjunct peptides systematically.

- Cancer screening should be current before starting. RATIONALE: while no causal cancer effect is established, GLP-1s have been associated with thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents and are contraindicated in MTC. Age-appropriate screening (mammogram, colonoscopy, PSA, skin exam, dermatology, thyroid ultrasound if neck symptoms) is appropriate.

- Pre-diabetic and metabolic syndrome patients without obesity benefit from microdose tirzepatide. RATIONALE: insulin sensitization, glucose normalization, and inflammation reduction occur at sub-weight-loss doses. The clinical phenotype is a thinner-but-insulin-resistant patient, often metabolically inflexible despite normal BMI.

- Reconstitution dose math must be confirmed by vial size — they vary significantly. The 60 mg/3 mL = 20 mg/mL = 5 mg/25 units is the most common in current compounded use. Always double-check the vial concentration before dosing.

### What it is

Survodutide (BI 456906) is a dual GLP-1 receptor / glucagon receptor agonist developed jointly by Boehringer Ingelheim and Zealand Pharma. Mechanistically, Survodutide sits between Tirzepatide (GIP/GLP-1) and Retatrutide (GIP/GLP-1/glucagon) — it adds glucagon receptor agonism to GLP-1 agonism but does NOT include GIP receptor activation. This dual-agonist design produces a distinctive metabolic profile: GLP-1 provides glucose-dependent insulin secretion, satiety, and gastric emptying delay; glucagon provides lipolysis, energy expenditure increase, and fatty acid oxidation in the liver. The net effect is robust weight loss with particular efficacy in hepatic fat reduction — making Survodutide a leading candidate for MASH/NAFLD indications. Phase 2 obesity trials demonstrated 19% weight loss at 48 weeks at the 4.8 mg weekly dose. The 2024 Phase 2 MASH data was striking: 83% of patients on the highest dose achieved MASH resolution with no worsening of fibrosis, and fibrosis improvement was significant. Phase 3 trials (SYNCHRONIZE-1 for MASH; SYNCHRONIZE-2 for obesity; further trials for cirrhosis) are ongoing. In compounded functional medicine practice, Survodutide is used for patients who want stronger effects than tirzepatide but where retatrutide's triple agonism is unnecessarily aggressive — particularly patients with prominent NAFLD/MASH features or those who don't tolerate retatrutide's intensity.

### Mechanism of action

- GLP-1 receptor agonism — same mechanism as semaglutide, tirzepatide, retatrutide. Produces glucose-dependent insulin secretion, postprandial glucagon suppression (paradoxically — this is the GLP-1 effect on alpha cells), satiety via hypothalamic centers, and delayed gastric emptying. RATIONALE: provides the foundational metabolic effects of all GLP-class drugs.

- Glucagon receptor agonism — the differentiating mechanism. RATIONALE: glucagon receptor activation in the liver drives gluconeogenesis (countered by GLP-1's glucose-lowering effect, producing net glucose-lowering), but more importantly drives hepatic lipolysis and fatty acid β-oxidation. This is the mechanism behind Survodutide's pronounced hepatic fat reduction.

- Glucagon also increases energy expenditure peripherally — supports weight loss beyond the appetite-suppression mechanism of GLP-1 alone.

- NO GIP receptor agonism — distinguishes Survodutide from Tirzepatide. RATIONALE: practitioners who avoid GIP agonism (because of theoretical concerns about adipogenesis or because of patient response patterns) prefer Survodutide. The clinical relevance of this distinction is debated.

- Net effect on hepatic fat: substantial reduction. RATIONALE: dual agonism on GLP-1 (reducing de novo lipogenesis) and glucagon (driving fatty acid oxidation) produces complementary mechanisms for hepatic fat clearance. Phase 2 MASH data (2024): 83% MASH resolution at high dose.

- Net effect on body weight: 19% weight loss at 48 weeks (Phase 2, 4.8 mg weekly). Comparable to tirzepatide; less than retatrutide.

- Net effect on glucose: glucose-lowering despite glucagon component. RATIONALE: GLP-1's glucose-lowering effect dominates over glucagon's gluconeogenic effect in the net balance, particularly when β-cells respond appropriately to GLP-1 stimulation.

- Half-life supports weekly dosing (~5-7 days).

- Activates hepatic AMPK signaling indirectly through glucagon receptor — supports muscle-preserving effects similar to other GLP-class agents.

### Clinical indications

- Obesity (BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with weight-related comorbidity)

- Type 2 diabetes mellitus (off-label, not FDA-approved)

- Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) — strongest emerging indication

- Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/MASLD)

- Metabolic syndrome with hepatic component

- Patients on tirzepatide who plateau and need additional mechanism (switch to Survodutide for glucagon component)

- Patients seeking stronger weight loss than tirzepatide but unable to tolerate retatrutide's intensity

- Visceral adipose-predominant obesity

- Diabetic dyslipidemia with hepatic steatosis

- Compensated MASH cirrhosis (under specialist coordination)

### Dosing rationale & timing

Standard titration mirrors GLP-class titration patterns to manage GI side effects. RATIONALE FOR SLOW TITRATION: glucagon component adds intensity beyond pure GLP-1 effects; faster titration produces more nausea, more decreased appetite, and more potential for excessive metabolic shift. Standard pattern: 0.6 mg/week × 4 weeks → 1.2 mg × 4 weeks → 2.4 mg × 4 weeks → 3.6 mg → 4.8 mg target maintenance. Total titration ~16-20 weeks to maximum dose. RATIONALE FOR 4.8 MG TARGET: Phase 2 trial maximum dose; produces ~19% weight loss; further dose increases were not extensively studied. Some clinical protocols target 3.6 mg as adequate maintenance for many patients. RATIONALE FOR WEEKLY DOSING: half-life supports once-weekly administration with stable steady-state. RATIONALE FOR SQ ROUTE: peptide stability requires injection; SQ provides reliable absorption with patient self-administration. RATIONALE FOR LOWER DOSES IN MASH-PRIMARY: some practitioners use Survodutide 1.2-2.4 mg weekly when the goal is hepatic fat reduction without aggressive weight loss — leverages the dual agonism for liver effects while moderating systemic intensity. RECONSTITUTION: 6 mg/mL = 60 mcg per unit; 600 mcg = 10 units, 1.2 mg = 20 units, 2.4 mg = 40 units, 3.6 mg = 60 units, 4.8 mg = 80 units. Refrigerate; stability per pharmacy.

### Evidence base

Phase 2 obesity trials demonstrated 19% weight loss at 48 weeks at 4.8 mg weekly (Le Roux et al., Lancet 2024). Phase 2 MASH trials (Sanyal et al., NEJM 2024) demonstrated 83% MASH resolution at the highest dose with significant fibrosis improvement — best-in-class data for an investigational MASH drug. Phase 3 trials in progress: SYNCHRONIZE-1 (MASH, expected readout 2026), SYNCHRONIZE-2 (obesity), SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT (cardiovascular outcomes), and trials in compensated cirrhosis. Mechanism studies establish the dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonism and the hepatic fat-reduction pathway through glucagon-driven β-oxidation. - Pregnancy and lactation. Discontinue ≥2 months before planned conception (prolonged half-life and limited fetal safety data).

- Active malignancy under treatment — coordinate with oncology.

- Severe hepatic decompensation (decompensated cirrhosis).

- Severe renal disease (eGFR <30) — limited data; coordinate with nephrology.

- Active gallbladder disease. RATIONALE: GLP-class agents increase cholelithiasis risk.

- Diabetic retinopathy with rapid HbA1c reduction risk.

- Active suicidal ideation — emerging psychiatric class concern.

### What it is

Retatrutide is a 39-amino-acid synthetic peptide that simultaneously activates THREE incretin receptors: GLP-1 receptor, GIP receptor, AND glucagon receptor. The triple agonism makes retatrutide a fundamentally different metabolic agent than dual agonists like tirzepatide. The glucagon component — counterintuitively, since glucagon raises blood sugar — drives hepatic fat oxidation, increases energy expenditure, and produces stronger fat loss effects than GLP-1/GIP alone. Phase 2 trials demonstrated 24% body weight reduction over 48 weeks at 12 mg/week — exceeding any other anti-obesity agent currently available. Eli Lilly's Phase 3 trials are ongoing. Compounded retatrutide is becoming available through research peptide channels for off-label use; this is currently the most aggressive metabolic peptide available outside formal pharmaceutical development. The triple mechanism produces stronger outcomes but also more pronounced side effects and more careful patient selection.

### Mechanism of action

- Triple receptor agonism: GLP-1R + GIP-R + glucagon receptor (GCGR).

- GLP-1R effects: same as tirzepatide — appetite suppression, gastric emptying delay, satiety, insulin sensitivity.

- GIP-R effects: same as tirzepatide — enhanced glucose-dependent insulin secretion, fat metabolism modulation.

- Glucagon receptor effects: stimulates hepatic glucose production AND hepatic fatty acid oxidation; increases energy expenditure (basal metabolic rate); decreases hepatic fat content directly through fatty acid oxidation.

- RATIONALE FOR GLUCAGON COMPONENT: glucagon at the receptor level promotes catabolism — hepatic glycogenolysis, fatty acid oxidation, increased energy expenditure. The classical concern (hyperglycemia from glucagon) is offset by the dominant GLP-1 and GIP-mediated insulin secretion. Net effect: similar or improved glucose control with significantly enhanced fat loss.

- Net effect: stronger weight loss than any dual agonist; superior NAFLD effects (direct hepatic fat oxidation via glucagon); enhanced metabolic flexibility.

- Increases basal metabolic rate by ~6-8% — meaningful contribution to weight loss beyond appetite suppression alone.

- Strong NAFLD/MASH effects via direct hepatic fatty acid oxidation.

- Anti-inflammatory effects (similar to tirzepatide).

- Cardiovascular protective effects in early trials.

### Clinical indications

- Severe obesity (BMI ≥35) where maximum weight loss is the goal

- Type 2 diabetes with severe obesity

- NAFLD/MASH — particularly with significant hepatic fat content

- Patients who have plateaued on tirzepatide and need additional intervention

- Severe metabolic syndrome with visceral adiposity

- Patients seeking maximum weight loss outcomes (with appropriate counseling)

- Sleep apnea improvement (weight-mediated)

- Some refractory T2DM cases

### Dosing rationale & timing

RATIONALE FOR DOSE CAP AT 12 MG: Phase 2 trials showed plateau in efficacy beyond 12 mg/week with continued increase in side effects. RATIONALE FOR WEEKLY DOSING: similar to tirzepatide; half-life supports weekly stable receptor occupancy. RATIONALE FOR MICRODOSING: emerging clinical practice — some practitioners use 1–2 mg/week for patients with severe metabolic dysfunction without severe obesity; this preserves the metabolic benefits while minimizing the catabolic effects. RECONSTITUTION: 12 mg / 1.2 mL = 10 mg/mL = 100 mcg per unit. So 2 mg = 20 units, 6 mg = 60 units, 12 mg = 120 units. The concentrated formulation allows easy unit-based dosing.

### What it is

Cagrilintide (NN9838) is a long-acting amylin analog developed by Novo Nordisk. Mechanistically, Cagrilintide represents a fundamentally DIFFERENT receptor class from the GLP-1 / GIP / glucagon class drugs — it acts on amylin receptors (AMY1, AMY2, AMY3 — calcitonin receptor + RAMP complex). Amylin is a 37-amino-acid peptide co-secreted with insulin from pancreatic β-cells. The endogenous amylin axis is the third major incretin-related pathway alongside GLP-1 and GIP, but it has been pharmaceutically underdeveloped until recently. The short-acting amylin analog Pramlintide (Symlin) was FDA-approved in 2005 for T1DM and T2DM but failed to achieve mass adoption due to thrice-daily dosing and modest effects. Cagrilintide solves the half-life problem with weekly dosing and produces more substantial weight loss — particularly when combined with GLP-1. The CagriSema combination (cagrilintide + semaglutide) is the lead Novo Nordisk obesity program; REDEFINE-1 (Phase 3, 2024) demonstrated 22.7% weight loss at 68 weeks, comparable to tirzepatide. Cagrilintide as monotherapy produces 10-15% weight loss in trials. In compounded functional medicine practice, Cagrilintide is used either as monotherapy for amylin-mechanism-preferred patients, or as add-on to GLP-1 for stalled weight loss or maximum effect. The mechanism complementarity (amylin + GLP-1) means combination doesn't produce additive toxicity from same-class additivity.

### Mechanism of action

- Amylin receptor agonism (AMY1, AMY2, AMY3) — calcitonin receptor + RAMP complex. RATIONALE: amylin is the natural co-secreted partner of insulin; supplementing amylin signaling restores a physiological pathway deficient in obesity and T2DM.

- Delays gastric emptying — similar to GLP-1 but through different receptor mechanism. RATIONALE: produces postprandial satiety and reduces glucose excursion.

- Suppresses postprandial glucagon — important for glucose control. Distinct mechanism from GLP-1 effect on alpha cells.

- Increases satiety via central nervous system action — amylin receptors in the area postrema and hypothalamus signal meal termination. RATIONALE: distinct from GLP-1's hypothalamic satiety signaling; the two systems are additive.

- Reduces food intake centrally — animal data shows amylin is one of the most robust meal-termination signals in the brain.

- Modulates leptin signaling — amylin and leptin act synergistically on hypothalamic feeding centers. Improves leptin sensitivity in obesity-associated leptin resistance.

- Bone effects via calcitonin receptor cross-activity — amylin binds calcitonin receptor with reduced affinity; some bone-modulating effects.

- Half-life supports weekly dosing (~7-9 days) — major advantage over Pramlintide's short half-life.

- Net weight loss: 10-15% as monotherapy; 22.7% combined with semaglutide (CagriSema, REDEFINE-1 Phase 3).

- Net glucose effect: glucose-lowering through delayed gastric emptying + postprandial glucagon suppression.

- Distinct mechanism from GLP-class — does NOT produce GLP-class side effects through GLP-1 receptor; has its own side effect profile (typically less nausea, more taste/appetite changes).

### Clinical indications

- Obesity (BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with comorbidity) — monotherapy or combination

- Type 2 diabetes mellitus (off-label for cagrilintide; pramlintide is approved)

- GLP-1 plateau — addition of cagrilintide to existing GLP-1 to break stalled weight loss

- Patients who don't tolerate GLP-class drugs (severe GLP-1-related nausea, gastroparesis-spectrum) — amylin alternative

- Patients who prefer different mechanism class than GLP

- Maximum-effect weight loss protocols (CagriSema-equivalent combination)

- Insulin-using diabetics who need additional postprandial glucose control

- Patients with prominent leptin resistance pattern

### Dosing rationale & timing

Standard titration mirrors other peptide weight-loss agents. RATIONALE FOR SLOW TITRATION: amylin is a potent satiety signal; rapid increase produces excessive appetite suppression that can compromise nutrition. Standard pattern: 300 mcg/week × 4 weeks → 600 mcg × 4 weeks → 1.2 mg × 4 weeks → 2.4 mg × 4 weeks → 4.5 mg target. Total titration ~16-20 weeks. RATIONALE FOR 4.5 MG TARGET: trial maximum dose; produces ~10-15% weight loss as monotherapy. Some practitioners stop at 2.4 mg if response is adequate, particularly when combined with GLP-1. RATIONALE FOR WEEKLY DOSING: half-life supports weekly with stable steady-state. RATIONALE FOR SQ ROUTE: peptide stability requires injection. RATIONALE FOR COMBINATION DOSING WITH GLP-1: when adding cagrilintide to existing GLP-1, start cagrilintide low (300-600 mcg) and titrate slowly while maintaining current GLP-1 dose; mechanism complementarity produces additive weight loss without same-class toxicity. CagriSema standardized: cagrilintide 2.4 mg + semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly (REDEFINE-1 Phase 3 protocol). RECONSTITUTION: 10 mg / 2 mL = 5 mg/mL = 50 mcg per unit; 300 mcg = 6 units, 600 mcg = 12 units, 1.2 mg = 24 units, 2.4 mg = 48 units, 4.5 mg = 90 units.

### Evidence base

Phase 2 monotherapy trials demonstrated 10-15% weight loss at 26 weeks at 4.5 mg weekly. The CagriSema (cagrilintide + semaglutide) combination has stronger Phase 3 evidence: REDEFINE-1 (2024, n>3,400) showed 22.7% weight loss at 68 weeks — comparable to tirzepatide head-to-head. REDEFINE-2 in T2DM and REDEFINE-3 in cardiovascular outcomes are ongoing. Pramlintide (the short-acting amylin analog, FDA-approved 2005) provides decades of safety data for the amylin receptor class — modest weight effects (~3%) but well-characterized safety profile. Mechanism studies establish the amylin receptor pharmacology and the AMY1/AMY2/AMY3 receptor distinctions. The hypothalamic amylin signaling and area postrema satiety effects are well-documented in animal models.

- Hypersensitivity to amylin or any amylin analog.

- Type 1 diabetes mellitus — relative contraindication; coordinate with endocrinology if used (pramlintide IS approved for T1DM with insulin).

- Active gastroparesis. RATIONALE: amylin delays gastric emptying intrinsically.

- History of severe hypoglycemia (within 6 months) — particularly if on insulin.

- Severe renal disease — limited data.

Sulfonylureas — additive glucose-lowering. Other diabetes medications — generally compatible. GLP-1 receptor agonists — COMPLEMENTARY mechanism; combination is mechanistically valid and increasingly used; CagriSema is the prototype. Not 'stacking GLP-class' — amylin is a different receptor class. Oral medications — delayed gastric emptying may reduce absorption. Compatible with most peptides. No CYP450 interactions documented.

### Clinical pearls

- Cagrilintide is the third major axis in incretin-related obesity therapy — alongside GLP-1 and GIP. RATIONALE: amylin is mechanistically distinct from GLP-class; understanding this opens combination therapy possibilities without same-class additive toxicity.

- CagriSema is the obesity blockbuster of 2024-2025. RATIONALE: REDEFINE-1 Phase 3 showed 22.7% weight loss at 68 weeks — comparable to tirzepatide. Novo Nordisk's CagriSema is positioned to compete with tirzepatide and retatrutide.

- If patient has severe GLP-class intolerance, Cagrilintide monotherapy is a viable alternative for weight loss. RATIONALE: ~10-15% weight loss as monotherapy is meaningful clinically.

## Required adjunct supplements and lifestyle

- Adequate protein: 1.2–1.6 g/kg total weight (tirzepatide); 1.4–1.8 g/kg (retatrutide). Total weight, not lean mass.

- Resistance training 3×/week minimum — non-negotiable for muscle preservation.

- Creatine monohydrate 5 g/day.

- Adequate sleep 7-9 hours.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Treating GLP-1 therapy as a 'just give the shot' intervention — sarcopenic obesity is the predictable outcome without the muscle preservation stack

- Ignoring body composition tracking — scale weight conceals lean mass loss; DEXA every 6 months is essential

- Inadequate protein counseling — most GLP-1 patients eat 30-50% less protein than they need without explicit instruction

- Skipping resistance training — without mechanical loading, no peptide can preserve muscle adequately

- Rapid titration producing severe GI side effects and dropout — slower escalation produces better long-term outcomes

- Aggressive weight loss rate (>2 lb/week) — produces disproportionate skin laxity, hair loss, and lean mass loss

- Missing the OS-01 opportunity in patients who can't yet exercise — 'exercise in a capsule' bridges the gap

- Not adjusting insulin/sulfonylurea doses when starting — predictable hypoglycemia

- Forgetting micronutrient monitoring — predictable B12, iron, vitamin D, calcium deficiencies over months

- Initiating multiple new peptides simultaneously with GLP-1 — establish GLP-1 stability for 2-3 months first, then layer adjuncts

- Ignoring hair loss complaints — usually telogen effluvium with adequate nutrition, will reverse with intervention

- Treating skin laxity as inevitable — slower weight loss + protein + GHK-Cu + OS-01 topical can substantially prevent and address it

# Tissue Repair Peptides — Category Overview

Tissue repair is one of the most clinically valuable application areas for peptide medicine. The body's intrinsic repair capacity is finite — declining with age, blunted in chronic illness, overwhelmed by major injury. Peptides provide targeted amplification of repair signaling that can dramatically accelerate healing and improve outcomes.

Three peptides anchor this category. Each has a distinct mechanism but they overlap clinically — the right choice depends on the indication, the severity, and the comorbidities.

TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4) is the actin-sequestering and stem cell mobilizing peptide. Its primary value is in indications where cellular migration and stem cell recruitment matter most — tendon and ligament injury, cardiac repair, hair regrowth, and complex chronic wound healing. The Goldstein lab provenance (same researcher as Thymosin Alpha-1) gives it substantial scientific credibility.

GHK-Cu is the gene modulation and collagen synthesis peptide. With approximately 4,000+ genes modulated by GHK-Cu, it is one of the most epigenetically active small molecules known. Its primary clinical value is in skin (anti-aging, scarring, wounds), hair (regrowth via stem cell mobilization in the bulge region), and broader senotherapeutic effects. The Pickart lab continues to publish supporting research decades after the original discovery.

Wolverine is the combination of BPC-157 (covered in Volume 3) and TB-500 used together for major tissue injury. The complementary mechanisms (BPC-157 = angiogenesis + fibroblast activation; TB-500 = stem cell mobilization + actin remodeling) cover the full spectrum of tissue repair signaling. Reserved for major injury where individual peptides would be insufficient.

### What it is

TB-500 is a synthetic peptide fragment of Thymosin Beta-4 (Tβ4) — a 43-amino-acid endogenous polypeptide that is one of the most abundant cellular proteins in mammalian tissues. Tβ4 is found in particularly high concentrations in platelets, white blood cells, and wound fluid, where it functions as the primary intracellular actin-sequestering protein and a master regulator of tissue repair. The 'TB-500' designation refers to a specific 17-amino-acid fragment containing the active region of Tβ4, although in clinical compounded use the term is often applied to full-length Tβ4 as well — providers should verify with their compounding pharmacy which form is supplied. Tβ4 was originally characterized by Allan Goldstein's group at George Washington University (the same lab that developed Thymosin Alpha-1) and is one of the most extensively studied tissue repair peptides in the literature. RegeneRx Biopharmaceuticals has pursued formal pharmaceutical development of Tβ4 (RGN-259, RGN-352) for ophthalmic and cardiac applications. In functional medicine practice, TB-500 is a cornerstone of orthopedic, cardiovascular, and tissue repair protocols.

### Mechanism of action

- Sequesters G-actin (monomeric actin) in the cytoplasm — the foundational molecular function. RATIONALE FOR CLINICAL EFFECT: by regulating the G-actin/F-actin equilibrium, TB-500 controls cellular shape change, motility, and migration — all essential for tissue repair processes.

- ACE-mediated cleavage of TB-4 generates Ac-SDKP (N-acetyl-Ser-Asp-Lys-Pro) — the 4-amino-acid bioactive fragment responsible for the strongest anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects. RATIONALE: this is the 'pathway activation' that TB-4 dosing must achieve. Insufficient substrate concentration limits ACE-mediated conversion and dampens the clinical effect. The same ACE-SDKP pathway is partly why ACE inhibitors have anti-fibrotic effects beyond their blood pressure mechanism.

- SDKP fragment effects: blocks IκB phosphorylation → prevents NF-κB activation → suppresses TNF-α and IL-1β. Downregulates M1 macrophage phenotype while sparing M2. Reduces MMP-9 activation in injured tissues. Inhibits cardiac fibrosis, glomerulosclerosis, and intestinal/colonic fibrosis in animal models.

- Promotes cell migration via actin cytoskeleton remodeling — fibroblasts, endothelial cells, keratinocytes, and stem cells all migrate more effectively to injury sites in the presence of Tβ4.

- Strong angiogenic effects — upregulates VEGF and promotes new blood vessel formation in injured tissues. Mechanism complementary to BPC-157 but operates through different pathways.

- Recruits and mobilizes endogenous stem cells (cardiac progenitor cells, hair follicle stem cells, bone marrow-derived stem cells) to sites of injury. RATIONALE: this is one of the most clinically valuable mechanisms — TB-500 doesn't just repair tissue, it brings the body's own repair machinery to where it's needed.

- Anti-inflammatory effects via downregulation of NF-κB and inflammatory cytokines (mediated largely through SDKP fragment).

- Anti-fibrotic effects — reduces TGF-β1-mediated scarring in healing tissues. Particularly valuable in cardiac repair and post-surgical contexts.

- Antimicrobial peptide effect at higher concentrations — direct activity against several pathogens.

- Crosses tissue planes readily due to small size and water-soluble nature — distributes systemically and reaches injured tissues throughout the body, not just at injection site.

- Activates the PI3K/Akt pathway — promotes cell survival in damaged tissues.

- Modulates hair follicle stem cell migration from the bulge region — basis for hair regrowth applications.

- Cardioprotective effects — reduces infarct size and promotes cardiac progenitor cell mobilization in MI models.

- Corneal and ocular surface repair — basis for the dry eye disease and corneal injury applications.

### Clinical indications

- Tendon, ligament, and muscle injuries — partial tears, chronic tendinopathy, post-surgical repair

- Joint cartilage degeneration (adjunct to standard care)

- Frozen shoulder / adhesive capsulitis

- Plantar fasciitis (refractory)

- Achilles tendinopathy

- Post-surgical recovery (orthopedic, cardiac, abdominal, ENT)

- Cardiovascular tissue repair — post-MI recovery (with cardiology coordination)

- Chronic non-healing wounds — diabetic ulcers, venous stasis ulcers

- Hair regrowth (alopecia areata, androgenetic alopecia adjunct)

- Dry eye disease and corneal injuries (specialized formulations)

- Post-radiation tissue injury

- Burns recovery

- Inflammatory bowel disease (emerging — Tβ4 has anti-inflammatory and barrier repair effects)

- Equine and veterinary use is extensive — useful talking point for patient education

- Stroke recovery (research stage with promising data)

- Multiple sclerosis adjunct (research stage — neuroprotective effects)

### Dosing rationale & timing

TB-500 works through PULSED SATURATION, not linear dose accumulation. RATIONALE: 5 × 1 mg ≠ 1 × 5 mg in clinical effect. The peptide activates a THRESHOLD-DEPENDENT cascade — above threshold, the full repair program engages (actin polymerization, angiogenic sprouting, fibroblast recruitment, satellite cell stimulation, fibrosis reversal, cell motility); below threshold, only mild anti-inflammatory effects occur. Think of TB-500 like PRP, stem cell signaling, growth factor pulses, or shockwave therapy — it requires a big enough 'push' to activate the cascade, not a steady micro-dose drip. DOSE-RESPONSE CLINICAL TIERS: • 1 mg daily — DOES NOT reach threshold. No fibroblast recruitment, no angiogenic trigger, no actin pathway activation. Works only as maintenance anti-inflammatory and tissue circulation support. Most common dosing error in TB-500 use. • 2.5 mg SQ 2× weekly — STANDARD pulse for structural repair. Hits the biological threshold for fibroblast recruitment, starts actin remodeling, promotes angiogenic sprouting, stimulates satellite cells in muscle and tendon, engages SDKP-mediated anti-fibrotic effects. Standard for moderate orthopedic injury. • 5 mg SQ 2× weekly — MAXIMUM signaling wave. Reserved for major injuries, post-surgery, frozen shoulder/adhesive capsulitis, severe fascial damage, post-radiation tissue injury. Creates the strongest pulse for maximal healing cascade activation. MOLECULAR FOUNDATION FOR THRESHOLD BIOLOGY: TB-4 functions partially as a precursor — it must be cleaved by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) into its active 4-amino-acid fragment N-acetyl-Ser-Asp-Lys-Pro (Ac-SDKP). SDKP is the moiety responsible for the strongest anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects (NF-κB inhibition via blocked IκB phosphorylation, M1 macrophage downregulation, MMP-9 reduction). The pulse must be large enough to (1) reach cellular receptor activation thresholds AND (2) provide sufficient substrate for ACE-mediated SDKP generation. Daily 1 mg dosing fails on both counts. RATIONALE FOR PULSE TIMING (twice weekly): TB-500 has moderate half-life with persistent tissue distribution; once threshold is crossed, downstream cascades operate for 48-72 hours; twice-weekly pulsing maintains pulsatile activation without continuous receptor occupancy. Some practitioners use 3× weekly during initial loading for severe injury — acceptable but not necessary. RATIONALE FOR REGIONAL DOSING: for orthopedic targets, SQ near the injured tissue enhances local concentration AND local ACE-mediated SDKP generation. For knee injury inject quadriceps; shoulder, deltoid; back, paraspinal. For systemic indications (cardiac, multi-site, hair regrowth), abdominal SQ. RATIONALE FOR CYCLING: chronic continuous pulsing without breaks may eventually produce diminishing returns; 4-8 week courses with 4-8 week breaks are standard for chronic conditions. Acute injury courses may run 8-12 weeks continuous, then taper to weekly maintenance. RECONSTITUTION: 5 mg / 2 mL = 2.5 mg/mL = 25 mcg per unit; 2.5 mg = 100 units, 5 mg = 200 units. 10 mg / 2 mL = 5 mg/mL = 50 mcg per unit; 2.5 mg = 50 units, 5 mg = 100 units. 10 mg / 1 mL = 10 mg/mL = 100 mcg per unit; 2.5 mg = 25 units, 5 mg = 50 units. Refrigerated stability 28-30 days post-reconstitution.

### Evidence base

Strong mechanistic foundation — Tβ4 has been characterized at the molecular level since the 1960s and is one of the best-studied tissue repair peptides in the literature. Animal data spans cardiac repair, wound healing, hair regrowth, ophthalmic applications, and neuroprotection across hundreds of publications. Human clinical trial data is more limited but growing — RegeneRx has conducted Phase 2/3 trials in dry eye disease (RGN-259) and cardiac applications (RGN-352). Compounded TB-500 has decades of clinical use with substantial clinical track record in orthopedic and tissue repair applications. The Goldstein lab and Allan Goldstein's continued research provide foundational support. Equine veterinary use is extensive and provides additional safety/efficacy data.

### Contraindications

- Active malignancy. RATIONALE: Tβ4 promotes angiogenesis, cell migration, and stem cell mobilization — all theoretical concerns for tumor support. Insufficient human data in active cancer to establish safety. Coordinate with oncology in cancer survivors (5+ years remission with normal tumor markers may be appropriate candidates with oncology coordination).

- Pregnancy and lactation — limited human data; precautionary.

- Active hemorrhage. RATIONALE: Tβ4 affects platelet function and angiogenesis; not characterized in active bleeding states.

- Recent stroke (within 4 weeks). RATIONALE: vascular effects in acute cerebrovascular state are unclear; defer until stable.

- Known peptide hypersensitivity.

- FDA regulatory status: Tβ4 has been on Category 2 review status with possible reclassification. Verify current sourcing reliability.

### Drug interactions

Pharmacodynamic considerations: synergistic with BPC-157 (the classic 'Wolverine' combination — see dedicated section in this volume). Synergistic with GHK-Cu for tissue repair via complementary mechanisms (TB-500 provides cell migration and stem cell mobilization; GHK-Cu provides ECM synthesis and gene modulation). Synergistic with GH peptides (CJC/Ipa, Tesamorelin) — IGF-1 elevation supports the muscle protein synthesis substrate for the tissue repair effects. Compatible with most pharmaceuticals — no CYP450 interactions. Caution with active anti-VEGF cancer therapy (theoretical mechanism conflict; coordinate with oncology). Caution with high-dose anticoagulants in active hemorrhagic states (theoretical platelet effect). Compatible with anti-inflammatory peptides (KPV) and antimicrobial peptides (LL-37) for complex chronic illness protocols.

### Baseline labs & monitoring

- Baseline: CBC with platelets (verify normal — assess platelet status before starting), comprehensive metabolic panel, hs-CRP, vitamin D.

- Cancer screening per age-appropriate guidelines BEFORE starting (mammogram, colonoscopy, PSA, skin exam) given the angiogenic/migration mechanisms.

- Imaging at baseline for orthopedic targets — MRI for major tendon/ligament injury, ultrasound for tendinopathy. Document the injury before starting to allow objective response assessment.

- Subjective: pain scale, function scale (disability index appropriate to the injury), range of motion measurements where applicable.

- Mid-cycle (week 4): symptom assessment, side effect review, injection tolerance.

- Post-cycle (week 8-12): repeat imaging if substantial baseline injury, repeat function scales.

- Long-term users (cycling for chronic conditions): annual CBC, hs-CRP, age-appropriate cancer screening.

- RATIONALE FOR CANCER SCREENING: Tβ4's angiogenic and stem cell mobilization mechanisms theoretically could support occult tumor growth. Annual screening is defensive practice given long-term use patterns.

### Side effects

*Common (mild, dose-limiting only if severe):*

- Mild injection site reaction — redness, transient nodule, especially with regional dosing.

- Mild fatigue in first 1-2 weeks (energy demands of active tissue repair).

- Transient mild headache.

- Mild flu-like symptoms in week 1 (rare).

- Most patients report no acute side effects — TB-500 is generally well tolerated.

*Serious (stop and reassess):*

- Theoretical: tumor support in undiagnosed malignancy via angiogenic and stem cell mobilization mechanisms — basis for cancer screening recommendation. Not documented but biologically plausible.

- Bleeding events in patients with platelet dysfunction (theoretical — Tβ4 has platelet effects).

- Severe Herx-like reaction in patients with significant biofilm or pathogen burden — rare but possible.

- Anaphylaxis (rare; any peptide).

- Severe injection site abscess — rare; may indicate sourcing/sterility issue.

### Stacking & synergy

TB-500 is a foundational tissue repair peptide that pairs widely. Pairs especially well with: (1) BPC-157 — the classic 'Wolverine' combination for major tissue injury; complementary mechanisms (BPC-157 = VEGFR2 angiogenesis + FAK fibroblast activation; TB-500 = actin remodeling + stem cell mobilization). See dedicated Wolverine section; (2) GHK-Cu — additive ECM synthesis and gene modulation; (3) CJC-1295 + Ipamorelin or Tesamorelin — IGF-1 mediated muscle protein synthesis substrate; (4) Collagen peptides 20 g/day, adequate protein 1.2-1.6 g/kg, and resistance training (for orthopedic indications) — substrates and stimulus for the repair mechanisms TB-500 activates; (5) BPC-157 + KPV for gut barrier repair with anti-inflammatory support; (6) GHK-Cu + retinoids for hair regrowth protocols (cross-reference Volume 11); (7) Nutritional adjuncts: vitamin C 2-4 g/day for collagen synthesis, zinc 30-50 mg/day for tissue repair, magnesium glycinate 300-600 mg/day, omega-3 EPA/DHA 2-4 g/day. AVOID stacking concerns: avoid in active malignancy without oncology coordination; avoid in active hemorrhagic conditions; coordinate with cardiology in active cardiac disease.

### Clinical pearls

- TB-500 is a PULSE peptide, not a daily peptide. RATIONALE: this is the single most common dosing error in TB-500 use. Patients accustomed to daily peptide dosing (BPC-157, GHK-Cu) try to apply that pattern to TB-500 and get poor results. TB-500 works through THRESHOLD ACTIVATION — bigger less-frequent pulses work; small daily drips do not.

- The clinical dose tier system: 1 mg daily = inadequate (anti-inflammatory only, never reaches structural repair threshold). 2.5 mg twice weekly = STANDARD (hits structural repair threshold). 5 mg twice weekly = MAXIMUM (major injury, post-surgery, frozen shoulder, severe fascial damage). RATIONALE: think of TB-500 like PRP, growth factor pulses, or shockwave — needs a bolus to activate the cellular cascade.

- Indications for the 5 mg pulse: rotator cuff partial tears, ACL/MCL injuries, meniscal damage, post-surgical major orthopedic recovery, severe chronic low back injury, frozen shoulder/adhesive capsulitis, fibrosis reversal, severe myofascial collapse, post-radiation tissue injury, mold/Lyme connective tissue degeneration, multi-site injuries. RATIONALE: these indications require maximum signaling wave to engage the full repair cascade.

- The molecular foundation for the pulse threshold: TB-4 must be cleaved by ACE into Ac-SDKP (the 4-amino-acid active fragment) for the strongest anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects. The pulse must be large enough to (1) reach cellular activation thresholds AND (2) provide sufficient substrate for ACE-mediated SDKP generation. This is why ACE inhibitors have known anti-fibrotic effects through the same SDKP pathway.

- TB-500 is one of the cornerstone tissue repair peptides. RATIONALE: actin sequestration, stem cell mobilization, AND SDKP-mediated anti-fibrotic effects together address fundamental mechanisms in tissue repair; few peptides have such broad clinically valuable actions.

- Regional dosing matters for orthopedic injury. RATIONALE: while TB-500 distributes systemically, local SQ injection near the injured tissue increases regional concentration AND enhances local ACE-mediated SDKP generation. Knee injury → quadriceps; shoulder → deltoid; back → paraspinal.

- The stem cell mobilization mechanism is what differentiates TB-500 from other repair peptides. RATIONALE: TB-500 doesn't just repair — it brings endogenous stem cells (cardiac, hair follicle, bone marrow) to injured tissues. This explains the breadth of clinical applications.

- TB-500 + BPC-157 (Wolverine) is the classic combination for major orthopedic injury — but ONLY when used at structural-repair-threshold pulse doses. Sub-threshold Wolverine dosing produces only anti-inflammatory effect, missing the structural repair benefits. See dedicated Wolverine section.

- Cardiac applications are real but require cardiology coordination. RATIONALE: post-MI Tβ4 has been studied in animal models with promising data — particularly the SDKP-mediated reduction in cardiac rupture risk and M1 macrophage modulation. Not standard care; specialist domain.

- Hair regrowth is an underused indication. RATIONALE: TB-500 mobilizes hair follicle stem cells from the bulge region. Combine with topical or oral PTD-DBM, GHK-Cu (topical/microneedling), and standard hair care for synergistic effect. See Volume 11.

- FDA Category 2 status: Thymosin Beta-4 fragment (LKKTETQ) was placed on the bulk substance Category 2 list — restricted from 503A injectable compounding. Acetylated TB-4 frag is currently available as an oral dietary supplement (anecdotally less potent than the injectable form but useful for general immunity and tissue support). Track FDA PCAC for ongoing reclassification.

- The Goldstein lab provenance gives TB-500 substantial scientific credibility. RATIONALE: Allan Goldstein characterized both Tβ4 and TA-1 — same researcher behind two of the most clinically valuable peptides in functional medicine. The science is solid.

- Cancer history is the most common contraindication question. The honest answer: theoretical concern via angiogenesis + stem cell mobilization mechanisms; no documented harm in human use; most longevity-medicine clinicians avoid in active cancer; many use cautiously in 5+ year remission patients with oncology coordination and normal tumor markers. Annual cancer screening is reasonable for long-term users.

- Equine veterinary use is extensive — TB-500 has been used in racing horses for tendon and joint repair for decades. Useful patient education talking point about the safety track record.

- Patients describing 'I just feel better all over' on TB-500 are reporting a real systemic effect. RATIONALE: Tβ4 is one of the most abundant intracellular proteins; supplementing it has effects beyond the targeted injury. Common to see general improvements in skin quality, hair, energy, and mood alongside the targeted application.

- Reconstitution math by vial type: 5 mg / 2 mL = 25 mcg/U so 2.5 mg = 100 U, 5 mg = 200 U. 10 mg / 2 mL = 50 mcg/U so 2.5 mg = 50 U, 5 mg = 100 U. 10 mg / 1 mL = 100 mcg/U so 2.5 mg = 25 U, 5 mg = 50 U. Verify vial concentration with pharmacy — they vary.

- If TB-500 produces no improvement in a documented orthopedic injury at 8-12 weeks, reassess in this order: (1) Was the dose actually at threshold? (1 mg daily fails) — recalculate; (2) Was the dose pulsed or daily-divided? (matters); (3) Sourcing quality; (4) Comorbidities (uncontrolled diabetes, severe nutritional deficiency, ongoing biotoxin exposure, untreated MCAS); (5) Wrong indication (some injuries don't respond to peptides alone — consider surgical opinion).

- Don't combine TB-500 initiation with multiple new peptides simultaneously. RATIONALE: when something works, you want to know what worked. Establish TB-500 response over 4-8 weeks before adding adjuncts.

### What it is

GHK-Cu is the copper-bound complex of the tripeptide glycyl-histidyl-lysine (Gly-His-Lys) — discovered in the early 1970s by Loren Pickart, who characterized GHK as a naturally occurring human plasma peptide that declines progressively with age. Plasma GHK levels at age 60 are approximately one-third of levels at age 20, providing the clinical rationale for supplementation. The copper-bound form (GHK-Cu) is the biologically active configuration; copper is essential for the peptide's effects on lysyl oxidase, superoxide dismutase, and ceruloplasmin. GHK-Cu is one of the most extensively studied tissue repair peptides in the literature with applications spanning skin, hair, wound healing, cognitive support, and broader anti-aging effects. The 2010 Pickart genome modulation paper documented that GHK-Cu modulates expression of approximately 4,000+ human genes — making it one of the most epigenetically active small molecules known. RegeneRx and other companies have pursued formal pharmaceutical development of GHK-Cu derivatives. In functional medicine and cosmetic dermatology, GHK-Cu is a workhorse peptide for skin, hair, and tissue repair.

### Mechanism of action

- Modulates expression of approximately 4,000+ human genes — including down-regulation of pro-aging genes and up-regulation of regenerative pathways. RATIONALE: this is one of the most extensively documented gene modulation effects of any natural peptide; it explains the breadth of clinical applications across skin, hair, wound healing, cognition, and tissue repair.

- Stimulates collagen synthesis (Type I and Type III) by fibroblasts via lysyl oxidase activation and direct gene expression effects.

- Stimulates elastin synthesis — supports skin firmness and elasticity.

- Stimulates glycosaminoglycan and proteoglycan synthesis — supports skin hydration and joint health.

- Provides bioavailable copper for SOD (superoxide dismutase), ceruloplasmin, and lysyl oxidase — copper-dependent enzymes essential for ECM crosslinking and oxidative stress management.

- Anti-inflammatory effects via NF-κB modulation.

- Stimulates fibroblast and keratinocyte proliferation and migration.

- Promotes wound healing — accelerates re-epithelialization, granulation tissue formation, and angiogenesis.

- Stimulates hair follicle stem cells in the bulge region — basis for hair regrowth applications.

- Reverses cellular senescence in fibroblasts and keratinocytes — true senotherapeutic effect.

- Modulates skin pigmentation toward normalization (lightens hyperpigmentation, supports vitiligo repigmentation in some cases).

- Cognitive effects — crosses blood-brain barrier; documented effects on neuroinflammation and neurogenesis.

- Antimicrobial effects at higher concentrations.

- Cardiovascular protective effects in animal models (less clinically applied currently).
